title: Verified public camera feeds as a data source: working adapter + free API
body: Your README's CCTV shot is what got me here, so I built the data source for it: public traffic cameras fetched by viewport, live frames projected onto the globe. Branch: **** (renderer-agnostic client, deck.gl binding, no-build demo, MIT). ![Three live downtown Austin cameras projected as ground footprints on a 3D map, with a frame inspector showing each decoded frame, its attribution and a live pixel read](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/00hello/gods-eye-view/datumfeed-source/sources/datumfeed/demo/proof.png) That's three downtown Austin cams, live, rendered headless, not a mockup. The strip on the right reads a pixel back from every decoded frame, which only works because CORS is actually solved: most camera servers taint the canvas, so `` works but `texImage2D` doesn't. The API proxies every frame with real CORS headers, bytes untouched. It runs on [Datumfeed](https://datumfeed.com), a free API I run: 8,970 public cameras across 6 registries (Austin, Caltrans, WSDOT, Ontario 511, Ottawa, London UK), each one health-polled instead of taking the registry's word for it. Turns out that matters. As of Aug 17, 639 of them are provably lying: dead feeds, coordinates outside the city, one shared "unavailable" card behind dozens of different ids. The adapter filters those before they reach the globe, so the map doesn't ship half dead. Honest numbers: anonymous access keeps about 5 cameras live (300 frames/hr per IP); a free key handles whole-city Austin. Attribution and per-registry poll cadence are enforced in the code, not left to the caller. If it's useful, take it. Happy to reshape it for whatever v1's source interface ends up being, or to strip it back to just the client if you'd rather write the layer yourselves. Full API doc is one file your agent can read: .

title: Make the app deployable to GitHub Pages and the top chrome responsive
body:
The fork could not be published as a static site and the wordmark overran narrow viewports. Both are fixed here.

Responsive top row

  #title-bar and #style-indicator were the only fixed top-row chrome with no
  fluid sizing: 26px type at 8px tracking, a 52px logo and hard 32/36px insets.
  At 1440px that is 395px wide, so from ~721px down the wordmark ran straight
  through the centred action buttons and off the right edge. A single hard
  step-down existed at 720px, which left the 721-1090px range uncovered and
  still collided under ~500px.

  Type, tracking, logo, gap and insets are now clamp()-scaled, so the full-size
  design is reached at ~1090px and degrades continuously below it — 1440px
  renders byte-identical to before. Under 640px the action row un-centres to
  the right rail and the style readout stacks beneath it, which is the only
  way three items fit one row on a phone. The now-redundant 720px overrides
  are removed; leaving them would freeze the fluid scale.

  .hud-summary-wrap had the same problem: a flat 420px cap overran a 390px
  viewport by ~70px, and since it is the widest child it dragged the whole
  intel readout with it. Capped against the viewport too.

  Verified 320-1440px: no horizontal overflow and no overlapping chrome.

Static hosting

  Every live feed is brokered by configureServer middleware in vite.config.js,
  so it runs under `vite dev` only. A static host cannot run it, and /api/*
  does not exist there. That is a property of static hosting, not a bug — and
  the globe, styles, share links, bundled datasets and the CORS-open feeds
  (USGS, GBFS) never needed a backend at all.

  - Builds use a relative base, so one artifact is valid at any URL prefix. This also avoids vite-plugin-cesium copying its runtime to dist/<base>/ when a non-root absolute base is set. Dev keeps '/'.
  - Runtime-assembled asset paths (aircraft GLBs, logo, mic) resolve against document.baseURI via a new appAssetUrl helper. The source strings stay put since several are identity keys pinned by tests.
  - A missing GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY no longer aborts init. MapStackController already fell back to the keyless OSM stack; the app now boots on it and explains itself instead of showing an error on a black screen.
  - Static builds answer their own /api calls with an explanatory 503, so each layer's existing error surface reads "needs the local server" rather than choking on the host's 404 HTML. GEV_STATIC_BUILD=0 opts out.
  - A one-time notice states which half of the app is live and accepts the two browser-side keys into localStorage, so a keyless deployment is still useful — visitors can point it at their own quota without a rebuild.

Adds the Pages workflow (keys optional, via repo secrets), docs/GITHUB-PAGES.md and README/.env.example pointers. Full suite passes (2587).


Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FhXFJjdiwFFMcdou5QbeAQ

title: [Feature Request] WiGLE Wi-Fi Network Layer
body:
Summary

Add an optional WiGLE Wi-Fi data layer that displays geolocated wireless-network observations on the 3D globe.

WiGLE feels like a natural addition to God's Eye View because it adds another real-world, publicly sourced radio-frequency dataset alongside aircraft, AIS, satellites, cameras, traffic, etc.

Suggested behavior
Optional WiGLE layer in the layer controls.
Use the WiGLE API with BYOK credentials, with credentials kept server-side.
Query only the current viewport / surrounding area rather than attempting to download huge geographic areas.
Cache results and respect WiGLE API limits.
Cluster observations at wide zoom levels and expand them into individual access points when zoomed in.
Clicking an observation could display available metadata such as:
SSID
BSSID
Encryption/security type
Channel/frequency
First/last observation time
Coordinates
Source/freshness
Allow filtering by age, such as:
recently observed
last year
all available observations
Clearly mark WiGLE observations as crowdsourced observations rather than live RF detections.
If WiGLE credentials are unavailable, the layer should report UNAVAILABLE rather than simulate data.
Add WiGLE attribution/licensing information to DATA_SOURCES.md and the in-app attribution system.
Possible later extension

WiGLE observations could eventually support derived infrastructure identification using known SSID patterns or vendor/OUI information.

Those results should be explicitly labeled as inferred rather than confirmed.

This could potentially complement layers such as ALPR/Flock camera mapping without conflating a WiGLE observation with a confirmed device.

title: [Feature Request] Public ALPR / Flock Safety Camera Layer
body:
Summary

Add a layer showing publicly mapped automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras, including Flock Safety cameras.

A good starting source appears to be DeFlock / OpenStreetMap, which already maintains crowdsourced locations of ALPR infrastructure.

This would fit very naturally beside the existing CCTV and infrastructure layers.

Suggested behavior
New ALPR Cameras layer.
Optional filter for:
All ALPR cameras
Flock Safety
Other manufacturers
Use publicly documented/crowdsourced camera locations rather than private Flock systems.
Possible sources:
DeFlock data
OpenStreetMap / Overpass
DeFlock PMTiles if appropriate
Cluster cameras at wide zoom levels.
Render individual cameras when zoomed in.
If direction information exists, render a small camera-facing cone/heading indicator.
Clicking a camera could show:
Manufacturer
Camera/system type
Operator, when publicly documented
Direction
Source
Last verification/update
Clearly distinguish:
confirmed/tagged Flock cameras
generic ALPR cameras
uncertain/crowdsourced reports
Label this as mapped surveillance infrastructure, not a live camera feed.
Preserve OpenStreetMap/DeFlock provenance and required attribution.
Scope / privacy boundary

This request is only for the physical locations and public metadata of surveillance infrastructure.

It would not involve:

license plate records
vehicle histories
Flock customer accounts
private Flock APIs
camera imagery unavailable to the public

The goal is simply to visualize publicly documented surveillance infrastructure as another OSINT layer.

Nice-to-have

Because God's Eye View already has a click-to-track/contact concept, it could eventually support things such as:

"Show ALPR cameras within 10 km"

or

"Show surveillance infrastructure near this location."

That would make the layer especially useful without needing access to any private surveillance data.

title: [Feature Request] Meshtastic Public Node Layer
body:
Summary

Add an optional Meshtastic node layer showing nodes that have voluntarily published themselves through Meshtastic's public map-reporting system.

This seems particularly appropriate for God's Eye View because Meshtastic already has an explicit mechanism for publishing node information and approximate locations to public maps.

Suggested behavior
New Meshtastic layer.
Consume only nodes published through the public/opt-in Meshtastic map-report system.
Possible source:
Meshtastic public MQTT MapReport data
an official/community map API if one is preferable for web clients
Display available public MapReport information such as:
node short/long name
node ID
hardware model
node role
firmware version
LoRa region
modem preset
altitude
approximate position
number of locally heard nodes
last report/freshness
Cluster nodes when zoomed out.
Show individual nodes when zoomed in.
Potentially visualize areas of high Meshtastic activity or node density.
Location privacy

The implementation should respect the position precision chosen by the node owner.

If a node publishes an approximate location, God's Eye View should preserve that uncertainty rather than placing the node at an artificially precise point.

For example, approximate locations could be rendered as:

a translucent uncertainty circle
an approximate-location marker
a marker plus a displayed precision radius
Freshness

Nodes should expose the same sort of honest source state used by other God's Eye View layers:

LIVE/RECENT
STALE
UNAVAILABLE

The timestamp of the last MapReport should be visible.

Scope

This layer should consume public map-report metadata only.

It should not expose private Meshtastic messages, encrypted-channel traffic, private MQTT brokers, or information that a node operator has not opted to publish.

Possible future extension

A later version could visualize publicly reported mesh characteristics such as:

node density
routers/repeaters
approximate coverage areas
regional LoRa presets
local-node counts

That could make the Meshtastic layer a useful visualization of decentralized communications infrastructure.

title: [Feature Request] TAK / ATAK Cursor-on-Target Integration
body:
Summary

Add optional TAK / Cursor-on-Target (CoT) integration to God's Eye View.

Rather than targeting only ATAK, this could use the broader TAK ecosystem's Cursor-on-Target protocol, potentially allowing interoperability with:

ATAK
WinTAK
iTAK
WebTAK
TAK Server
OpenTAKServer
FreeTAKServer
Other CoT-compatible systems

This would let God's Eye View function as another visualization client for TAK data while potentially allowing selected God's Eye View data to be shared into an authorized TAK environment.

Phase 1: TAK Data Layer

Add a TAK / CoT layer that connects to a TAK Server or compatible CoT endpoint configured by the user.

Display authorized CoT objects on the God's Eye View globe.

Potentially supported objects include:

Team/user locations
Points of interest
Markers
Vehicles
Aircraft
Other position reports
Routes
Lines
Areas/shapes
Emergency markers
Sensor locations

Where possible, God's Eye View should preserve the original CoT:

UID
type
callsign/name
coordinates
altitude
heading
timestamp
stale time
affiliation/category
source

Objects should automatically disappear or be marked stale according to their CoT stale timestamp.

3D Visualization

TAK information could be especially interesting inside God's Eye View because it could combine TAK's collaborative situational-awareness data with the existing 3D environment.

For example:

TAK Unit → God's Eye View 3D Marker

Clicking the marker could expose the CoT metadata and existing God's Eye View contextual information for the surrounding area.

Routes, polygons, circles, and other compatible objects could be projected directly onto the Cesium globe.

Authentication

TAK connections should be explicitly configured by the user.

Potential configuration:

TAK Server hostname
Port
Protocol
Client certificate
Private key
CA certificate
Username/password where applicable

Credentials and certificates should remain server-side and never be exposed to the browser.

No default connection to a private or third-party TAK network should occur.

If no TAK connection is configured, the layer should simply report:

UNAVAILABLE

Phase 2: God's Eye View → TAK

A later extension could provide an optional way to publish selected God's Eye View objects as CoT.

For example, a user could click a supported public-data object and choose:

Send to TAK

Potential examples:

Aircraft
Ships
Satellites
Weather events
Wildfires
Cameras
Meshtastic nodes
Public infrastructure
User-created points of interest

God's Eye View would convert the selected object's position and metadata into an appropriate CoT event and send it to the user's configured TAK Server.

This should be an explicit user action rather than automatically broadcasting every God's Eye View data source into TAK.

Interesting Combination With Other Proposed Layers

TAK integration becomes particularly useful when combined with additional God's Eye View layers such as:

Meshtastic
WiGLE
Public ALPR / Flock camera locations

For example, God's Eye View could visualize these datasets normally while allowing a user to selectively share an object into their own TAK environment.

That would make God's Eye View a useful bridge between traditional public OSINT/GIS sources and the TAK ecosystem.

Architecture Suggestion

Because browsers cannot directly behave like a normal TAK TCP/TLS client in many configurations, the integration would probably be best implemented as a server-side TAK connector.

Conceptually:

TAK Server

↓

God's Eye View CoT Connector

↓

normalized internal objects

↓

Cesium / God's Eye View UI

For outbound data:

God's Eye View object

↓

CoT conversion

↓

TAK connector

↓

TAK Server

There are already open-source libraries and projects that demonstrate converting CoT XML into structured/GeoJSON data, so the integration would not necessarily require implementing the entire TAK ecosystem from scratch.

Privacy / Security Boundary

TAK networks frequently contain private location and operational information, so this integration should be BYOS — Bring Your Own Server.

God's Eye View should:

Never attempt to discover TAK servers.
Never connect to a TAK server without explicit configuration.
Never bypass TAK authentication.
Keep client certificates/private keys server-side.
Clearly distinguish private TAK data from public God's Eye View sources.
Never expose one user's TAK feed to another user.
Avoid persisting TAK position history unless explicitly configured.
Respect CoT stale times.

The purpose is interoperability with a TAK network the user is already authorized to access, not discovery of or access to third-party TAK systems.

Nice-to-Have

A particularly useful long-term feature would be an OSINT → CoT bridge.

A user could select supported God's Eye View objects and share them into their TAK environment without needing a separate conversion tool.

That could turn God's Eye View into both:

A high-quality 3D TAK visualization client.
A bridge between public geospatial intelligence sources and the wider TAK ecosystem.

title: Render Performance Suggestions
body:
Super cool project, thank you!

Explored the repo — it's a CesiumJS globe app that's already had several documented perf passes (render governor, throttled preRender ticks, billboard collections). Remaining high-value wins, ranked:

## Top 5 rendering-performance improvements

1. **Remove/gate `preserveDrawingBuffer: true`** — src/main.js:122
   Forces the browser to preserve the full-screen WebGL drawing buffer every frame, defeating the zero-copy buffer-swap fast path. It's only needed for screenshots/recording — gate it to those modes (or use `scene.canvas.toDataURL()` immediately after render).

2. **Drop `msaaSamples: 4` to 2 or make it adaptive** — src/main.js:119
   4× MSAA over Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles is one of the biggest fixed GPU costs per frame; brutal on integrated GPUs. Expose as a quality setting (the app already has a perf-investigation precedent for this pattern).

3. **Cut the 58 `backdrop-filter: blur()` rules** — style.css (58 occurrences)
   Every blurred HUD panel forces the compositor to read and blur the WebGL canvas beneath it *every frame*, and panels stack. Replacing with pre-baked translucent gradients/opaque backgrounds on the heaviest surfaces (command dock, trays, chips) is likely the single largest paint-cost win.

4. **Replace the compass-tape `innerHTML` rebuild** — src/ui.js:1450-1457
   On heading change it re-parses/rebuilds 7 `<span>`s via `innerHTML` string concat → parse + layout + GC churn during exactly the most interaction-heavy moments (camera motion). Build the strip once and slide it with a `transform: translateX` update (compositor-only).

5. **Split the monolithic render-blocking CSS** — index.html:8 (`style.css`: 247 KB / 9,163 lines) + 3 synchronous Google Fonts stylesheets (index.html:11-13)
   All of it blocks first paint even though much of the UI (cockpit mode, trays, modals, per-style themes) is hidden initially. Inline critical above-the-fold CSS, lazy-load the rest, and self-host/preload the two font families.

Honorable mentions: cap the world-overlay canvas backing store DPR (~19 MB at DPR 2, src/overlays/worldOverlay.js:1102) and coalesce the scattered HUD poll timers (250 ms/500 ms/60 ms in src/hud.js:216-238, src/ui.js:9188-9216) into one ticker.

title: Issue 4 wigle wifi
Issue 7 tak cot
Add NIFC wildfire incidents layer
body:
New layer showing confirmed wildfire incidents from NIFC's public WFIGS ArcGIS Feature Service — deliberately distinct from the existing FIRMS layer, which shows raw VIIRS satellite thermal-anomaly detections. NIFC data is human-reported incident tracking (name, cause, acreage, percent contained), same complementary relationship as ALPR sits next to CCTV.

Public, CORS-open, keyless ArcGIS endpoint — fetched directly from the browser exactly like earthquakes.js fetches USGS, no server proxy needed. Verified live: real endpoint returns 602 current incidents matching the exact query/fields the layer uses. Scoped to IncidentTypeCategory IN ('WF','CX') — wildfires and complexes; prescribed burns (RX) are excluded at the query level as out of scope for a wildfire-incidents layer.

Marker size scales with acreage (sqrt, clamped); color reflects containment (uncontained/partial/contained, unset reads as uncontained). Click shows cause, discovery date, acreage, percent contained, state.

Registered in main.js + layerState.js (token 'v' — 'z' was already a hardcoded "unknown token" test sentinel in two test files; caught by the full suite before committing), voice/text aliases, attribution in dataCredits.js and DATA_SOURCES.md.

title: Add public ALPR / Flock Safety camera layer
body:
Closes #5.

New optional layer showing crowdsourced ALPR camera locations from OpenStreetMap's DeFlock tagging (`man_made=surveillance` + `surveillance:type=ALPR`), fetched viewport-bounded through the existing generic `/api/overpass` proxy — no new server route needed.

- `src/data/alprCameras.js`: viewport-bounded fetch/render, patterned on `militaryInstallations.js` (moveEnd-debounced, unavailable-retry backoff, click-to-select entity context). Flock-operated cameras render in a distinct color from other tagged ALPR vendors; a `camera:direction`/`direction` tag draws a short facing-direction line.
- Registered in `main.js` + `layerState.js` for the auto-built toggle panel and share-link serialization.
- Voice/text aliases in `gevActions.js`.
- Attribution in `dataCredits.js` and `DATA_SOURCES.md`.
- `src/data/alprCameras.test.mjs`: unit tests for the pure helpers (tag normalization, Flock classification, destination-point math, retry backoff).

Mapped surveillance infrastructure only — no plate records, vendor accounts, or private Flock/OSM data.

Includes a follow-up commit fixing a bug a code-review pass found: `numTag()` treated a present-but-blank OSM tag value as a fabricated `0` instead of missing (`Number('') === 0`), which would have rendered a camera with no real facing data as pointing due north.

title: Add public Meshtastic node layer
body:
Closes #6.

New optional layer showing nodes that opted in to Meshtastic's own public Map Reporting feature — the network's built-in "publish yourself to a public map" mechanism, over MQTT.

**Server**: `meshtasticProxy` (`vite.config.js`) keeps one persistent MQTT connection to `mqtt.meshtastic.org` (the project's own public broker, published read-only credentials), subscribed only to `msh/+/2/map/#`. It decodes exclusively unencrypted MapReport packets (portnum 73) via the official `@meshtastic/protobufs` definitions and never inspects or attempts to decrypt anything else on the wire — encrypted channel packets are dropped without being touched. An in-memory cache (capped 8000 nodes, swept every 15 min, 24h eviction, true LRU) is served as plain JSON from `/api/meshtastic/nodes`; validated live against the real broker end-to-end.

**Client**: `src/data/meshtasticNodes.js` polls that snapshot like any other layer. A node's `position_precision` (bits retained) is honored rather than flattened into a false-precision pin — meaningful uncertainty renders as a translucent circle, a high-precision report as a plain point. Per-node LIVE/STALE opacity independent of overall layer status.

`src/data/meshtasticMapReport.js` holds the pure helpers (id formatting, uncertainty radius, freshness bucketing) shared by server and client; `src/data/meshtasticDecode.js` isolates the protobuf-dependent decode so it never reaches the browser bundle (confirmed via a production build). Registered in `main.js` + `layerState.js`, voice/text aliases, attribution in `dataCredits.js` and `DATA_SOURCES.md`.

Includes a follow-up commit fixing two bugs a code-review pass found:
- `update()` could resolve to `false` on a transient fetch failure, which `manager.js`'s enable-lifecycle treats as a fatal enable failure and bounces the layer's toggle back off instead of leaving it enabled to report the failure via `getStats()`.
- The node-cache cap silently dropped brand-new nodes once full instead of evicting the oldest-seen one — fixed to true LRU.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Require auth and hard rate limits for /api/realtime/token
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- `/api/realtime/token` mints OpenAI realtime client secrets using the server `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
- The only limiter is opt-in; the default is unlimited.
- If the Vite dev or preview server is reachable by other clients, they can spend the project OpenAI quota.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:5045-5213` implements the endpoint and calls `/v1/realtime/client_secrets`.
- `vite.config.js:427-479` makes the limiter optional/unlimited by default.
- `.env.example:41-49` documents the OpenAI limiter as optional.

Suggested fix:
- Require an explicit auth boundary before minting a token.
- Make rate limiting default-on and fail closed when not configured for exposed deployments.
- Consider disabling this endpoint outside localhost unless the deployment has real authentication.

This was found during an adversarial repository review; impact depends on how the dev/preview server is exposed.

title: Require auth and hard rate limits for /api/openai/hud-summary
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- `/api/openai/hud-summary` sends requests to OpenAI Responses using the server key.
- The route is unauthenticated and the limiter defaults to unlimited.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:4960-5020` implements the route and calls OpenAI.
- `vite.config.js:4970-4971` only applies the opt-in limiter.
- `vite.config.js:4973` reads `OPENAI_API_KEY` server-side.

Suggested fix:
- Require authentication/authorization for cost-bearing OpenAI calls.
- Make server-side quota controls mandatory for any non-local bind.
- Return a hard configuration error instead of silently running unlimited.

This was found during an adversarial repository review; impact depends on how the dev/preview server is exposed.

title: Protect /api/google/nearby-places from unauthenticated quota spend
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- `/api/google/nearby-places` proxies Google Places requests with the server Google key.
- The route is unauthenticated and the limiter defaults to unlimited.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:5274-5384` implements the nearby places proxy.
- `vite.config.js:5284-5293` applies only the optional limiter.
- `vite.config.js:5296` reads `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY`.
- `.env.example:13-22` documents Google proxy rate limiting as optional.

Suggested fix:
- Require auth or restrict the route to trusted local use.
- Make request budgets mandatory before enabling the proxy on a reachable interface.
- Add telemetry for rejected and accepted quota-bearing requests.

This was found during an adversarial repository review; impact depends on how the dev/preview server is exposed.

title: Protect /api/google/text-search from quota spend and invalid coordinates
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- `/api/google/text-search` proxies Google Places text search with no auth and optional-only throttling.
- It only checks that `lat` and `lon` are finite, not that they are valid latitude/longitude ranges.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:5390-5499` implements the proxy.
- `vite.config.js:5398-5407` applies only the optional limiter.
- `vite.config.js:5418-5423` validates presence/finite values but not coordinate bounds.

Suggested fix:
- Require auth and mandatory rate limits for exposed use.
- Validate latitude in `[-90, 90]` and longitude in `[-180, 180]` before forwarding upstream.
- Fail before contacting Google on invalid input.

This was found during an adversarial repository review; impact depends on how the dev/preview server is exposed.

title: Rate-limit and validate Street View fallback in CCTV frame proxy
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- `/api/cctv/frame/:id` can fall back to Google Street View using client-supplied `lat`, `lon`, `heading`, `fov`, and `pitch`.
- There is no route-specific rate limit before calling Google Street View.
- Unknown camera IDs can still reach the fallback path when finite coordinates are supplied.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:4620-4628` accepts query parameters that override source coordinates.
- `vite.config.js:4459-4489` calls Google Street View using `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY`.
- `vite.config.js:4653` invokes the fallback after upstream image failure.

Suggested fix:
- Apply mandatory quota controls before any Street View request.
- Require a known registered camera source for fallback, or remove client-supplied coordinate fallback.
- Validate coordinate and camera parameter bounds before contacting Google.

This was found during an adversarial repository review; impact depends on how the dev/preview server is exposed.

title: Do not disable Vite host protection when binding to 0.0.0.0
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- When `HOST=0.0.0.0` or `HOST=::`, the config sets `allowedHosts: true`.
- That disables Vite host-header protection exactly when the server is exposed beyond localhost.
- This increases DNS rebinding/host-header risk for the same process that brokers API keys.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:7364-7370` sets `allowedHosts` to `true` for wildcard binds.
- `vite.config.js:5216-5223` and `5503-5510` install cost-bearing proxy routes into the same server.

Suggested fix:
- Keep a concrete allowlist even for LAN binds.
- Require explicit configured hostnames instead of accepting every host header.
- Document the required LAN hostnames instead of disabling the guard.

This was found during an adversarial repository review; impact depends on how the dev/preview server is exposed.

title: Do not expose key-broker API routes from vite preview by default
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- The OpenAI and Google proxy middleware is installed in both Vite dev server and Vite preview server.
- `vite preview` is easy to mistake for a deployable preview while it still brokers server API keys.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:5216-5223` registers OpenAI proxy middleware for dev and preview.
- `vite.config.js:5503-5510` registers Google proxy middleware for dev and preview.

Suggested fix:
- Require an explicit environment flag before enabling key-bearing routes in preview.
- Fail closed if required auth/rate-limit settings are absent.

title: Enforce streaming byte and duration caps for CCTV media responses
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- CCTV media responses are only rejected when upstream declares an oversized `Content-Length`.
- Chunked or missing-length responses can stream indefinitely through the proxy.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:4320-4359` implements `proxyMediaResponse`.
- `vite.config.js:4335-4343` checks declared `Content-Length > 64 MB`.
- The subsequent stream piping has no accumulated byte cap, idle timeout, or duration cap.

Suggested fix:
- Count bytes while streaming and destroy the upstream/response once the cap is exceeded.
- Add idle and total-duration timeouts.
- Prefer a smaller default cap for image/video preview routes unless larger media is required.

title: Cap CCTV image response bodies before buffering them
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- CCTV image fetches buffer the full upstream body with `arrayBuffer()` after only checking content type.
- A malicious or compromised configured source can return a large image body and exhaust memory within the timeout window.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:4374-4400` implements `fetchCctvImageFromUpstream`.
- `vite.config.js:4392` performs `Buffer.from(await upstream.arrayBuffer())` with no response-size cap.

Suggested fix:
- Enforce `Content-Length` before reading when present.
- Stream with an accumulated byte cap when length is absent or untrusted.
- Return a clear upstream-too-large error instead of buffering unbounded input.

title: Harden server-registered CCTV URLs against SSRF
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- CCTV source URLs can come from env JSON or a configured JSON file.
- The proxy accepts arbitrary `http:`/`https:` URLs from those registered sources.
- There is no private-address rejection, DNS pinning, or redirect hardening on these fetches.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:3493-3506` loads `CCTV_SOURCES_FILE`.
- `vite.config.js:3514-3522` loads `CCTV_SOURCES_JSON`.
- `vite.config.js:4074-4101` preserves `url` and `snapshotUrl` strings.
- `vite.config.js:4549` and `4374-4400` fetch registered HTTP(S) sources.

Suggested fix:

- Reject loopback, link-local, private, multicast, and otherwise non-public destinations unless explicitly allowed.

title: Enforce GBFS response limits while streaming bytes
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- The GBFS proxy reads the entire response body before enforcing the configured maximum.
- A missing or false `Content-Length` can still force memory growth before the cap is checked.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:3317-3330` checks `Content-Length`, then calls `await upstream.text()`.
- The size check happens after the whole decoded body has been materialized.

Suggested fix:
- Stream the response and count bytes as they arrive.
- Abort once the configured maximum is exceeded.
- Preserve the existing content-type validation before parsing.

title: Use byte counts, not JS string length, for GBFS body limits
body:
Reviewed commit: 880a672b5e16ad3e41d318801d3a5203f9201923

Problem:
- `GBFS_MAX_BODY_BYTES` is a byte limit, but the proxy compares it to JavaScript string length after decoding.
- Character count is not equivalent to byte count for non-ASCII payloads.

Evidence:
- `vite.config.js:3317-3330` calls `await upstream.text()` and compares `body.length` to `GBFS_MAX_BODY_BYTES`.

Suggested fix:
- Enforce the byte cap before text decoding.
- Use `Buffer.byteLength` only after a bounded read if a full string is still required.
- Rename variables so byte limits and character limits cannot be confused.

title: Feature Request: Add Docker & Docker Compose installation/deployment option
body:
### Summary
Currently, God's Eye View requires a local Node.js environment (specifically Node.js 24.14.x or 26.x) and manual dependency installation. Adding a containerized setup with a `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml` would make self-hosting, homelab setups, and cross-platform execution effortless without needing to manage local Node version managers.

### Proposed Solution
Provide:
1. A multi-stage `Dockerfile` (or lightweight Alpine Node runtime).
2. A `docker-compose.yml` that passes environment variables (e.g. `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`) via `.env` file.
3. Updated instructions in `README.md` under Quick Start for Docker deployment.

#### Example `Dockerfile`:
```dockerfile
FROM node:24-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app ./
EXPOSE 4173
CMD ["npm", "run", "dev", "--", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "4173"]
```

#### Example `docker-compose.yml`:
```yaml
version: '3.8'

services:
  gods-eye-view:
    build: .
    container_name: gods-eye-view
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "4173:4173"
    env_file:
      - .env
```

### Benefits
- Zero Node.js version conflicts on host systems.
- 1-command deployment with `docker compose up -d`.
- Simplifies reverse proxy setups (Traefik, Nginx, Caddy).

title: test:track: ground-3d probe expects 4 sampleHeight calls but only makes 3 (fails on clean main)
body:
Running npm run test:track on a fresh clone fails one check, and it isn't tied
to any local change. It reproduces on a clean main (release commit 880a672).

The check that fails:

  ground-3d: ground snap + mesh-floor probes are one-shot/per-poll bounded
  (no per-frame sampling). sampleHeight is called 3 times after the models
  come up; the check wants at least 4 (a snap plus a mesh cell for each of the
  two grounded planes). The per-frame guard itself is fine: growth over ~60
  frames is 1.

So it's 99 passed, 1 failed with a valid Google Maps key, and it isn't a
browser artifact: it reproduces identically on the pinned Chrome-for-Testing
145.0.7632.77 the harness targets, and on a newer system Chrome (151). Without
a key you also get three "no console errors" failures from the tiles 400, but
those clear once a real key is in place.

A few things I noticed while digging in:
- It's consistent, not flaky: always 3, on both the pinned v145 and system v151.
- Only the initial count is short. The "no per-frame sampling" half passes.
- The terrain upstream (terrain.reearth.land) is up and quick for single
  points (200 in about 2s), so it isn't an outage. On a cold cache, though, a
  batch can run past the 30s window on first load.

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 26.4.0, pinned Chrome-for-Testing 145.0.7632.77.

Is the "at least 4" right for two grounded planes, or can one of them
legitimately produce a single sampleHeight call depending on timing? Happy to
help chase it if it's a real gap.

title: fix: measure GBFS response cap in bytes, not string length
body:
The GBFS proxy is supposed to cap upstream responses at 5 MB, but it was
checking body.length after decoding. That's a character count, not bytes, so
for multi-byte (non-ASCII) responses a body could go over the byte limit and
still pass the check.

Fix is one line: compare Buffer.byteLength(body, 'utf8') against the cap
instead. ASCII traffic under the cap behaves exactly as before; this only
tightens the edge case for multi-byte bodies.

Closes #32

### Testing
- npm run build and npm test are both green (2587 tests, 0 failures).
- npm run test:track: 99/100 on the pinned Chrome-for-Testing v145. The one
  failure (a ground-3d probe that expects 4 sampleHeight calls but sees 3)
  isn't from this change. It reproduces the same way on a clean main checkout
  and lives in the terrain/ground-snap code, which this PR doesn't touch.
  I've opened #44 for it.
- Checked the actual path by hand too: hitting /api/gbfs with Austin's
  station_information.json still returns 200 and valid JSON.

title: fix: reject out-of-range coordinates in Google text-search proxy
body:
/api/google/text-search validated that lat and lon were finite, but not that
they were actual coordinates. Anything finite got forwarded to Google Places,
so an out-of-range value spent quota on a request that could never return a
useful result.

This adds a bounds check right after the existing finite check: latitude has
to be within [-90, 90] and longitude within [-180, 180], otherwise the route
returns 400 before contacting Google. Valid coordinates are unaffected.

Scope note: issue #19 also mentions auth and rate limits for exposed use.
That is a broader concern shared across the other Google and OpenAI proxy
routes (#16, #17, #18), so I kept this PR to the coordinate-validation half,
which is the self-contained correctness fix. Using Refs rather than Closes so
the auth part can stay tracked.

Refs #19

### Testing
- npm run build and npm test are both green (2587 tests, 0 failures).
- npm run test:track: 99/100 on the pinned Chrome-for-Testing v145. The single
  failure is the pre-existing ground-3d probe tracked in #44, unrelated to this
  change and reproducible on a clean main.
- Verified by hand against a running dev server:
  - lat=999 and lon=-200 both return 400 with "lat must be within [-90, 90]
    and lon within [-180, 180]", with no upstream call made.
  - valid coordinates (lat=12.97, lon=77.59) pass the check and reach Google
    as before.

title: Feature Request: Simplify deployment for non-developers (Docker & One-Click Cloud Deploy)
body:
Loving what you've built here! Right now, testing out *God's Eye View* requires a full local dev setup—cloning the repo, setting up Node/npm, and managing `.env` files.

For non-developer users like OSINT researchers, spatial analysts, or people just wanting to evaluate the app, that setup creates a pretty high barrier to entry.

Since the app relies on a Node/Vite server layer to proxy API calls securely (as noted in `SECURITY.md`), static hosting like GitHub Pages isn't ideal. However, there are two low-maintenance ways we could make onboarding way easier without breaking security or adding support overhead:

**1. Pre-built Docker Image (`ghcr.io`)**

* Add a basic `Dockerfile` and a GitHub Action (`docker-publish.yml`) to automatically push container images to GitHub Container Registry.
* This eliminates local Node version mismatches and OS quirks entirely. Users could just run:
```bash
docker run -d -p 5173:5173 --env-file .env ghcr.io/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view:latest

```



**2. One-Click Cloud Deploy (Vercel or Render)**

* Add a basic `render.yaml` or server-compatible `vercel.json` and a "Deploy" button to the `README.md`.
* Users could spin up their own cloud instance in minutes and paste their API keys into a web interface instead of using the terminal.

**Suggested Roadmap:**

* [ ] Add `Dockerfile` and test local builds.
* [ ] Add GitHub Action for automated container pushes.
* [ ] Add Cloud Deploy config (`render.yaml` / `vercel.json`).
* [ ] Update `README.md` with container and deploy instructions.

I don't code myself, but I'd be more than happy to help out by thoroughly testing pre-built Docker containers or cloud deployments across different browser environments if someone picks this up!

title: Serving from localhost on Windows not working
Stop rebuilding the compass tape through innerHTML on every heading change
body:
Small one, from the render-performance list in #8 (item 4).

`src/ui.js` around the compass tape rebuilt all seven tick spans through
`innerHTML` on every heading-bucket change: new template string, parse,
throw away the old nodes. The `--slot`/`--depth` position each span sits at
never actually changes though, only which heading division ends up inside
it does.

This builds the seven spans once (lazily, on the first update) and caches
the references, then on a heading-bucket change just sets `textContent` and
toggles the `active` class on the cached nodes. Same signature-comparison
guard as before, so it still only touches the DOM when the heading crosses
into a new bucket, not every frame.

No visual or behavioral change. Positions, labels, and the active-tick
styling are identical, just fewer allocations and no re-parse on the
interaction-heavy path (camera turning).

Verified:
- `npm test`: same pass/fail set as a clean checkout of `main` (several
  suites fail with no API keys configured either way, unrelated to this).
- `npm run build`: clean.
- Confirmed nothing else in the codebase touches `#cockpit-compass-tape`'s
  children or relies on it being rebuilt (CSS keys entirely off the inline
  `--slot`/`--depth` custom properties and the `active` class, both still
  set exactly the same way).

title: feat: typed multi-provider AI agent (OpenAI / OpenRouter / Ollama)
body:
## Summary

Adds a **typed AI agent console** that drives the existing 28 tools over any
OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint — **OpenAI, OpenRouter, or a local Ollama** —
and moves the five-word AI HUD summary onto the same provider registry.

Voice is untouched and unchanged. The two transports run side by side.

Also adds an optional **Cesium ion route for the photorealistic globe**, so the
project no longer strictly requires a billing-enabled Google Cloud account.

![The typed console running "zoom out to full planet view" on a local qwen3:4b](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/darrendignam/gods-eye-view/refs/heads/main/docs/media/text-agent-zoom-to-globe.png)

## Why

Voice is excellent and expensive. Audio tokens dominate the bill, an open mic
bills for silence, and the Realtime API has no open-source equivalent speaking
its WebRTC protocol with native speech-to-speech plus tool calling.

Typing removes all three at once: the same agent, the same tools, roughly **50x
cheaper**, and reachable by back ends that will never implement Realtime —
including a model on the operator's own GPU.

| | Per command |
|---|---|
| gpt-5-nano | ~$0.00015 |
| gpt-5-mini | ~$0.0008 |
| Ollama | free |

against roughly $0.10–$0.30 per minute of open-mic voice.

## What it does not change

- **Voice is byte-identical.** The 50-directive operating manual moved from the
  inline Realtime session config into `src/agent/instructions.js`, and the voice
  modality emits a byte-identical string (asserted in tests). Text overrides
  only five channel-specific directives.
- **Defaults are unchanged.** An install that sets none of the new variables
  behaves exactly as before: the HUD summary uses OpenAI and `gpt-5-nano`, and
  returns the same `503 "OPENAI_API_KEY is not set"` the L9 gate asserts.
- **`gevActions.js` is untouched.** It was already provider-agnostic — 3,455
  lines with zero LLM knowledge — so the panel drives the same runner voice does.

## Architecture

```
src/agent/
├── providers.js      # registry, normalization, capability gating, cost
├── instructions.js   # the 50-directive manual, shared with voice
├── toolSchema.js     # Realtime→chat reshape, JSON Schema validation
├── conversation.js   # transcript sanitizing, bounded history
├── upstream.js       # provider HTTP, injectable fetch
├── diagnostics.js    # silent-failure detection
├── agentLoop.js      # client-side tool loop
└── agentPanel.js     # the panel
```

Credentials stay server-side; the browser executes the tools because they drive
its own viewer. Malformed tool calls are corrected server-side, because Ollama's
compatible endpoint does not support `tool_choice`.

New endpoints: `GET /api/agent/config`, `GET /api/agent/models`,
`POST /api/agent/command`.

## Two silent failures this had to solve

Both were found on real hardware, and both return **HTTP 200** with a plausible
answer, so neither surfaces as an error:

1. **Truncated tool prefix.** The app sends ~11,300 tokens of prefix. Ollama's
   stock context is 4096, which silently cuts the tool list; the model then
   writes a `<function-call>` block as prose and picks the wrong tool. The
   capability gate cannot catch it because `/api/show` reports the model's
   *architectural* context, not the runtime window. Detected from the returned
   prompt token count instead, with the remedy named.

2. **Reasoning overflow.** A reasoning model spends its whole output budget
   thinking about a five-word summary and returns empty content — still thinking
   at 1024 tokens after 86 seconds. Detected and told to use an instruct model.

## Cesium ion route

`createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset` falls back to an ion-brokered tileset
whenever `GoogleMaps.defaultApiKey` is undefined, and ion's free tier includes an
allowance. Startup previously threw on a missing Google key before Cesium could
take that path.

Either credential now suffices; Google wins when both are set. The ion route
loses Google geocoding (both geocoders already guarded for a missing key, so
nothing new throws) while fixed-coordinate city presets keep working.

## Docker

Optional `compose.yaml` with an Ollama GPU sidecar. Runs the **dev server**, not
a build, because ten of the nineteen proxies register only on `configureServer`
and a preview container silently loses them.

## Testing

All three gates from CONTRIBUTING.md are green:

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm test` | **2797 passed**, 0 failed (+198 new) |
| `npm run build` | clean |
| `npm run test:track` | **100 passed**, 0 failed |

Plus two new browser harnesses: `npm run qa:agent-panel` drives a real typed
command through the tool loop to a state change, and `npm run qa:tileset-route`
asserts which upstream authorized the globe.

Verified end to end on an RTX 3070 with Ollama 0.18.2 and `qwen3:4b`.

## Docs

`docs/TEXT-AGENT.md`, `docs/LOCAL-MODELS.md`, `docs/DOCKER.md`,
`docs/MAP-CREDENTIALS.md`, all registered in the canonical docs order, with
`CURRENT-STATE.md` updated as its maintenance rule requires.

## Note for reviewers

This is a large change (40 files, ~6,400 lines) and arrives as one branch. Happy
to split it — the ion route is genuinely independent of the agent work and could
land separately — or to close it and open a smaller discussion first if a new
transport is not a direction you want.

title: Feature request: Toggle to enable sending any chosen radio output to the Voice Model so it can answer questions about it
fix: add an upstream connect timeout to the CCTV media proxy
body:
The CCTV media proxy (/api/cctv/media/:id) fetched the configured upstream
with no timeout. A slow or hung source could keep a proxy request open
indefinitely and tie up resources.

This wraps the upstream fetch in an AbortController with a bounded connect
timeout (15s) and returns a 504 when the upstream stalls, instead of a
generic 502. The important detail for streaming: the timer is cleared as soon
as response headers arrive, so a healthy live video stream is never cut off.
It follows the same pattern the GBFS proxy already uses in this file.

Scope note: this covers the connect timeout the issue calls out (the media
fetch had no AbortSignal). Idle and total-duration limits while a stream is in
flight are a separate concern tracked in #26.

Closes #25

### Testing
- npm run build and npm test are both green (2587 tests, 0 failures).
- npm run test:track: 99/100 on the pinned Chrome-for-Testing v145. The one
  failure is the pre-existing ground-3d probe tracked in #44, unrelated to
  this change and reproducible on a clean main.
- Verified both paths by hand against a running dev server:
  - A healthy camera returns 200 image/jpeg in well under a second, so normal
    proxying is unaffected.
  - A source pointed at a deliberately hung upstream now returns
    504 "Upstream media timeout" right at the 15s bound, instead of hanging.

title: qa:map-source-tray fails on clean main: long Enter hold check races the disclosure debounce
body:
`npm run qa:map-source-tray` fails deterministically on a clean checkout of `main`, on the check **"long Enter hold cannot strand the disclosure keyboard path"**.

Raising it because CONTRIBUTING lists the QA gates as things that must stay green before a PR, and this one does not start green.

## Reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git
cd gods-eye-view && npm install
GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY="…" CESIUM_ION_TOKEN="…" npm run dev -- --host localhost --port 4173
QA_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4173 npm run qa:map-source-tray
```

```
[PASS] exact four-source presentation; the retired left Map Stack panel is gone
[PASS] compact wing is a semantic disclosure
[PASS] Enter opens the tray and hands focus to a Map Source tile
[PASS] Escape closes the tray and restores disclosure focus
[PASS] Space opens the tray through the same keyboard path
[FAIL] long Enter hold cannot strand the disclosure keyboard path — {"expanded":"false","activeStack":null}
```

The run then aborts on the next step (`Node is either not clickable or not an Element` at `qa-map-source-tray.mjs:194`), because the tray is closed when the following check expects it open.

**6/6 runs failed**, identical output every time. Not flaky.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Commit | `880a672` (unmodified `main`) |
| Node | **24.14.0** (also reproduced on 24.4.1) |
| Puppeteer | 24.37.5, Chrome 145.0.7632.77, headless |
| OS | Linux 6.8.0 |
| Keys | real Google Maps key with Map Tiles API enabled, real ion token |

Reproduced on a supported Node specifically to rule the version out.

## This may be the harness, not the app

Walking the same key sequence manually against the same build, but with an extra
snapshot between the `Enter` release and the following `Escape`, reaches the
state the check wants:

```
Escape (close)              {"expanded":"false", active:"control-panel-toggle"}
Enter HELD 320ms (down)     {"expanded":"true",  active:"control-panel-toggle"}
Enter released              {"expanded":"true",  active:"photoreal"}
Escape after hold           {"expanded":"false", active:"control-panel-toggle"}
Enter (expect reopen)       {"expanded":"true",  active:"photoreal"}   ← what the check wants
```

So the disclosure does recover from a long hold; the keyboard path is not
actually stranded.

The disclosure open/close is debounced (`scheduleOpen` / `scheduleClose` in
`src/ui.js`, each behind `openDelayMs` / `closeDelayMs` with `:hover` and
`:focus-visible` guards), while the QA script drives it with fixed 300 ms and
320 ms sleeps. That reads like the harness racing the debounce rather than a
defect in the tray — the assertion samples state at a fixed offset that lands on
the wrong side of a pending timer.

If that is right, the fix is for the check to wait on controller truth
(`aria-expanded` settling) the way the later Bing step already does with
`page.waitForFunction`, instead of a fixed sleep.

I have not proposed a patch since I am not sure whether the intended contract is
"recovers eventually" or "recovers within 300 ms" — happy to send one either way
if you confirm which.

## Possibly related

#44 reports another QA gate failing on clean `main`.

title: [Feature Request] Rayhunter (EFF) cellular IMSI-catcher tap layer
body:
Add a local-only data layer that connects to a locally-running EFF Rayhunter instance (https://github.com/EFForg/rayhunter, typically flashed onto an Orbic mobile hotspot at its default local address/port) and surfaces its IMSI-catcher / cellular-anomaly warnings on the globe at the user's current location.

Rayhunter has no GPS of its own — it just flags suspicious cellular behavior seen by the hotspot it runs on. So this is inherently a **personal, opt-in, local-network** layer: the user points the app at their own Rayhunter's local API, and detected warnings get plotted at wherever the user currently is (or was) when the warning fired, not at any public/global endpoint.

Scope:
- User-configurable local Rayhunter base URL (default to the project's documented default address/port).
- Poll its API for warnings/analysis results; exact endpoint shape should come from the real EFForg/rayhunter API docs/source, not guessed.
- Plot warnings on the globe at the user's live location with severity/detail in the click card.
- Off by default (opt-in local-network layer), like other locally-sourced data.

Filed to track implementation.

title: [Feature Request] Local RTL-SDR / dump1090 receiver tap layer
body:
Add a local-only data layer that connects to a user's own local dump1090/readsb ADS-B receiver (RTL-SDR dongle), typically exposed at http://localhost:8080/data/aircraft.json (or a user-configurable host/port), and shows exactly what that receiver is hearing on the globe — independent of the existing public-feed Flights layer.

Why separate from the existing Flights layer: Flights already shows public aggregated ADS-B (one polling interval behind, aggregator coverage). This layer shows only what the user's own antenna actually receives right now — useful for verifying receiver performance/range and seeing genuinely first-hand local data with zero third-party aggregation.

Scope:
- User-configurable local receiver base URL (default to the common dump1090-fa/readsb default of http://localhost:8080).
- Poll aircraft.json (or tar1090-compatible equivalent) on a short interval.
- Plot received aircraft on the globe, visually distinguished from the public Flights layer.
- Off by default (opt-in local-network layer).

Filed to track implementation.

title: feat(data): add SLF Alpine measurement stations layer
body:
Adds the WSL/SLF IMIS network as a keyless CC BY 4.0 layer: ~207 automatic stations across the Swiss Alps, mostly above the tree line, reporting snow depth, wind, and temperature every 30 minutes.

Fetched through a new /api/slf/stations proxy because measurement-api.slf.ch sends no CORS headers, unlike USGS. The proxy also joins stations to measurements so the browser receives ~207 ready-to-render records rather than the ~9,400 raw rows upstream returns, and caches for five minutes against a 30-minute feed.

Snow depth is drawn as a vertical stem, following the dam-stem recipe in localGeojson.js: polyline and point on one entity that carries a position, explicit graphics constructors, anchored on the sampled ground floor rather than the station's published elevation, and scaled to camera altitude so it stays legible at any zoom while preserving the ratio between stations.

Units come from the published OpenAPI schema, not guessed. An absent reading stays null rather than becoming zero, because 0 cm is a real August measurement and the two must not be conflated.

Station detail renders as world-overlay cards; the viewer runs with infoBox: false, so Cesium entity descriptions would render nowhere.

title: Google 3D is unavaiable
Make the Google Maps key optional
body:
### The problem

`src/main.js` throws when `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` is absent, before the viewer is constructed. The app therefore cannot start at all without a billing-enabled Google Cloud account.

That is a hard gate in front of everything that needs no credentials. Ten of the thirteen layers are keyless — flights, military ADS-B, satellites, earthquakes, CCTV, radio, bikeshare, launches, mapped installations, and every bundled dataset — and none of them are reachable without first setting up Google billing.

I hit this as a new user: enabling Map Tiles requires a billing account, and the signup flow is easy to get stuck in. The README's promise that most of the globe is 🟢 isn't reachable until that's resolved.

### The change

`MapStackController` already treats a null Google tileset as the ion/OSM regime, so very little needed to move.

- **`main.js`** — the throw becomes a warning. With no key the photoreal tileset fetch is skipped and the Cesium globe stays visible.
- **`main.js`** — the initial map stack now resolves `photoreal` → `bing-aerial` → `osm` by what's actually configured. Previously `'osm'` was hardcoded whenever the Google tileset was absent, so an available Cesium ion token was ignored and users with ion got flat OSM tiles instead of Bing aerial.
- **`locations.js`** — `searchAndFlyTo` threw `No Google Maps API key available for geocoding`, breaking search entirely. It now falls back to OpenStreetMap Nominatim, reusing the existing `geocodeNavigationMode` / `flyToViewportBounds` / `flyToLandmark` framing rather than introducing a second policy.

**With a key present, every path is byte-for-byte unchanged.** The fallbacks are reached only when the key is absent.

### Limitations, stated honestly

The keyless geocoder has no viewport bias and no Places-near-view recovery, so ambiguous names ("Sixth Street") can land in the wrong city. That's documented in the JSDoc rather than papered over. Nominatim place classes are mapped onto the Google geocode types `geocodeNavigationMode` already understands, with a two-step lookup on `addresstype` then `type` — Nominatim reports airports as `addresstype: aeroway`, `type: aerodrome`, and only the latter maps cleanly.

Users without Google lose photorealistic 3D building meshes. Everything data-driven — tracking, orbits, trails, detection, cockpit — is unaffected.

### Testing

- `npm test` — **2601 passing, 0 failing**, on this branch in isolation.
- Verified in-browser keyless: app boots, map stack reports `Aerial` with an ion token and `OSM` without one, no console errors, all live layers populate (OpenSky, adsb.lol, AISStream, FIRMS, TomTom).
- Verified with a Google key present: photoreal path unchanged.

title: Feat: GBFS v3 support for station names
body:
GBFS v3 uses `LocalizedString` for `name` and `short_name` of the stations. This caused stations from v3 to have names like `[object Object]`.

This commit makes the code handle v3 names. It default to locale 'en' then fallbacks to the first option in the array.

Documentation for v3: https://gbfs.org/documentation/reference/#station_informationjson

Also, removed the GBFS 2.x constraint from a comment since station_id was and is present in all version of the standard.

title: fix: restore Google 3D on EEA billing accounts via Cesium ion, add OSM Buildings
body:
## The problem

`createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset` returns **403 for every Google Cloud project on an EEA billing account** created on or after 8 July 2025. The restriction follows the **billing address, not the requester**, so it is contractual rather than technical: no key configuration recovers it, and there is nothing an EU developer can fix on their side. Google's notice: https://developers.google.com/maps/comms/eea/map-tiles

Today that developer sees the app quietly drop to the plain Cesium globe with `Google 3D Tiles unavailable` in the loader status. The README says one Google Maps key is the whole entry fee, and for them it buys nothing.

## The fix

Cesium ion resells the identical tileset under its own (non-EEA) Google contract as **asset `2275207`**. When the direct call throws, `src/main.js` now retries through ion before falling back to the globe:

```
direct createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset()
  → 403 on EEA billing
  → Cesium3DTileset.fromIonAssetId(2275207)     ← new
    → still failing → existing Cesium globe fallback, unchanged
```

Verified serving from Hungary, 2026-08-25. It needs a `CESIUM_ION_TOKEN`; without one the behaviour is exactly what it is today. Same imagery, same Google terms, different contracting party, so the "Google" attribution requirement is unchanged.

## Also here: Cesium OSM Buildings

The globe map stacks (Bing Aerial, Bing Labels, OSM) render a flat photo where the photoreal stack has real geometry. Cesium OSM Buildings (ion asset `96188`, ≈350M OpenStreetMap-derived extrusions, free with any ion token) fills that in.

`src/main.js` owns the tileset; `MapStackController` only toggles its `show`, mirroring how it already handles `googleTileset`. It is **hidden on `photoreal`** on purpose: the photogrammetry already contains buildings, and drawing both puts grey boxes inside the real ones. Load failure is cosmetic and logged, never fatal.

## Verification

- `npm run build` clean.
- `npm test`: 2,589 passed, 0 failed.
- `npm run test:track`: **96 passed, 4 failed** on my machine. All four are consequences of the EEA condition itself, not of this diff:
  - three are `no console errors` assertions, failing on `403 tile.googleapis.com/v1/3dtiles/root.json`. Chrome logs that network failure before any application code can catch it, so an EEA account cannot make those assertions pass, with or without this change.
  - one is `ground-3d: ... probes are one-shot/per-poll bounded`, which expects ≥4 `sampleHeight` calls and sees 3. **It fails identically on my other two PR branches, neither of which touches ground sampling.** The invariant the check actually guards still holds: growth over ~60 frames was 0.
  - On a non-EEA account the direct path succeeds, the new fallback never runs, and the harness should be green as before. I cannot verify that from here, and would appreciate a second run by someone who can.

## Docs updated

`CHANGELOG.md` (Added + Fixed), `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` (Map Stack Switcher), `DATA_SOURCES.md` (both ion assets with their terms and attribution), and a `README.md` note in Keys & Costs pointing EEA developers at the ion token before they conclude their Google key is broken. Cesium's free tier is non-commercial, and the README says so.

title: fix: reject impossible ground samples that hide local-layer markers
body:
## The bug

Over a partially-streamed Google photoreal tileset, `scene.sampleHeight` returns values around **-6,600 m**. The plausibility guard in `localGeojson.js` was symmetric:

```js
if (!Number.isFinite(sampled) || Math.abs(sampled) > GROUND_SAMPLE_MAX_ABS_HEIGHT_M) return false; // 9000
```

so -6,600 passed, was accepted as ground, and every stem in the layer was rebuilt 6.6 km below the ellipsoid, where the horizon occluder correctly hid it.

The failure mode is the bad part. `getStats()` still reported every feature loaded with `error: null`, so the layer chip stayed green and nothing logged. The markers were simply **not on screen at close range**, while rendering fine at country zoom and on every globe stack, which reads as a rendering quirk rather than bad data.

## The fix

The Earth is not symmetric, so the band should not be either. Real surfaces run from about -430 m (Dead Sea shore) to 8,849 m:

```js
const GROUND_SAMPLE_MIN_HEIGHT_M = -500;
const GROUND_SAMPLE_MAX_HEIGHT_M = 9000;
```

A sub-surface sample is now rejected rather than trusted. Rejecting leaves the record **unsampled**, which matters: it keeps its place on the existing bounded retry schedule and draws from ellipsoid zero meanwhile, which is the pre-existing keyless behaviour. Nothing about the retry budget, the capability gate, or the render-governor interaction changes.

Measured on a dams-layer feature, camera at 20 km:

```
before   base -6,606 m   hidden
after    base    114 m   drawn on the real surface
```

## Tests

Two, both in `src/data/localGeojson.test.mjs`:

1. A unit test on the newly exported `isPlausibleGroundHeight`, pinning the -6,600 m case, both real-surface extremes, and the `undefined`/`NaN` that `sampleHeight` actually returns when no tile is hit.
2. A behavioural test on the existing `createRealLocalLayerHarness`: drive `sampleHeight` at -6600, assert the stem stays at ellipsoid height, then let a later good sample ground it. **It fails against the old symmetric guard** — I reverted the source line to check, and it was the only failure of the 24 in that file.

## Verification

- `npm run build` clean.
- `npm test`: 2,589 passed, 0 failed.
- `npm run test:track`: 96 passed, 4 failed on my machine. None relate to this diff. Three are `no console errors` assertions failing on a `403` from `tile.googleapis.com`, which my Google billing account gets unconditionally under Google's EEA Map Tiles terms and which Chrome logs before any code can catch. The fourth (`ground-3d: ... probes are one-shot/per-poll bounded`, expecting ≥4 `sampleHeight` calls, seeing 3) **fails identically on a branch of mine that does not touch ground sampling at all**, and the invariant it guards still holds: growth over ~60 frames was 1, against ~60+ for per-frame sampling.

## Docs updated

`CHANGELOG.md` (Fixed) and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`, under the local-infrastructure layer contract where the stem/ground-sample rules already live.

title: fix: broker Google Geocoding, Places and Street View through a server-side key
body:
## The problem

Google rejects referrer-restricted keys for its web-service APIs outright:

```
Geocoding  →  "API keys with referer restrictions cannot be used with this API"
Places     →  "Requests from referer <empty> are blocked"
```

Verified against both, 2026-08-26. Enabling the API does not help; the restriction is on the key.

That breaks three things for anyone who follows this repo's own security advice. SECURITY.md and the README both say to put an HTTP-referrer restriction on `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY`, and they are right to: it is injected into the bundle for Map Tiles and readable in devtools. But that same key was being used for:

- **Geocoding**, called straight from the browser in four places (`locations.js` search box, `annotationResolver.js`, and two paths in `voice/gevActions.js`),
- **Places**, called from the server by `/api/google/nearby-places` and `/api/google/text-search`,
- **Street View**, called from the server as the CCTV frame fallback.

The server calls carry no referrer at all, so they fail on a referrer-restricted key. The only way to make the current code work is to strip the restriction from a key that ships in the bundle, which leaves a publicly readable key anyone can spend.

## The fix: one credential per audience

```
GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY     browser, referrer-restricted, Map Tiles only
GOOGLE_SERVER_API_KEY   server only, no application restriction,
                        Geocoding + Places + Street View
```

`serverGoogleKey()` resolves `GOOGLE_SERVER_API_KEY`, then `GOOGLE_GEOCODING_API_KEY` (an earlier name, kept working), then `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` — so **single-key setups with an unrestricted key behave exactly as before** and nothing breaks for existing users.

Geocoding also needed a proxy, since it was the one Google call still made from the browser. `/api/google/geocode` handles forward (`address`) and reverse (`latlng`), and **allowlists the parameters it forwards** (`address`, `latlng`, `bounds`, `region`, `language`, `result_type`). Passing the caller's query string through wholesale would let a page append its own `key` and turn this into an open relay billed to someone else. It shares the existing Google rate limiter, returns Google's own error shape so callers need no special case, and never echoes the upstream URL, which carries the key. All four client call sites now use it.

`dev-fresh.sh` reads the new key from Keychain (service `google-server-api`, falling back to `google-geocoding-api`) and reports it at startup. It also now accepts a Cesium ion token filed under `api-key` as well as `token` — a token under the unexpected account name silently dropped the app to OSM imagery while every other startup line still printed clean.

## One test-fixture note worth reading

Five mock branches in `annotationEngine.test.mjs` / `annotationResolver.test.mjs` discriminated the geocode call by its Google host, and stopped matching once it became same-origin. The fall-through read as a **transient** miss, so affected tests burned their real 8s/25s backoff ladders: the suite went from 10s to over 10 minutes **while still passing**, which is exactly the kind of failure nobody investigates. They are now behind an `isGeocodeCall()` helper matching both forms. Suite back to ≈13s.

## Verification

- `npm run build` clean.
- `npm test`: 2,587 passed, 0 failed, 12.9s.
- End to end against live Google: "Budapest" resolves to 47.4979, 19.0402; nearby-places returns real results; the CCTV Street View fallback works.
- `npm run test:track`: 96 passed, 4 failed on my machine, none related to this diff. Three are `no console errors` assertions failing on a `403` from `tile.googleapis.com`, which my Google billing account gets unconditionally under Google's EEA Map Tiles terms and which Chrome logs before any code can catch. The fourth (`ground-3d: ... probes are one-shot/per-poll bounded`) fails identically on my other two PR branches, neither of which touches ground sampling.

## Docs updated

`SECURITY.md` gains the key-per-audience table and the reason one key cannot serve both. `.env.example` and the README Keys & Costs section carry the same split. `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` documents `serverGoogleKey()`, the `/api/google/geocode` allowlist, and the `dev-fresh.sh` precedence. `CHANGELOG.md` records it under Fixed and Security.

title: FIRMS proxy fails with fetch failed on Node 24 when IPv6 is unavailable, but there's a fix
body:
## FIRMS proxy fails with `fetch failed` on Node 24 when IPv6 is unavailable

### Environment

* OS: Linux Mint
* Node.js: `v24.19.0` via nvm
* Gods Eye View: current `main`
* FIRMS API key: valid and working
* Network: IPv4 works; IPv6 is unavailable from this machine

### Problem

The FIRMS proxy repeatedly logs:

```text
[firms-proxy] VIIRS_NOAA20_NRT fetch failed: fetch failed
[firms-proxy] VIIRS_NOAA21_NRT fetch failed: fetch failed
[firms-proxy] VIIRS_SNPP_NRT fetch failed: fetch failed
[firms-proxy] refresh failed (all FIRMS sources failed) — serving cache if any
```

The FIRMS API itself is reachable and the key is valid.

For example, this works correctly with `curl` and returns HTTP 200 plus valid CSV data:

```bash
curl -4 \
"https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/api/area/csv/${FIRMS_MAP_KEY}/VIIRS_NOAA20_NRT/world/2"
```

The FIRMS key-status endpoint also returns HTTP 200.

However, Node's built-in `fetch()` fails:

```bash
node -e "
fetch('https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/')
  .then(r => console.log('HTTP', r.status))
  .catch(e => console.error(e.cause))
"
```

Result:

```text
AggregateError [ETIMEDOUT]

Error: connect ETIMEDOUT 198.118.194.34:443
Error: connect ENETUNREACH 2001:4d0:241a:40c0::34:443
```

Using:

```bash
node --dns-result-order=ipv4first
```

does not resolve the problem.

However, disabling Node's network-family auto-selection fixes it immediately:

```bash
node --no-network-family-autoselection -e "
fetch('https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/')
  .then(r => console.log('HTTP', r.status))
  .catch(e => console.error(e.cause))
"
```

Result:

```text
HTTP 200
```

Running Gods Eye View with:

```bash
NODE_OPTIONS="--no-network-family-autoselection" npm run dev -- --host localhost --port 4173
```

also fixes the FIRMS proxy.

### Expected behaviour

FIRMS requests should succeed on systems where IPv4 works but IPv6 is unavailable or unrouted, without requiring a global Node networking option.

### Possible improvement

Would it make sense for the FIRMS proxy to use a more targeted connection strategy for this endpoint, or otherwise handle Node's IPv4/IPv6 auto-selection failure?

For example, this could potentially be handled only for FIRMS requests rather than requiring:

```text
NODE_OPTIONS=--no-network-family-autoselection
```

for the entire application.

It may also be useful for the FIRMS error logging to include `error.cause`, since the current log only reports:

```text
fetch failed
```

whereas `error.cause` revealed the underlying `ETIMEDOUT` / `ENETUNREACH` errors.

title: 🎉 Google 3D Tiles WORKING from Europe / EEA — solution inside
body:
# 🎉 Google 3D Tiles WORKING from Europe / EEA — solution inside

**Good news: Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles are working in God's Eye View from Europe / EEA. 🎉**

I tested this on **Windows 11 from Prague, Czech Republic (EEA)**.

The normal Google Maps Platform route doesn't work for new EEA billing accounts because Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles are unavailable through the Map Tiles API for these accounts.

However:

## ✅ Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles DO work through Cesium ion

And the workaround is surprisingly simple.

No VPN, no non-European Google billing account, no proxy.

I'm currently running the full photorealistic 3D view in Prague using a normal **Cesium ion Community account**.

### Proof — running in Prague 🇨🇿

![Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles working in Prague](https://i.imgur.com/w8LGZJF.jpeg)

---

# 🚀 Want it working right now?

This is basically a **one-line code change + one `.env` value**.

## 1. Create a Cesium ion account

Create/sign in to a Cesium ion account and open:

**Access Tokens**

For personal/testing use, the free Community account works.

The default token is enough for testing. It already has the public:

```text
assets:read
geocode
```

scopes.

You can also create a dedicated token with only:

```text
assets:read
```

No private/write permissions are required.

---

## 2. Make sure Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles are in My Assets

In Cesium ion:

**Asset Depot → Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles**

Add/open it so it appears under **My Assets**.

The asset ID is:

```text
2275207
```

This is the Cesium ion asset ID for Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles — it is not a user-specific ID.

![Cesium ion Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles asset 2275207](https://i.imgur.com/2FWZomd.png)

---

## 3. Put your Cesium token into `.env`

```env
CESIUM_ION_TOKEN=YOUR_CESIUM_ION_TOKEN
```

Do **not** post your token publicly.

---

# ✨ 4. The actual one-line workaround

In:

```text
src/main.js
```

the project currently loads Google directly with:

```javascript
tileset = await Cesium.createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset({
  onlyUsingWithGoogleGeocoder: true,
});
```

Replace that with:

```javascript
tileset = await Cesium.Cesium3DTileset.fromIonAssetId(2275207);
```

That's it.

The project already sets:

```javascript
Cesium.Ion.defaultAccessToken = cesiumToken;
```

from `CESIUM_ION_TOKEN`, so no additional authentication code is required.

Restart the Node/Vite process completely.

Then launch God's Eye View again.

## Result:

**Full Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles. In Prague. From an EEA account. Working. 🎉**

---

# Why this works

God's Eye View currently accesses Google 3D directly using:

```javascript
Cesium.createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset()
```

which uses a Google Maps Platform API key.

For EEA billing accounts, Google's Map Tiles API does not return Photorealistic 3D Tiles.

But Cesium ion also provides Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles as a global ion asset:

```text
2275207
```

CesiumJS can load that asset directly:

```javascript
Cesium.Cesium3DTileset.fromIonAssetId(2275207)
```

So instead of:

```text
God's Eye View
      ↓
Google Maps Platform API
      ↓
EEA restriction ❌
```

we can do:

```text
God's Eye View
      ↓
Cesium ion
      ↓
Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles
      ↓
WORKING ✅
```

---

# 🛠 Suggestion for an upstream fix

It would be great if God's Eye View supported both methods automatically.

Currently `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` is treated as mandatory near startup.

Instead, Google Maps Platform could remain the preferred backend when a Google API key exists, with Cesium ion used as a fallback.

Something along these lines:

```javascript
const cesiumToken = import.meta.env.CESIUM_ION_TOKEN;
const googleApiKey = import.meta.env.GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY;

if (cesiumToken) {
  Cesium.Ion.defaultAccessToken = cesiumToken;
}

if (googleApiKey) {
  Cesium.GoogleMaps.defaultApiKey = googleApiKey;
  window.__GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY__ = googleApiKey;
}
```

Then for the photorealistic tiles:

```javascript
let tileset = null;

try {
  if (googleApiKey) {
    // Preferred existing path
    tileset = await Cesium.createGooglePhotorealistic3DTileset({
      onlyUsingWithGoogleGeocoder: true,
    });
  } else if (cesiumToken) {
    // Cesium ion / EEA path
    tileset = await Cesium.Cesium3DTileset.fromIonAssetId(2275207);
  }

  if (!tileset) {
    throw new Error(
      'No Google Maps API key or Cesium ion token available.'
    );
  }

  viewer.scene.primitives.add(tileset);
  viewer.scene.globe.show = false;
} catch (tileError) {
  console.warn(
    '[Init] Photorealistic 3D Tiles unavailable, falling back to Cesium globe:',
    tileError
  );

  viewer.scene.globe.show = true;
}
```

Even better would be:

```text
1. Try direct Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles
                ↓
             success ✅

             OR

                ↓ fails
2. CESIUM_ION_TOKEN available?
                ↓
   load ion asset 2275207
                ↓
             success ✅

             OR

                ↓ fails
3. Fall back to OSM / Cesium globe
```

That would preserve the current behavior for users outside the EEA while allowing EEA users to get the **actual photorealistic God's Eye View experience instead of the flat OSM fallback**.

---

## Notes from testing

Tested successfully with:

```text
Windows 11
Czech Republic / EEA
Node.js 26.7.0
npm 11.19.0
Cesium ion Community account
Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles asset: 2275207
```

One small gotcha:

After changing `CESIUM_ION_TOKEN` in `.env`, Vite detected the change and reported that it restarted the server, but the new token still returned `401`.

After **fully terminating the Node/Vite process and starting it again**, the same token worked immediately.

So if somebody sees a Cesium `401` after editing `.env`:

```text
STOP THE SERVER COMPLETELY → START IT AGAIN
```

before assuming that the token is invalid.

I also verified the same token + asset independently in Cesium Sandcastle before changing God's Eye View.

---

Hopefully this can become an official fallback — it makes a **huge** difference for EEA users. 🚀🌍
