title: I suggest to rename the tool
body:
I’d like to suggest renaming the “God’s Eye View” tool. I think there are several strong reasons why the current name may not be the best fit for the project.

The biggest issue is that the name sets expectations far beyond what the tool can currently deliver. “God’s Eye View” implies an almost complete, omniscient view of the world — seeing everything from everywhere. However, the actual tool has significant limitations in geographic coverage and 3D visualization. There are important locations where the expected 3D experience does not work properly, including places such as the Golden Gate Bridge and Burj Khalifa. When the name promises an all-seeing perspective, these limitations become much more obvious to users and can make the product feel less reliable than it actually is.

Another concern is searchability and discoverability. “God’s Eye View” is a very common phrase used across religion, philosophy, literature, movies, games, photography, and other subjects. As a result, it is difficult for a user searching for this specific tool to distinguish it from unrelated content. If Google is not indexing or ranking the tool properly, the ambiguity of the name is something worth investigating. A unique technical name would give the project a much stronger identity in search engines.

The name also doesn't immediately tell a new user what the tool actually does. Someone encountering “God’s Eye View” for the first time has no obvious way of knowing whether it is a mapping tool, 3D visualization system, geographic explorer, analytics feature, or something else. A more descriptive name would reduce that confusion.

There are also some branding problems:

It overpromises functionality. The name suggests complete visibility and coverage, while the actual product necessarily has technical and geographic limitations.
It creates an unrealistic mental model. Users may expect every location to be available in detailed 3D.
It is difficult to make unique in search results. The phrase already has an enormous amount of unrelated content associated with it.
It makes SEO harder. A distinctive name would give the project a much clearer search identity.
It is difficult to turn into a recognizable software brand. A unique technical term would be easier to associate specifically with this project.
It isn't functionally descriptive. The name describes a metaphor rather than the actual capability of the tool.
It may become increasingly inaccurate as the project evolves. If coverage remains incomplete, the “all-seeing” implication will continue to conflict with the actual experience.
It can make technical limitations feel like failures. Missing 3D coverage is normal for mapping/visualization technology, but it feels much more significant when the product is branded as an “all-seeing” view.
A neutral, descriptive name would be easier for documentation and communication. Developers could immediately understand what the tool is intended to provide.

Finally, there is also a cultural and religious consideration. “God’s Eye View” has an explicit religious reference, and people from different religious and cultural backgrounds may interpret that differently. Even if the name is intended purely as a metaphor, a technical project aimed at a broad international audience may benefit from avoiding religious terminology altogether. A neutral name would make the project feel more universally accessible without changing its functionality.

I’m not suggesting the current name was chosen with bad intentions. I think the underlying concept is good, but the name creates unnecessary expectations, search/discoverability problems, branding challenges, and potentially cultural concerns.

A name such as “Global View,” “World View,” “Spatial View,” “3D Overview,” “Omni View,” “Map Overview,” or another distinctive technical name could communicate the concept more accurately while giving the project a stronger identity.

For those reasons, I think a rename would be worth seriously considering.

title: fix: isolate ACL verify PowerShell from pwsh7-polluted PSModulePath
body:
## Summary

On Windows machines with a side-by-side **PowerShell 7** install, the credential-file hardening step (`hardenCredentialFile` in `src/keySetupHardening.mjs`) fails closed and refuses to write provider keys.

### Root cause

PowerShell 7 prepends its own module trees to `PSModulePath` at startup:
```
C:\Users\<user>\Documents\PowerShell\Modules
C:\Program Files\PowerShell\Modules
c:\program files\powershell\7\Modules
...
```
The Windows hardening path spawns the **system PowerShell 5.1** (`powershell.exe`) to verify the exact DACL of the credential file. That process inherited the polluted `PSModulePath` from the caller. When 5.1 tried to autoload `Get-Acl` (from `Microsoft.PowerShell.Security`), it hit the incompatible **7.x module manifest** first and failed with `CouldNotAutoloadMatchingModule`:

```
Get-Acl : 找不到模块"Microsoft.PowerShell.Security"中的 Get-Acl 命令...
```

`hardenCredentialFile` returns `false` → provider settings refuse to save any key on such machines. This is also a **security gap**: the verify interpreter must never load modules from an environment an untrusted caller can steer.

### Fix

Reset `PSModulePath` for the **verify subprocess only** to the 5.1 system module tree, derived from the already-validated `powershell.exe` path (`<systemRoot>\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules`). This matches the file's existing fail-closed posture toward inheritable environment steering (the same reasoning that refuses `PATH`-shadowed tools and redirected system roots). No other environment is touched, and the surrounding `environment` spread is preserved.

### Test

New regression test `Windows hardening isolates the verify PowerShell from a pwsh7-polluted PSModulePath` simulates a polluted `PSModulePath` and asserts the verify subprocess receives only the 5.1 system module tree.

Verified locally on Windows:
- `src/keySetupHardening.test.mjs`: **13/13 pass**, including the real-DACL integration test (`Windows production hardener applies its exact DACL with native tools`), which previously failed on this machine.
- Full suite: **exit 0** (2677 tests).

title: fix(overpass): rotate mirrors on any refusal, and never cache one as data
body:
## What's wrong

`/api/overpass` lists four mirrors but only rotates on `5xx`. Anything else — including a `4xx` — falls through to `return payload`, so the fan-out ends at the first mirror that declines, with the remaining mirrors untried.

The refusal is then cached. The cache guard reads `payload.status < 500`, so a `406` HTML error page is written to memory **and** to disk, and the serve-stale guard uses the same threshold and so declines to replace it. Boundary-class queries hold a month-long TTL, so one refusal can outlive the outage that caused it by weeks.

This affects every Overpass-backed feature: road geometry for traffic, annotation outlines, and place lookup.

## How it shows up

Measured against the live mirrors, byte-identical request, only the endpoint changing:

| Mirror | Response to the proxy's `User-Agent` |
|---|---|
| `overpass-api.de` | **406** |
| `lz4.overpass-api.de` | **406** |
| `overpass.kumi.systems` | 200 |
| `overpass.private.coffee` | 200 |

The same request with `User-Agent: curl/8.5.0` gets `200` from `overpass-api.de`, so the refusal is User-Agent filtering at that operator rather than a bad query. Whatever the reason, the proxy already lists mirrors that answer — it just never reaches them.

On the machine this was found on, **4 of 23** disk-cache entries held that Apache error page, stored with `status: 406` and `contentType: text/html`, and were being served to the client as data.

## The change

Both decisions now go through one predicate:

```js
export function overpassPayloadIsData(payload) { … }   // 2xx, not rate-limited, not a body-level runtime error
```

- **Rotation**: any non-2xx moves to the next mirror.
- **Caching**: only data is cached.
- **Serve-stale**: anything that is not data is eligible for a stale replacement.

Using one predicate for the last two is deliberate — they drifted apart before, which is what let a refusal be both stored and un-replaceable.

A refusal every mirror agrees on is still reported with the **first** mirror's status and body, so a genuinely malformed query still says what upstream said — after every mirror has had its chance, rather than instead of it.

`fetchOverpassPayload` now takes optional `endpoints` / `fetchImpl`, so the rotation is covered without touching a live mirror. Defaults are unchanged.

## Verification

- `npm test` — 2682 tests, 0 failures (6 new in `src/overpassProxy.test.mjs`)
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm run test:track` — 108 passed, 0 failed
- Restoring either half of the old behaviour (`status >= 500` rotation, or a `< 500` predicate) turns the new tests red.
- Live A/B on the same query at the same moment: on `main` one query poisons the disk cache with the error page; on this branch the cache stays clean.

One honest caveat on the live evidence: mirror health fluctuates. During development the fix returned a normal 200 (151 KB) by rotating past `overpass-api.de` to `kumi.systems`. At the time of writing, `kumi.systems` is timing out and `private.coffee` is unreachable, so all four mirrors fail and the proxy correctly returns the first refusal **without caching it** — which is the half that can still be demonstrated side by side against `main` right now.

## Notes

- No behaviour change when a mirror answers normally.
- `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` updated per CONTRIBUTING.
- No new data source, so `DATA_SOURCES.md` is untouched.

title: feat(layers): add Civic Offices, a viewport layer that states its own limits
body:
## What it adds

A viewport data layer for **police stations, town halls and government offices** from OpenStreetMap, through the existing `/api/overpass` proxy, debounced on camera `moveEnd`. One self-contained module implementing the layer interface, following the pattern CONTRIBUTING points at.

Classification is by declared order, so a building tagged both `amenity=police` and `office=government` is a police station rather than whichever tag was read first.

## The part worth reviewing

This layer's gaps do not look like gaps. A missing aircraft is obviously missing; an unmapped district renders **exactly** like a district with no office, so a reader takes the absence for a fact about the world rather than about the data. The ground rule about not misrepresenting public-data inference as authoritative intelligence lands, for this layer, almost entirely on one line of text — the row's meta line.

So that line is built from measurements the response actually carries, not from a disclaimer:

- **`out count`** is requested alongside the features, so the row reads `400 of 437 in view` when the query cap truncated the set. A silently truncated list reads as a complete one.
- **`osm3s.timestamp_osm_base`** is the snapshot date of whichever mirror answered. They lag — two mirrors gave `2026-05-06` and `2026-06-01` during development — so the row shows the date it got, not today's.
- A response **without** a count reports no total rather than reusing the drawn length, which would turn "unknown" into "this many".
- Above a **2°** viewport the layer clears and says `zoom in to load — too wide to map`. `0 in view` over a continent is a false statement about the world, and leaving the previous city's offices drawn over it is worse.

Nothing is accumulated across viewports. The claim is always "in view", and the tests assert the string never contains *total*, *all*, *complete* or *every*.

## Rendering

Names go through `worldOverlay`, not a Cesium entity `label`. Entity labels were the first attempt and rendered nothing — no layer here uses them, `infoBox` is off, and all on-globe text is placed by the overlay's collision arbiter, so a label outside it has nothing keeping it off its neighbours.

## Verification

- `npm test` — **2698 tests, 0 failures** (12 in `src/data/civicOffices.test.mjs`)
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm run test:track` — **108 passed, 0 failed**
- CI on this branch: Node 24.14.0, Node 26.x and Windows onboarding all green
- Live in Chromium over Hanoi (`0.077° × 0.144°`): **76 offices**, row reads `OpenStreetMap · 76 in view · mapped to 2026-06-01`, labels place correctly (`UBND phường Nhật Tân`, `Công an phường Bồ Đề`). Zooming to the globe (180° × 360°) clears the layer and the row reads `zoom in to load — too wide to map`. No console errors.

That capture predates #165, which has since merged. Re-checked on this branch rebased onto current `main`: the layer draws again — `25 in view · mapped to 2026-06-01` over central Hanoi at a wider `0.30° × 0.16°` box, `error: null`, nothing truncated. Before #165 landed it reported `UNAVAILABLE · OpenStreetMap · Overpass 406` and drew nothing, which was correct degradation on its side.

## Notes

- `DATA_SOURCES.md` and `dataCredits.js` gain the matching ODbL attribution.
- The registry assertion in `layerState.test.mjs` moves 16 → 17. It exists to make adding a layer deliberate, so it is updated here on purpose. The layer takes share-link token `o`.
- Nothing is bundled; all data is fetched at runtime.

This is a new layer, so it is a product call rather than a fix — happy to close it if Civic Offices is not a direction you want, or to split the meta-line honesty work out of it if the layer itself is the part in question.

title: test(locations): check the destination preset table as data
body:
## Why

`CITY_POIS` is the only place in the app where a landmark's position is written by hand, and nothing validates it. Every other test in the suite exercises code. The table's failure mode is different, and that is what makes it worth a file: a wrong entry **looks like working software** — the pill lights up, the camera flies, and it frames the wrong place.

## The invariant that pays for it

Every POI must lie inside its own destination's `viewBounds`. That rectangle is what "fly to \<city\>" opens on, so a landmark outside it is one the destination advertises but its own overview never shows.

**These pass clean on the current eight destinations.** This is a guard for the next entry, not a fix for an existing one — I'd rather say that plainly than imply it found something here.

It was written while adding destinations to a fork, where it caught one immediately: a landmark sitting 15 km outside its destination's western edge, added by hand a fortnight earlier and never noticed, because the camera still flew somewhere that looked reasonable.

## The rest

Structural rather than stylistic, so an entry framed unusually is still free to be added:

- coordinates finite and on Earth
- `viewBounds` corners the right way round (a swapped pair frames nothing, but the framing code still runs)
- pitch pointing downward, heading in `[0, 360)`, positive `alt`
- required keys present

title: Add index.html analysis, smoke test, font-vendor script, and key-setup opt-out
body:
Why

This PR adds documentation and developer tooling to make the app shell easier to inspect, test, and package for hardened/offline deployments. It documents index.html mappings, introduces a lightweight smoke test to catch runtime import/ui regressions, and provides a simple font-vendor helper for airgapped builds. It also prevents accidental exposure of the in-app key entry surface in production via a build/runtime opt-out.

What I changed (approach)

- Documentation: docs/dom-id-mapping.md (maps major index.html IDs to source modules), docs/external-resources-audit.md (fonts/icons audit + vendor plan), docs/smoke-test-instructions.md (how to run the smoke test).
- Tests/tooling: scripts/test-smoke.mjs (Puppeteer smoke test) and npm script "smoke:test" exposed in package.json. The smoke test starts the dev server, opens the app headless, asserts core UI elements render, and checks for runtime errors.
- Packaging helper: scripts/fetch-fonts.mjs — fetches Google Fonts CSS and woff2 assets into public/fonts/ and writes a local-fonts.css that can be added to index.html for offline use.
- Key-setup safety: src/keySetup.js now respects a build-time flag (VITE_DISABLE_KEY_SETUP=true) or runtime global (window.__GEV_DISABLE_KEY_SETUP = true) to entirely remove the key-setup UI from the page. This prevents accidental exposure of key entry surfaces in production builds or embedded contexts.
- package.json: added npm script "smoke:test" to run the smoke test.

Files changed (high level)

- src/keySetup.js (opt-out guard for key-setup)
- package.json (script)
- docs/* (three new docs)
- scripts/* (two new helper scripts)

Notes and review checklist

- The smoke test uses Puppeteer and assumes a dev environment where headless Chromium can run. CI should provide suitable runners or this job should be gated.
- The fetch-fonts script is a simple helper; it fetches and rewrites CSS references. For release packaging, consider invoking it from a CI/release workflow and committing the results into `public/fonts/`.
- Key-setup opt-out: set VITE_DISABLE_KEY_SETUP=true at build time (e.g., in your CI or local build) or set `window.__GEV_DISABLE_KEY_SETUP = true` in embeds to disable the UI entirely.

Testing performed

- Committed changes, created a fork, and pushed branch.
- Local smoke-test script added; team should enable a CI job to run it.

Notes for reviewers

- Focus review on the runtime opt-out in `src/keySetup.js` and the smoke test script security (it spawns the dev server). The other files are docs and helper scripts.

Proposal: add a Cesium-free spatial query utility for shared distance/selection logic
body:
I’d like to contribute a small, reusable spatial primitive rather than another data layer.

### Proposed scope
Add a pure, Cesium-free utility for point-based spatial queries:

- great-circle distance in metres
- radius queries returning matches ordered by distance
- nearest-entity lookup
- deterministic tie handling
- finite-coordinate validation

The API would operate on caller-supplied position accessors so it does not couple the utility to aircraft, vessels, CCTV, or a specific entity shape.

### Why this fits the current codebase
I noticed that great-circle calculations currently exist in multiple spatially relevant modules (for example `trafficBounds.js` and `routePlausible.js`). A small shared primitive could reduce duplication without forcing a larger architectural refactor.

I would keep this PR deliberately narrow:

- no UI changes
- no new data source
- no Cesium dependency in the utility
- node:test coverage for normal cases, dateline crossing, exact radius boundaries, invalid coordinates, and deterministic ordering

A later PR could consume the utility from an existing feature, but I would keep the first change independently reviewable.

Would this direction be useful to the maintainers? I can prepare the focused implementation and tests against `main`.

title: cctv: live HLS/RTMP video feeds (proxy-owned segment store, hls.js, native video texture)
body: ## Summary CCTV can now play live video instead of only refreshed stills. Tested against DelDOT (Delaware), whose Wowza server turned out to be a good stress test. Most of what's below exists because of how that server behaves. ## What this adds - **Proxy**: `/api/cctv/media//...` sub-path resolution with origin pinning, manifest rewriting, and a proxy-owned segment store with two strategies: - `createHlsPuller` for `.m3u8` upstreams. Polls the chunklist, re-resolves the master when a session is refused, and keys segments by the stream-global number in the filename so session rotations stitch with no overlap or loss. No ffmpeg. - `createHlsRemuxer` for RTMP and other stream kinds. Runs ffmpeg (`-c copy`) as a disposable segment producer with instant respawn, a stall watchdog, and a proxy-generated playlist with continuous numbering and discontinuity tags at respawn boundaries. **ffmpeg is optional.** Without it, `.m3u8` still plays through the puller and the stills path is untouched. - **Client**: hls.js (dynamic import, so stills-only catalogs don't load it), with a Brave-safe branch and network/media recovery. Cesium's native video texture, sized from the real stream and rebound on resolution change. A playback-rate governor for cameras whose encoder clock runs slow relative to wall time. DelDOT delivers about 52 s of content per real minute; cameras with honest clocks sit at 1.0 and never leave it. - **Panel**: the preview card plays live video via `captureStream()` of the active camera's element (one decoder, two surfaces) and widens for it. Stills keep the existing `` path. - **Delaware pack**: two calibrated DelDOT cameras in `config/cctv_sources.delaware.json` as a working example of a video-capable source. They use `rtmpt://video.deldot.gov:80/...` (RTMP tunneled over HTTP, which proved steadier). `rtmp://video.deldot.gov:1935/...` is the same stream over native RTMP. - **Docs**: README (live-video section, CCTV row), SECURITY (origin pinning, ffmpeg spawn constraints), TESTING (soak scenario), DATA_SOURCES (DelDOT). - Minor: OSM imagery capped at z19 so the provider stops requesting tiles that don't exist. ## Why it looks like this DelDOT's Wowza restarts every publish on a 60-second timer. Over HLS that loses about 15 s per minute (a discarded partial segment plus the first-chunk delay). Over RTMP it loses about 1 s, so the remuxer prefers an RTMP URL when the catalog has one. Separately, the cameras deliver less content time than wall time, which no transport can fix, so the client governs playback rate. The measurements are in the commit history and I can write them up in a doc if that's useful. ## Testing Activate a Delaware camera and let it run. On DelDOT it holds indefinitely with roughly a 30 s live delay. TESTING.md section 6 has the soak script. Stills-only setups are unchanged. ## Known limitations - DelDOT rate-limits by client IP. Rapid activate/reload cycles from one host (tuning, testing) trip it, and it shows up as 404s and stalls that clear after a quiet minute. Not a pipeline fault. Leave a minute between test runs. - If hls.js rebuilds its pipeline mid-stream, the preview card can hold its last frame while the projection plane keeps playing. Re-activating the camera clears it. ## Not in this PR A DelDOT loader (per-agency catalog fetch, Caltrans-style) and a WebGL render path for the card. Both follow separately.

title: Proposal: MAPA.UA Ukraine air-threat tracks layer (needs license + capacity check)
body:
## Context

While porting community features, we have a working **MAPA.UA** layer that proxies the public JSON API at [mapa.ua/docs](https://mapa.ua/docs/) (`GET /api/v1/current`) for live Ukrainian air-threat tracks (drones / missiles / bombs), with safety copy that the data is approximate and not for operational decisions.

WarScope’s documented public events API was a better fit for an immediate PR (see #205). MAPA.UA is more sensitive for two reasons:

## Why this is an issue first, not a PR

1. **No written license / Terms of Use** on the public docs — only a volunteer-run free API with a safety disclaimer. Upstream CONTRIBUTING asks contributors not to add sources they do not have the right to redistribute/proxy.
2. **Volunteer wartime feed capacity** — re-proxying from a high-traffic open-source app could overload a small project. We would want an explicit OK (and preferably rate/cache guidance) from the MAPA.UA maintainers before shipping.

## Proposed shape (if approved)

- Same-origin Vite proxy to fixed `mapa.ua` host only (no client-supplied URLs).
- Aggressive memory cache + serve-stale + object/trail caps (as in our local prototype).
- Honest HUD attribution: approximate open-data estimates; not air-defence / safety guidance.
- Layer off by default (`enabled-only` disposition).

## Ask

- Is a MAPA.UA layer in scope for God’s Eye View if license/capacity are clarified?
- Preferred path: open an upstream issue here and separately ask MAPA.UA, or skip entirely?

Happy to follow maintainer guidance either way.

title: feat(cctv): add Traffic Scotland, Perth & Kinross, and Scottish mountain webcam sources
body:
## Summary

- Add **Traffic Scotland** trunk-road cameras as a keyless default CCTV pack alongside Austin, Caltrans and TfL. The public site's `/tsis/cameras` catalog (415 sites, 500 views, coordinates included) becomes one camera per view (`ts-<view id>`), capped at 300 nearest Edinburgh and Glasgow (`CCTV_TRAFFIC_SCOTLAND_MAX_SOURCES`; 500 covers the whole network), kill switch `CCTV_TRAFFIC_SCOTLAND_ENABLED=0`.
- Traffic Scotland publishes no image URLs: each site's stills arrive as base64 data URIs inside an HTML fragment. The proxy fetches the fragment, validates the JPEG/PNG bytes, caches every view at that site for four minutes (upstream republishes every ~5 min in the central belt, ~20 min elsewhere), shares one in-flight fetch across concurrent views, and serves a stale frame when a refresh fails. Both `/frame/:id` and `/media/:id` route through it so the fragment is never piped to the browser as an image.
- Add a **bundled, hand-curated Scotland pack** (`config/cctv_sources.scotland.curated.json`): Perth & Kinross Council's 23 road cameras (15-minute stills; headings taken from the caption burned into each frame, so 20 carry a CURATED badge) and 22 mountain/ski webcams (Cairngorm Mountain, Glencoe Mountain Resort via Winterhighland, Glenshee, Aboyne airfield, Ben Nevis from Loch Linnhe, Leadhills). Bundled packs load as additive peers of the live packs — unlike `CCTV_SOURCES_FILE` they never suppress them — and `CCTV_BUNDLED_PACKS_ENABLED=0` skips them.
- Sources may now carry `frameRefreshMs` (server → `/api/cctv/sources` → client `staticFrameRefreshMs`), so a pack states its operator's cadence instead of relying on the provider-name table. Traffic Scotland is also added to that table at five minutes.
- `CCTV_MAX_SOURCES` default rises 900 → 1,150 so no default pack is silently truncated.

Existing packs, the SSRF posture (server-registered URLs only; the Traffic Scotland resolver additionally pins the official fragment origin and a `ts-<digits>` id shape), the fallback chain, and all client pose/calibration behaviour are unchanged. All new cameras start as RAW PRIOR or CURATED priors and calibrate with the existing gizmo.

## Data sources and terms

- **Traffic Scotland** — the catalog and fragment endpoints are the ones the public traffic.gov.scot site uses, not a documented API; the documented developer route is a registered FTP service. The site describes its information as freely available and the developer hub asks that Traffic Scotland be clearly credited, which the Data attribution popover now does. Frames already carry Traffic Scotland's own watermark and timestamp. Images are withheld upstream while a camera is in operational use, so individual views go dark without warning.
- **Perth & Kinross Council** and the **mountain webcam operators** publish plain still URLs with no stated reuse licence. Frames are proxied live, never stored or redistributed, polled at each operator's stated interval, and every operator is credited by name and link. `DATA_SOURCES.md` records this and says to remove an entry if an operator objects.
- Positions: trunk-road council sites reuse Traffic Scotland's published coordinates; the rest are placed from OSM features matching the council's own descriptions, so treat them as ±100 m priors. The Ben Nevis frame is ~1.6 MB per fetch and is the heaviest camera in the catalog.

## Validation

- Node 26.8.1: `npm test` — 2,715 passed, zero failed, one skip (allocation microbenchmarks are calibrated for Node 24 and skip on 26).
- `npm run build` — passed; existing chunk-size warning only.
- `npm run test:track -- --url http://localhost:4199` — 108 passed, zero failed, zero skipped. (With my local, restricted Google Maps key left in `.env`, the three "no console errors" checks fail because Google 3D tiles return 403 for that key; blanking the key makes the same run fully green, so the failures are environmental rather than caused by this change.)
- New unit coverage: `src/data/trafficScotlandCctv.test.mjs` (loader, origin pin, fragment decoder, shared in-flight fetch, cache expiry, stale fallback, timeout) and `src/data/curatedCctvPacks.test.mjs` (shipped pack schema — unique ids, https only, Scottish bounding box, bounded cadence, curated entries must carry a heading — plus loader filtering and kill switch).
- Live dev server: `/api/cctv/sources` registered 1,145 cameras (300 Traffic Scotland, 23 Perth & Kinross, 22 mountain); 53 Traffic Scotland cameras fall within 15 km of Edinburgh. Frames for A720 Dreghorn, both A702 Boghall views, every Perth & Kinross sample, and each mountain operator returned `image/jpeg` with `X-CCTV-Source: upstream-image`; a repeat Traffic Scotland fetch was served from the site cache in under a millisecond; `/media/ts-43` and `/stream/ts-43` behave as for other still packs; `/health` reports the new cameras as `ok/snapshot`.

title: feat: add a Docker install path
body:
Adds a Docker install path: `docker compose up` builds a pinned Node image and serves the app on `http://localhost:4173` with no local Node install. Refs #43, #48.

Rebased onto current `main`. Two commits: the Docker path, then the container-to-host key-setup fix @jklaze reported in this thread.

### ~~Why another one~~

~~I found #94, #55 and #42 after writing this, and I'm happy to fold this into any of them rather than add noise to the queue, say the word.~~

Kept for the record: that offer stood, and this PR was chosen as the Docker path in the thread. #94 by nitsuah, #55 by DarshSinghKushwaha and #42 by samaritan-maxjb covered the same ground first, and #55 in particular carries the GHCR publishing work that this PR does not attempt.

### What's in it

**The published port binds loopback, not every interface.** Docker's usual `"4173:4173"` publishes on `0.0.0.0`. On a dev server that brokers whatever provider keys the user has configured, that quietly makes the README's "Sharing an instance" warning the default rather than an opt-in. `"127.0.0.1:4173:4173"` keeps the container's posture identical to `npm run dev`.

**The repo is bind-mounted, so state survives the container.** Without a mount, `.env`, `.gev-cache` and `.gev-logs` all die with the container. `node_modules` stays in the image (anonymous volume) so a host install can't shadow the Linux-built `sharp`.

**Provider Settings works in the container.** Docker delivers the host's own browser from the container network's gateway, never from `127.0.0.1`, so the loopback-only admission gate refused every save with a 403. `scripts/docker-start.mjs` reads the default gateway from `/proc/net/route` and sets `GEV_KEY_SETUP_TRUSTED_PEERS` to exactly that address; the gate admits an exact-address list alongside loopback, and nothing else is relaxed. Unset trusts nothing, so every other launcher is unchanged. `--network none` trusts nothing.

**No `env_file:`.** Vite's `loadEnv` already reads `/app/.env` off the mount, and a compose `env_file: .env` hard-fails when the file is absent, which is the documented keyless-start path.

**`git` is installed in the image.** `npm test` builds fixtures with `git init`, so the suite cannot run in a container without it.

Two smaller notes: the container runs as the host user, since everything it writes lands in your working tree (Vite's dep optimizer still needs to write inside the image's `node_modules`, hence the two loosened dirs); and `PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD=1` keeps Chromium out of the image, as it's only needed by the QA harness.

### Corrections to the first revision of this PR

Things I claimed here that were not true, the first two found by reviewers rather than by me:

1. **"Keys pasted into Provider Settings persist to your host `.env`."** False until the fix above. I had verified the storage layer, the host `.env` being read inside the container and the mount being writable, and inferred the rest without ever driving the panel. @jklaze built the branch and got the 403. README and CHANGELOG are corrected.
2. **"`npm test` runs fine in the container."** False: 71 failures, all `spawnSync git ENOENT`, because `node:24-slim` ships no `git`. Fixed by installing it rather than by softening the claim.
3. **"`npm run test:track` could not run because puppeteer's Chrome download is broken on my host."** The fact was right, the reason was wrong: my checkout had puppeteer 24 installed against a `package.json` that pins 25. A plain `npm ci` fixed it and the harness runs.

### Verified

On a clean build, in the container, on Docker Desktop for Windows (WSL2 backend), linux/x86_64:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Cold build, `--no-cache` | builds and boots |
| Launcher gateway detection | `[Docker] Provider Settings trusts the container gateway (172.22.0.1).` |
| `GET /api/setup/status` from the host | 200, was 403 |
| Paste key, then SAVE | writes the bind-mounted `.env`, `0600` in the container |
| Survives `compose down` / `up` | yes |
| REMOVE | comments the key back out; status goes to `set: false` |
| Foreign Origin / foreign Host / proxy header | 403 / 403 / 403 |
| Sibling container on the same network | 403 |
| `--network none` | trusts nothing, still boots |
| `npm run doctor`, `npm test`, `npm run build` | exit 0; 5067 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed |
| `npm run test:track` | 109 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped, against the containerized server |

The save, removal and persistence rows were driven by hand through the panel, not scripted.

### Untested

One environment only. Not covered: Docker Engine on native Linux, macOS and Apple silicon, any arm64 build, and NAS or hypervisor hosts such as Synology DSM, TrueNAS and Proxmox. The `user:` line is a no-op on Docker Desktop, so the uid mapping is exactly the piece that has not met a host where it does something. IPv6-only Docker networks are documented but untested: the launcher finds no IPv4 gateway, logs that it is staying loopback-only, and the panel refuses.

title: fix(ui): recover off-screen panels with bounded viewport clamping
body:
### Overview

Fixes the issue documented in `docs/KNOWN-ISSUES.md` where panels (such as the CCTV panel or Display controls) can restore off-screen or appear missing following layout refactors, screen resolution changes, or collapsed-state restoration.

title: feat(transit): live public-transit vehicles from open GTFS-Realtime feeds (#70)
body:
## Why

Issue #70 asked for a transit layer, and two people offered feeds. Beyond aviation and maritime, public transit is the busiest thing moving in any city, and many operators publish it live with no key. This adds it as one layer package plus one provider, in the current component layout, following the registered-URL-only proxy rule in SECURITY.md.

## What

**Transit layer** (`src/layers/transit/`, one instance per catalog) — buses, trams, metros, trains and ferries as point primitives colored by mode, moving on the globe.

- Seven keyless, openly licensed GTFS-Realtime feeds ship in `src/data/transitFeeds.js`: MBTA Boston, CapMetro Austin, Metro Transit Minneapolis–St Paul, HSL Helsinki, OVapi Netherlands, Entur Norway, TransLink South East Queensland. Each row carries its license, license URL and attribution; each operator is credited in the Data attribution popover the moment its vehicles render.
- Only feeds whose coverage circle contains the camera's look-at point are polled (below a 3,000 km altitude gate, 40 km hysteresis once active). A session over Boston costs one MBTA request per 15 s and nothing elsewhere.
- Motion: every poll gives a vehicle a new fix, and the point glides from where it was drawn to that fix over the next 15 s. One interval behind real time, no extrapolation snap-back (the same trade the flights layer makes). Vehicles absent from two polls are removed; fixes older than ten minutes are ignored.
- Height: near the ground a vehicle reads the shared ground floor (`cachedGroundFloor`) and stays hidden until its cell answers — cells are warmed at most 300 per poll and re-read on a short timer, never per frame. From 60 km up the fleet renders at the ellipsoid, always visible through the mesh.
- Click a vehicle for a shared-host card: route, speed, heading, stop status, occupancy, report age. It follows the vehicle; Escape or a click on empty globe clears it. The handler is ambient: it yields while any tool holds the pointer and never claims it.
- Holds continuous render only while it has vehicles. Share links carry the layer as token `h` (the 19th registry entry).

**Provider** (`server/providers/transit.js`, pure mechanics in `src/data/transitProxy.js`) — `GET /api/transit/feeds` (public catalog) and `GET /api/transit/vehicles/<id>`. The browser names a registered id, never a URL. https only (a redirect must land on https), 8 MB cap, protobuf decoded server-side, 15 s in-memory cache with single-flight refresh, serve-stale for up to 10 min on upstream failure (`X-GEV-Cache: STALE-ERROR`, which the layer shows as STALE). No disk cache. Adds `readResponseBytesCapped` to `server/providers/common/http.js`.

**Decoder** (`src/data/gtfsRealtime.js`) — a minimal GTFS-RT FeedMessage → VehiclePosition reader on the existing `pbf` dependency. No `gtfs-realtime-bindings`, no protobufjs, no new dependency. Unknown and extension fields skip cleanly (OVapi and Entur carry them).

**Composition.** `src/app/layers/transit.js` binds the scene owners (render governor, sprite order, pick registry, world overlay, ground floor, pointer arbiter, credits); `src/data/transit.js` binds the source slot; `constructCatalog` constructs the layer from the supplied source and `layerSources` supplies the standalone one. Package exports `./layers/transit`, `./sources/transit` and `./server/providers/transit` with their boundary groups (`transit-layer`, `transit-source`, `transit-provider`); the new modules join the formatter scope.

## Licenses

All seven feeds are keyless and licensed for display with attribution; the per-feed terms are in `DATA_SOURCES.md` and in the registry. Entur's required `ET-Client-Name` header and OVapi's identify-yourself User-Agent are sent by the proxy. NYCT's subway feed is deliberately absent: it publishes stop-relative positions without coordinates.

## Verification (main @ 96a6b49)

- `npm test`: 3,623 tests, 3,622 pass, 1 skipped (the Node 24 allocation gate; run on Node 22). New: the decoder against hand-encoded protobuf; the registry (unique ids, https, licenses, coverage incl. "Helsinki polls HSL only"); proxy route resolution and cache policy; and the layer through its factory with fake services — two catalogs share no state, enable over Helsinki polls HSL alone and draws its vehicles, a second poll glides them and drops one that vanished, cold floor cells hide the vehicle and are warmed while warm ones place it at floor plus lift, from 1,500 km nothing is warmed, clicks select/clear and yield while a tool holds the pointer, a failing feed degrades without dropping what is drawn, and the source refuses unregistered ids.
- `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`: green.
- `node scripts/qa-transit.mjs` (new harness, real feeds, keyless, system Chrome): 22/22 — Helsinki polls HSL alone; 99 vehicles anchored to the floor and shown across bus/tram/subway/rail; 30 of 40 sampled vehicles moved after the second poll; a real click opened the card and Escape cleared it; HSL credited with its license; Norway from 1,500 km swapped to Entur alone with 467 vehicles shown at the ellipsoid; switching off dropped everything; no page or console errors.
- Decoder timing on live feeds: MBTA 0.7 ms, HSL 4 ms, Entur (1.4 MB, 6,949 entities) 15 ms.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- Detection/HUD integration and voice tools for transit.
- Route shapes and stop names from static GTFS; direction arrows.
- More feeds — one row each, with the license link. Mobility Database lists hundreds of keyless ones.

title: feat(directions): keyless A→B directions with turn-by-turn steps and FLY
body:
## Why

Routing already exists in God's Eye View — voice can say "route from A to B" and `/api/route` asks the FOSSGIS OSRM servers for a street-following path — but it is unreachable without an OpenAI key (voice) and a Google key (geocoding the waypoints), and it returns geometry with no turn-by-turn steps. For a globe that boots keyless, directions should work keyless too. This is the click-to-set front end to the routing that is already there, plus steps.

## What

**Directions layer** (`src/data/directions.js`) — the row's chips are the whole interface:

- **DRIVE / WALK / BIKE** pick the OSRM profile (changing it reroutes).
- **SET A**, then click the globe; **SET B**, click again. Escape or a second press cancels. Markers clamp to the ground.
- With both placed, the route is requested and draped on terrain and 3D tiles (`ClassificationType.BOTH`) with the same flowing-dash material as voice routes (now exported from the annotation renderer), with one white dot per maneuver. Click a dot for a card: the instruction, the leg after it, and the next instruction.
- **SWAP** reverses A and B. **FLY** rides the camera along the route through the shared route-flight cinematic (`flyRoute`, the same code voice `fly_route` uses). **CLEAR** removes everything.
- The row reads `OSM routing · 3.4 km · 8 min · Drive`; while routing, `Routing…`; a router miss reads `No route found between A and B`. The layer never draws a straight line as a route.
- Continuous render is held only while a route is drawn (the dashes animate). Share links carry the layer as token `n`.

**`/api/route`** now accepts `steps=1` and returns turn-by-turn steps. The upstream is always asked for steps and the full response is cached, so the annotation engine (no steps) and this layer (steps) share one upstream OSRM call per route. `src/data/routeSteps.js` phrases OSRM's maneuver type / modifier / exit / road name into one plain-English sentence per decision and folds `exit roundabout` into the roundabout step it leaves.

**Two small shared changes.** `initCameraVerbs` accepts a missing view-target getter (so FLY works before any voice session) and never clears an installed one; the manager gains a public `refreshLayerStats()` so a layer whose state changes outside a tick (click placement, routing) can repaint its row.

**Attribution.** OSRM on the FOSSGIS servers is now credited in the Data attribution popover and documented in `DATA_SOURCES.md` with the fair-use terms; voice routes had been using it uncredited since launch.

## Verification

- `npm test`: 2,719 tests, 2,718 pass, 1 skipped (the Node 24 allocation gate; run on Node 22). 12 new: the instruction builder against OSRM maneuver types, roundabout folding, the step cap, chip and stats state tables, params validation, payload validation (a failed route never becomes a straight line).
- `npm run build`: green.
- Headless Chrome (1440×900, Metal ANGLE) against the dev server, keyless, over Helsinki: SET A + click, SET B + click → a 12-step drive; WALK → a 28-step walk; a maneuver dot clicked → card "Turn left onto Vallilantaival · Step 24 of 28 · then 64 m · 51 s · Then: Keep slightly right at the fork" (overlay diagnostics: one `directions-step` entry painted); FLY moved the camera; CLEAR reset the row. Two `/api/route` calls, both 200, no console errors.

## Relationship to the Transit PR

Independent of the Transit layer PR — both branch from `main`. They touch the same registration lines (`main.js`, `layerState.js` and its count, `spriteOrder.js`, `dataCredits.js`, the docs tables), so whichever merges second needs a trivial rebase; happy to do it.

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- Let voice `fly_route` see a Directions route, and a `get_directions` voice tool.
- Named endpoints once keyless search (#166) lands: type "Helsinki Central Station" instead of clicking.
- Alternative routes, avoid-highways, and an ETA that respects the Transit layer's live vehicles.

title: Idea: Mapillary street-level imagery layer
body:
Hi all,

First of all, thanks for building and maintaining God’s Eye View. I’ve been following the project for a while and I’d really like to contribute something useful.

One source I use quite often in investigations is Mapillary. I regularly switch between satellite imagery and street-level imagery, and Mapillary can be really useful because the imagery is uploaded by users. In my experience this sometimes gives you newer or additional images of a location that you don’t find on the usual street-view services.

I was wondering if it would be useful to add Mapillary directly to God’s Eye View.

My idea for a first version would be to keep it fairly simple: show nearby Mapillary images when you’re zoomed in, show the direction the camera was facing, the capture date and a thumbnail, and provide a link to the original image on Mapillary.

Later on it could possibly be expanded with things like browsing through sequences or using Mapillary detections, but I wouldn’t include that in the first version.

Before I start building anything, I mainly wanted to check if this is something you’d be interested in and if anyone is already working on something similar.

If it sounds useful, I’d be happy to build it and submit a PR.

title: fix(traffic): keep Street Traffic working when Overpass is unavailable
body:
## Summary

Street Traffic can remain stuck at `SYNCING ROAD NETWORK` when the public Overpass mirrors are unavailable, rate-limited, or return an upstream error. This makes the layer render no roads or vehicles even when the separate TomTom flow service is healthy.

This PR adds a bounded OpenStreetMap Standard Map API path for the exact road query emitted by Street Traffic. The response is parsed server-side into the existing Overpass-shaped payload, so the client layer and TomTom matching code keep the same contract.

## What changed

- Detect only the traffic layer's allow-listed `highway` query and validate its viewport bounding box.
- Request `https://api.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/map` with a 12-second timeout for those bounded road queries.
- Parse OSM XML nodes, ways, tags, and node references into the `{ elements: [{ type: 'way', tags, geometry }] }` shape already consumed by `src/data/traffic.js`.
- Keep the existing four-mirror Overpass rotation as a fallback when the Standard Map API fails.
- Leave arbitrary/non-traffic Overpass queries on the existing generic path, so installation context, annotation geometry, and place lookup behavior are unchanged.
- Preserve the existing cache, response caps, rate/concurrency controls, and same-origin `/api/overpass` route.
- Add parser and request-shape tests, plus update `CHANGELOG.md`, `DATA_SOURCES.md`, and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`.

## Why

In a local reproduction, every configured public Overpass mirror failed or refused the road request (502/406 responses and connection timeouts), while the TomTom flow endpoint remained healthy. Because road geometry is a prerequisite for rendering the traffic dots, the UI stayed in its loading state.

The standard OSM map endpoint returned the bounded road data successfully. With this change, the browser completed the traffic load and rendered the existing TomTom-backed traffic layer without any frontend-specific workaround or API-key change.

TomTom remains responsible only for live congestion flow and coverage. OpenStreetMap remains the source for road geometry, with the existing in-app attribution and ODbL documentation.

## Compatibility and trade-offs

- The Standard Map API is used only for a strict, bounded traffic query; arbitrary Overpass QL is never translated or sent to this endpoint.
- The fallback is server-side and preserves the current client response shape.
- Road geometry is still fetched at runtime and is not bundled or redistributed.
- If both OSM paths are unavailable, the existing stale-cache/error behavior remains in place.

## Validation

- `node --test src/overpassProxy.test.mjs` — 11 passed.
- `npm test` — 2,708 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed. The skipped test is an existing Node 24 allocation benchmark when run under Node 25.
- `npm run build` — passed; only the repository's existing large-chunk warnings remain.
- `npm run test:track -- --url http://localhost:4174` — 103 passed, 5 failed in existing `display-floor/corridor` invariants unrelated to this change; the full run reported clean console and HTTP 5xx checks. The tracking, share-link, voice-context, model, and arrival-rotation checks passed.
- Manual local proxy check — a traffic road request returned HTTP 200 with `X-Overpass-Upstream: https://api.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/map`, and the browser completed the Street Traffic load.

No API keys, environment files, cache files, logs, or generated artifacts are included in this PR.

title: fix(radio): resolve common country exonyms Intl.DisplayNames omits
body:
## What
The Radio layer's country parser (`src/data/radioCountry.js`) builds its name→code lookup from `Intl.DisplayNames`' primary English label. Common English names and exonyms that aren't that exact label therefore fail closed. This adds them as unambiguous aliases to the existing bounded map.

## Why
Two paths call `normalizeRadioCountryInput`:
- **Voice** (`src/voice/gevActions.js`) — a spoken *"play radio in Turkey"* passes free text. ICU 77 renders `TR` as "Türkiye", so "Turkey" returned **no stations**.
- **Dataset filtering** (`src/data/radio.js`) — stations whose `country` field carries one of these names (and no `countrycode`) were dropped from country matching.

Verified failing before this change (ICU 77.1), now resolving:

| Input | ICU primary label | Resolves to |
|---|---|---|
| Turkey / Turkiye | Türkiye | TR |
| Myanmar / Burma | Myanmar (Burma) | MM |
| UAE | United Arab Emirates | AE |
| Holland | Netherlands | NL |
| Swaziland | Eswatini | SZ |
| East Timor | Timor-Leste | TL |
| Cabo Verde | Cape Verde | CV |
| Vatican | Vatican City | VA |

## Fail-closed preserved
Only names that map to exactly one country are added. Ambiguous names (a bare "Congo" → CD/CG, "Korea" → KP/KR) still fail closed, and a test asserts that.

title: Add Readable Overlay Labels for Non-Latin OSM Place Names
body: ## Add Readable Overlay Labels for Non-Latin OSM Place Names ### Background OpenStreetMap place labels can be difficult to read when names are rendered only in non-Latin scripts, such as Cyrillic, Chinese, Arabic, and other local writing systems. A readable label overlay should be available as a data layer. It should not replace the original OpenStreetMap label. Instead, it should render an additional Latin-readable name near the original label, so users can still see both the local name and the readable overlay. ### Expected Behavior - Add a toggleable data layer for readable OSM place labels. - The layer should be enabled by default. - The readable label should appear below the original OSM label. - The user should be able to adjust the vertical offset. - A reset button should restore the offset to `0`. - Label placement should remain stable while zooming. - Labels must not become mirrored or flipped when the offset is changed. - Original OSM labels must remain visible. ### Current Problems 1. Changing the offset can make labels appear mirrored/flipped. 2. There is no reset button for returning the offset to `0`. 3. The offset changes visually while zooming. 4. The overlay label should stay consistently positioned relative to the original label. ### Technical Notes The layer is registered as a standard data layer: ```js dataManager.register(osmReadableLabelsLayer); It is included in the layer state registry so it can be enabled by default and persist options: Object.freeze({ id: 'osm-readable-labels', token: 'o', disposition: 'enabled+options', optionOwner: 'osm-readable-labels', defaultEnabled: true, }); For stable positioning, avoid changing the geographic/world position to simulate a visual offset. That can make the apparent offset depend on zoom level, terrain, camera angle, or globe orientation. Prefer a screen-space/pixel offset: label: { text: readableName, pixelOffset: new Cesium.Cartesian2(0, offsetPx), verticalOrigin: Cesium.VerticalOrigin.TOP, } This keeps the label displacement stable across zoom levels because the offset is measured in screen pixels. Avoid transforms that can invert text orientation. The readable label should always remain horizontally readable. ### UI Requirements Add controls to the readable OSM label layer: getRowControls() { return [ { type: 'range', id: 'labelOffset', label: 'Offset', min: -40, max: 80, step: 1, value: params.labelOffset ?? 0, }, { type: 'button', id: 'resetOffset', label: 'Reset', }, ]; } ### Acceptance Criteria - Readable OSM overlay labels are available for non-Latin place names. - The layer is enabled by default. - The layer can be turned on/off from the data layer panel. - The readable label appears below the original OSM label. - Offset adjustment does not mirror or flip labels. - Offset remains visually stable while zooming. - Reset button restores offset to 0. - Original OSM labels remain visible.

title: feat(cctv): add Ontario 511 (MTO) public-camera city pack

## What
Adds a **fourth CCTV city pack** alongside Austin, Caltrans, and TfL: ~250 public traffic cameras across Ontario (anchored on Toronto and Ottawa), fetched keylessly from the `511on.ca` developer API and served through the existing CCTV frame proxy. Directly answers the "Add a CCTV source pack" invitation in CONTRIBUTING.

## How it works
- **`vite.config.js`**: a pure, exported `normalizeOntario511Camera()` (official-host **origin pin** on `511on.ca`, strict numeric-coordinate guard) plus `loadOntario511SourcesFromOpenData()` mirroring the TfL/Caltrans loaders, wired into `getCctvSources()` behind `CCTV_ONTARIO_ENABLED` (default on) with `CCTV_ONTARIO_MAX_SOURCES` to cap the served count.
- The feed reports no camera heading (`Direction` is `"Unknown"` province-wide), so poses use the same low-confidence id-hash prior as TfL / headless Austin — calibrate by dragging the gizmo, per the existing model.
- Only server-registered upstream URLs are ever fetched (the frame proxy already forbids client-supplied URLs); the loader additionally pins the catalog host, matching the Caltrans `cwwp2.dot.ca.gov` / TfL S3 pins.

## Attribution / licensing
Open Government Licence – Ontario (public developer API, throttled 10 calls/60 s — the existing 15-minute catalog cache keeps hits well under that). Registered in `src/data/dataCredits.js` and documented in `DATA_SOURCES.md`. No logo is used.

## How verified (Node 24.14.0)
- `npm run build` — ✓ green
- `npm test` — ✓ full unit suite green, including a new `src/data/cctvOntario511.test.mjs` (5 tests: record→source mapping, official-host origin pin, coordinate/enabled-view rejection, name fallbacks)
- **Live dev server**: `GET /api/cctv/sources` lists the Ontario cameras (`provider: "Ontario 511 (MTO)"`, correct OGL license); `GET /api/cctv/frame/<id>` returns **real upstream frames** (`X-CCTV-Source: upstream-image` — mostly JPEG, occasionally a PNG placeholder, documented accordingly).

No client changes were needed — sources carrying a new `cityId` render through the existing graceful fallback in `src/data/cctv.js`. `npm run test:track` (Puppeteer) was not run locally.

title: feat: draw on the world by hand (DISPLAY ▸ Draw)
body:
## What

**DISPLAY ▸ Draw**: draw on the world by hand. Pick Area, Line or Pin, click the vertices on the real world, double-click or press Enter to finish, give it a label and a colour. Backspace removes the last vertex, Esc cancels the shape in progress, a second Esc leaves draw mode.

A drawn shape goes through the **same `annotationEngine.annotate()`** the voice agent uses, with its geometry supplied and `manual: true`. So it renders with the whiteboard look (draped area, flowing line, pin), persists, de-dups, shows up in `.list()` and the GeoJSON interchange, and clears with `clear_annotations` / `.clear()`. No geocoder, Places or Overpass call is made for a drawn shape.

## Why

The whiteboard today is voice-only, and a name is the only way in. Plenty of things people want to mark have no name on any map: the shed at the back of a wholesale market, a paddock, a yard, the far building. This lets a person point at exactly that and label it, and it lets a session build a board without a microphone (or a key).

## How

- `src/annotations/drawMode.js` (new, pure): the draw session, minimum vertices per shape, double-click de-dup at 0.5 m, length/area, hint text, and the `isDrawModeActive()` switch. Unit-tested.
- `src/annotations/drawTool.js` (new): the Cesium + DOM half. Vertices are world-anchored through the resolver's existing `pickWorldFromScreen` cascade (now exported), so a vertex on a roof lands on the roof. A dashed preview follows the cursor. The viewer's stock LEFT_DOUBLE_CLICK action is removed for the session and restored on exit. Exposed as `window.__gevDrawTool` for tests.
- `src/annotations/annotationEngine.js`: `resolveSpec` short-circuits manual specs (`isManualSpec` / `resolveManualSpec`). A drawn area is a real (not synthesized) outline; a drawn line is a `route` with `mode: 'manual'`, labelled with its length and never a travel time; a pin is a point.
- `src/data/trackingClickGesture.js`: while a session is open the gesture returns before `onClick`, so a vertex over an aircraft, military contact or camera is a vertex, not a selection.
- `index.html` / `style.css`: the Draw group in the DISPLAY panel, in the existing `pp-*` grammar (toggle, shape segment, label field, colour, one-line hint). Respects Clean UI like the rest of the panel.
- `src/main.js`: `initDrawTool({ viewer, annotations })` right after `initAnnotations`.
- Docs: `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` (new section), `CHANGELOG.md`, `README.md` (one line under *Annotate it*).

## Verified

- `npm run build` green (Node 24.21).
- `npm test` green: 2,720 pass, 0 fail (+ the calibrated allocation suite, 13 pass).
- `npm run test:track` green against the dev server: 108 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped (keyless boot).
- Headless Chromium (Playwright, ANGLE/SwiftShader): opened the DISPLAY panel, pressed Draw, four real mouse clicks on the Capitol grounds, double-click to finish → one `area` annotation, ring of 4, amber, `resolvedVia: manual`, `synthesized: false`, 3.3 ha in the hint; Esc twice leaves draw mode with the stock double-click restored. Same result on a keyless boot and with a Google key present.

## Notes for review

- Layers that bind their own LEFT_CLICK outside `bindTrackingClickGesture` (vessel and fire cards) still receive clicks during a draw session. Routing them through the same guard is a one-line follow-up if you want it; I kept this PR to the gesture module they already share.
- No new data source, no new key, nothing fetched.

title: feat(voice): local voice provider (Ollama / Anthropic) driving the same 28 tools — #212

title: feat(nav): keyless forward geocoding via a Nominatim proxy — fly_to_location works without a Google key

Today `searchAndFlyTo` throws `No Google Maps API key available for geocoding` when there is no key, so voice/typed navigation only reaches the eight preset cities — the keyless default stops at "take me to Tokyo".

## What

Returns the Google Geocoding subset the client reads (`status`, `results[0].formatted_address / geometry.location / geometry.viewport / types`), with Nominatim `class/type/addresstype` mapped onto the Google `types` the navigation-mode heuristic understands (country → region-overview, city → city-overview, road → street-corridor, …).

title: feat: browser My Location (GPS fly-to + follow)

title: perf: subset the icon font, and drop the second icon family nothing uses
body:
## Why

Loading the app pulls **442,061 bytes from Google Fonts over six requests**, and
**330,256 of them are the complete Material Symbols Outlined variable font** —
served so the interface can draw 28 glyphs.

The sixth request is `Material+Icons+Round`: a second icon family that no source
uses. `src/cockpitMarkup.test.mjs:694` already asserts the markup must not use
it. Its 173 kB font never downloads today, because nothing activates the family,
but the stylesheet is fetched and render-blocking on every boot.

Measured in headless Chromium against `npm run dev`, cold profile, 2026-09-09:

| | requests | bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | 6 | 442,061 |
| this branch | 5 | **115,319** |

## What changed

`index.html` asks Google for a subset with `icon_names=`. The same 28 glyphs
come back in **4,044 bytes** instead of 330,256, and the unused stylesheet is
gone. No new dependency, no vendored font, no build step — the CDN does the
subsetting.

## The part that can break silently, and the test that stops it

A glyph the subset does not carry gets **no missing-glyph box**. The ligature
never forms and the element renders the literal word, mid-cockpit. So the list
is not kept by hand: `src/materialSymbolsSubset.test.mjs` extracts the glyph
names from the sources and fails when one is missing from `icon_names`, naming
the file that asks for it.

It reads two shapes — the glyph as element text, and any string assigned to
`textContent`/`innerText`. The second is what catches
`icon.textContent = expanded ? 'right_panel_close' : 'right_panel_open'` in
`src/ui.js:1992`: the element is found by `querySelector('.material-symbols-outlined')`
and its glyph picked by a ternary, so `right_panel_open` appears nowhere in
`index.html`. A list written by reading the markup would have shipped the words
`right_panel_open` into the collapsed briefing panel.

The extractor errs wide on purpose. Google answers 200 and ignores an
`icon_names` entry it does not know (verified against the live endpoint), so a
false positive costs nothing, while a false negative costs the interface. Two
non-icon words ride along in the list for that reason.

## How it was verified

- `npm run build` — clean.
- `npm test` — 2,708 pass, 0 fail. (The two allocation microbenchmarks skip on
  Node 26.0.0, as `scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs` intends; no Node 24 on this
  machine.)
- `npm run test:track` — **does not finish on this machine, on `main` as much as
  on this branch**, so I have no green run to show either side. Three runs, zero
  `FAIL` lines in all three: `main` stopped after 9 assertions on a 30 s
  `waitForFunction` timeout at `scripts/track-regression.mjs:647` (the
  share-link reload waiting for the tracked aircraft to return); this branch
  stopped after 42 on a Puppeteer `ProtocolError`, then after the same 9 on the
  same timeout. Nothing in it touches fonts, and the branch never behaves
  differently from its base — but it is not the green run CONTRIBUTING asks for,
  so I would rather say so than imply otherwise.
- Removing `right_panel_open` from `icon_names` fails the new test with
  `right_panel_open (src/ui.js)`.
- In the live page, each of the 28 glyphs measures about **one em** wide via
  `canvas.measureText` under `20px "Material Symbols Outlined"`, against
  **369 px** for a name deliberately left out of the subset — so every glyph the
  app renders is really in the font, not merely requested.

title: fix(server): gate cost/log endpoints against cross-site requests and ship a full CSP
body: ## Summary Adds a same-site request gate to four dev-server endpoints that the credential panel's `admitKeySetupRequest` gate does not cover: `/api/realtime/token`, `/api/openai/hud-summary`, `/api/google/nearby-places` and `/api/realtime/debug-log`. Replaces the frame-ancestors-only header with a full Content-Security-Policy on the dev and preview servers. ## Threat With the dev server running, a hostile page open in the same browser can reach those endpoints cross-site. A `fetch` carries a foreign `Origin`; an `` carries no `Origin` at all but does carry `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site`. Either mints a paid Realtime token, spends OpenAI or Google quota, or appends attacker-chosen bytes to the conversation log. #354 has since bounded and rate-limited the log sink; this PR adds the missing origin check for all four routes. ## Change - `src/localRequestGate.mjs`: pure, import-free `admitSameSiteRequest`. Refuses reverse-proxy signal headers, a `Sec-Fetch-Site` other than `same-origin`/`none`, and a foreign or opaque `Origin`. It deliberately does not require a loopback socket, an `Origin`, or JSON, so the Node QA harnesses (no `Origin`) and the documented `HOST=0.0.0.0` LAN opt-in keep working. 14 unit tests. - `server/providers/common/same-site.js`: `admitSameSite(req, res)` answers 403 itself; `sameSiteGated(handler)` wraps a handler. - `server/providers/openai.js`: the three OpenAI routes are wrapped with `sameSiteGated`. `server/providers/places/google.js`: nearby-places gates before its method check, so a cross-site caller cannot map the method surface. - `build/vite.js`: `BROWSER_CSP` / `BROWSER_HEADERS` applied to both `server.headers` and `preview.headers`, pinned by `src/tooling/viteBuild.test.mjs`. - `scripts/package-boundaries.json`, `scripts/format-scope.json`: the two new modules are owned by the `openai-provider` and `place-providers` groups and adopted by the formatter. - `SECURITY.md`: documents the gate, its limit, and the CSP. `script-src` is `'self' 'unsafe-eval' blob:`. Knockout, bundled in `@cesium/widgets`, resolves the global object with `(0, eval)("this")` at load time, and the Cesium widget never initializes without `'unsafe-eval'`. In the built app Cesium's bundled workers bootstrap through `importScripts(blob:…)`, which a worker checks against `script-src`, so `blob:` is required under `vite preview` (the dev server loads workers by URL). Inline scripts and scripts from any other origin remain blocked. ## Known limit The gate does not survive DNS rebinding in the `HOST=0.0.0.0` mode. There Vite's host check is off, so a rebinding page has an `Origin` and `Host` that agree and a truthful `same-origin`. `SECURITY.md` says so next to the gate. In the default loopback mode the host check rejects a rebinding `Host` before any handler runs. ## Compatibility No new dependencies. Keyless fallbacks, the opt-in rate limiters and the strict credential gate are unchanged. ## Testing - `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm test` (4180 pass), `npm run build`. - `npm run test:track` served under the new policy: 109 passed, no console errors. - A headless-Chrome probe in both `npm run dev` and `vite preview` modes: cross-site, ``-style, proxied, same-origin and header-less requests to the four endpoints (403 / 403 / 403 / served / served), the CSP header, then a globe boot with a first-run tile click that fails on any CSP violation, CSP-related page error, or worker script-load error. - Not covered: voice sessions and radio playback with real keys, since the probe runs keyless. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: fix: pin PSModulePath for the Windows credential ACL verifier (Provider Settings save fails under PowerShell 7)
body:
## Summary

On Windows, saving keys from Provider Settings fails with **"could not restrict the credential file to your account; nothing was saved"** whenever the dev server was started from **PowerShell 7 (pwsh)**. The `icacls` step succeeds; it is the follow-up verification that fails.

`hardenCredentialFile` verifies the DACL by spawning Windows PowerShell 5.1 with `Get-Acl`, and it inherited the parent's `PSModulePath`. A pwsh 7 parent exports a `PSModulePath` that lists its own module folders first, so Windows PowerShell resolves `Microsoft.PowerShell.Security` to the PowerShell 7 copy and cannot load it:

```
Get-Acl : The 'Get-Acl' command was found in the module 'Microsoft.PowerShell.Security',
but the module could not be loaded.
```

The hardener correctly fails closed, so no key is ever saved. The same cause makes the unit test `Windows production hardener applies its exact DACL with native tools` fail on any Windows host where `npm test` runs under pwsh.

## Fix

Pin `PSModulePath` for the verifier spawn to `<SystemRoot>\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\Modules`, the built-in directory that holds the only module the script needs. This is always `System32`, even for a 32-bit host that reaches the tools through `Sysnative`, because the spawned `powershell.exe` is the native 64-bit binary. Pinning also keeps user-writable module directories out of the verifier's search path, in line with the module's existing no-PATH policy for the native tools.

## Tests

- New: the verifier receives the pinned `PSModulePath` even when the parent exports pwsh 7 folders; other inherited variables are untouched.
- New: the 32-bit `Sysnative` route still pins the module path under `System32`.
- Existing Windows production hardener test now passes on a pwsh 7 host.

## Verification

Windows 11 Enterprise LTSC 2024, Node 24.21.0, session started from PowerShell 7.5:

- Reproduced the failure by spawning `powershell.exe` from Node with the inherited environment (status 1, module load error) and confirmed the same command succeeds with the pinned module path.
- `npm test`: 2707 pass, 0 fail, 2 skipped (previously 1 fail).
- `npm run build`: succeeds.

title: feat: add Amsterdam public traffic cameras as a CCTV source pack
body:
Adds the City of Amsterdam's public traffic/ANPR camera register as a CCTV source pack — **rebased onto current `main` and reworked around @kvnloo's review**. The branch was based on a `main` 493 commits stale, from before the CCTV provider moved out of `vite.config.js` into `server/providers/cctv/*`; none of the original commit survives, so this is a clean re-implementation against the current pack interface.

## What changed since the review

> I would not ship these rows as ordinary live CCTV sources with `url: ''` and let Street View/synthetic fallback make them look like degraded cameras. […] I would represent them as `position-only` / `no-public-media` records and make the CCTV UI refuse the normal live-frame fallback for that source kind.

Done, and made explicit at the HTTP/client boundary rather than left implicit. Sources now declare `mediaAvailability`:

| value | meaning |
|---|---|
| `public` (default) | imagery is published; a missing frame is an **outage**, and the Street View / synthetic fallback chain is the right answer to it |
| `position-only` | the upstream is a survey of camera **positions** with no public imagery behind it — a permanent, documented state, so the chain is **refused** |

Concretely:

- `/api/cctv/sources` and `/api/cctv/stream/:id` carry the state; the stream payload advertises `frameUrl: null, mediaUrl: null`.
- `/api/cctv/frame/:id` and `/api/cctv/media/:id` answer **409** with `X-CCTV-Source: position-only`, **before** the fallback chain runs — so no Street View request is ever billed for a frame that would never change.
- `/api/cctv/health` reports `status: 'position-only'`, not `degraded`. It isn't a feed in trouble; it was never a feed.
- The client refuses symmetrically, so it never even earns that 409: the ambient-card pacer skips these cameras, the projection plane keeps a `NO PUBLIC FEED · POSITION ONLY` placeholder, and the panel badge reads the same.

Unknown values normalize to `public`, so a typo can never blind a pack that *does* have frames. Every existing pack is untouched and keeps the full chain.

The two facts stay separate, as you put it:

```text
observed fact: a public camera/ANPR installation exists here   → the pack contributes this
media state:   no public live frame is available               → declared, not discovered
```

Also dropped from the original PR: the whole `CCTV_MAX_SOURCES` section. `allocateSourceCap` now fills the cap round-robin and the default is 4000, so the starvation bug that PR described is already fixed upstream. Nothing here touches the cap.

## The pack

`loadAmsterdamSourcesFromOpenData` reads the DSO-API asset register filtered server-side to `objectSoort=Camera` — **404 cameras** today (mast traffic cameras plus the travel-time, environmental-zone, S100-ring and mobile ANPR networks), capped to the 250 nearest Dam square. Keyless; off with `CCTV_AMSTERDAM_ENABLED=0`. An optional `AMSTERDAM_DATA_API_KEY` rides as `X-Api-Key` ahead of the platform's announced key requirement.

Two wire details are load-bearing, and both fail **silently** — both are pinned by tests:

1. **`Accept: application/hal+json`.** The API answers **406** to a plain `application/json`, even with `_format=json` in the query.
2. **`Accept-Crs: EPSG:4326`.** The register is natively Rijksdriehoek (EPSG:28992) — six-figure metres like `[120997, 485841]`. The Amsterdam bounding box doubles as the datum guard *behind* that header: if the negotiation ever breaks, every row fails the check and the pack **empties** rather than scattering cameras.

No bearing exists anywhere in the register, so every row takes the headingless low-confidence RAW PRIOR pose as TfL does (id-hash heading, −18° / 44° / 145 m / 8 m, `headingConfidence: 'low'`). `groundElevationM: 2` is orthometric per `src/data/geoid.js`, matching the Caltrans/TfL convention.

### Why not the live Rijkswaterstaat feeds

There are publicly viewable live A10/A4/A9 cameras near Amsterdam. They are deliberately **not** used: their images come from `stream.inmoves.nl`, which serves `robots.txt: Disallow: /` and returns a **401 placeholder** unless the request carries a `Referer` of the operator's own site. Using them means forging a Referer to defeat hotlink protection against the operator's stated wishes. Recorded in `DATA_SOURCES.md` so it doesn't have to be re-derived.

## Verification

All gates green locally on Node 24.19.0:

- `npm test` — **5398 tests, 0 failures** (28 new across three files)
- `npm run build` — clean (only the pre-existing chunk-size advisory)
- `npm run check:boundaries` — clean (`src/sources/cctvTypes.js`, which now owns the shared media-availability vocabulary, is declared in the five packages that reach it)
- `npm run test:track` — **109 passed, 0 failed**, including `no console errors` and `no HTTP 5xx` across the full run
- `npm run doctor -- --json` — exit 0

Against the real API through the running dev server:

```
[CCTV] Loaded Amsterdam camera register: 404 cameras (using nearest 250; positions only, no public frames)
/api/cctv/sources            -> 3292 cameras · amsterdam-open-data: 250
  all position-only · unique ids 250 · all in bbox · all headingConfidence low · all groundElevationM 2
  non-Amsterdam: 3042 rows, all mediaAvailability "public"
GET /api/cctv/frame/ams-153tvk016   -> 409  X-CCTV-Source: position-only
GET /api/cctv/media/ams-153tvk016   -> 409  X-CCTV-Source: position-only
GET /api/cctv/stream/ams-153tvk016  -> {"frameUrl":null,"mediaUrl":null,"mediaAvailability":"position-only"}
GET /api/cctv/health                -> {"status":"position-only","message":"No public media published for this camera"}
GET /api/cctv/frame/354  (Austin)   -> 200  X-CCTV-Source: synthetic   # outage path intact
```

And in the browser, flown to Dam square with the layer live:

```
amsterdam in catalog        : 250   (frameUrl/mediaUrl all null)
other cameras               : 3042  (frameUrl present)
frame/media requests issued : 21
  ...for ams- cameras       : 0
4xx/5xx on /api/cctv/*      : 0      # the client never even earns the 409
panel source badge          : "NO PUBLIC FEED · POSITION ONLY"
```

Camera icons and ambient cards land on the canal ring at Dam, Silodam, Barentszplein and Van Diemenstraat, each labelled `CAM-<street> (<type>)`, with an empty preview pane rather than anything pretending to be live.

New tests live in `src/data/cctvAmsterdam.test.mjs` (pack contract, pose personality, orthometric datum, RD-coordinate rejection, camera-only + unique filtering, type-label mapping including its fail-open path and the upstream `Mileuzone` typo, malformed-payload tolerance, the two wire headers, off-origin paging refusal), `src/data/cctvPositionOnly.test.mjs` (the semantic end-to-end through the mounted proxy) and `src/layers/cctv/positionOnly.test.mjs` (the client refusal). The two refusal tests were mutation-checked — each fails when its guard is removed.

## Docs

`DATA_SOURCES.md` (table row, a note covering the position-only nature, and the Rijkswaterstaat decision), `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` (a dedicated pack section), `src/data/dataCredits.js`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `README.md`, `.env.example`.

README's walkthrough step 4 ("Turn on CCTV over Austin, London, or California") is deliberately **not** updated — that line is about looking through a live feed, which Amsterdam doesn't offer.
