title: feat(clouds): keyless NOAA GOES cloud cover layer
body:
## What

Adds a **Cloud Cover** data layer rendering near-real-time NOAA GOES-R full-disk **GeoColor** imagery (GOES-19 East, GOES-18 West) from the keyless NOAA/NESDIS STAR CDN, plus the geostationary→geographic reprojection core.

## Why

The app had no cloud/weather imagery layer. GOES is keyless, U.S. public domain, and already refreshed every ~10 min by NOAA. This is the first family of a broader "global cloud coverage" effort (Meteosat/FengYun/Himawari follow-ups); **GOES alone covers the Americas and adjacent oceans only, so this PR does not claim global coverage.**

## How

- `server/providers/geostationary/projection.js` — pure GOES-R ABI fixed-grid math (`satelliteNav`, `scanAnglesToGeodetic`, `geodeticToScanAngles`, `GOES_GRID_HALF_EXTENT_RAD`) with an exact ellipsoid visibility test.
- `server/providers/geostationary/raster.js` — inverse-resamples a full-disk RGBA image into equirectangular parts with an out-of-disk alpha mask, horizon binary-search bounds, and antimeridian splitting.
- `server/providers/goes.js` — `/api/goes/manifest`, `/api/goes/frames/<frameId>/<part>.png`, `/api/goes/status`. Fetches the STAR JPEG, reprojects with `sharp` (decode/encode only; the warp is pure JS), caches content-addressed frames for 5 min (single-flight, per-satellite failure isolation, last-good on failure).
- `src/layers/clouds/` + `src/data/clouds.js` — the layer owns only its own Cesium imagery layers, replaces frames without leaking, and reports guidance instead of drawing when the globe is hidden (Google Photorealistic 3D).
- Registered as `clouds` (token `h`), attribution added, docs updated.

## Coverage / limits

- Americas + adjacent oceans only (GOES-19 + GOES-18). Not a global mosaic.
- Requires a globe imagery stack (Satellite/OSM); photoreal mode hides the globe.
- GeoColor is a rendered scene (clouds/land/snow/night lights), not a cloud-only mask.
- Output is 1024 px tall per satellite frame to bound GPU texture memory.

## Verification

- `npm test` — 3412 pass, 0 fail (1 skipped; allocation microbenchmarks skip on non-Node-24).
- `npm run check:boundaries` — pass.
- Projection tests anchor on analytic values (sub-satellite point, disk edge, equator closed form), not just round-trips. Proxy tests cover manifest/frame/status, TTL caching, per-satellite failure, and last-good frames.

## Notes

No new keys. `sharp` is already a devDependency; the local dev/preview server needs dev dependencies installed.

title: feat(glm): keyless NOAA GLM lightning layer
body:
## What

Adds a **GLM Lightning** data layer showing recent lightning flash observations from NOAA's Geostationary Lightning Mapper on **GOES-19 (East)** and **GOES-18 (West)**, keyless via NOAA Open Data on AWS.

## How

- `server/providers/common/noaa-s3.js` — bounded S3 `ListObjectsV2` (XML), granule-key timestamp parsing, and capped object download.
- `server/providers/glm/flashes.js` — NetCDF-4 decode via `h5wasm/node`: `flash_count`, `product_time` units, packed `scale_factor`/`add_offset`/`_FillValue`, unsigned int16 fields, and per-flash records (`id`, `satelliteId`, lon/lat, time, energy, area, quality flag).
- `server/providers/glm.js` — `/api/glm` and `/api/glm/status`. Keeps a **bounded two-minute rolling window** of flashes, lists/downloads unseen granules (hour-rollover aware), dedupes by granule/flash id, expires old flashes, caps the response at 20,000 newest, and serves last-good on failure. Per-satellite failures never drop the other feed.
- `src/layers/glm/` + `src/data/glmLightning.js` — owns one Cesium `PointPrimitiveCollection`, stable flash ids, energy-bucketed color, truthful unavailable state. Registered as `glm-lightning` (token `l`).

## Validation

The decoder was run against a **real GOES-19 granule** (`GLM-L2-LCFA/2026/257/12/OR_GLM-L2-LCFA_G19_s20262571200000_...nc`): 236 flashes, correct 20 s time window, plausible Americas coordinates, unsigned flash ids, finite energy/area.

## Honest limits

These are **optical flash detections from a geostationary view**, not ground-truth cloud-to-ground strike records. Overlapping East/West views can observe the same physical flash, so counts are not globally deduplicated. Requires `h5wasm` (devDependency) on the local dev/preview server.

## Verification

- `npm test` — 3408 pass, 0 fail (1 skipped; allocation microbenchmarks skip on non-Node-24).
- `npm run check:boundaries` — pass.
- Tests cover S3 XML/granule parsing, packed-value decoding, provider window/dedupe/expiry/truncation/stale behavior, and the client layer lifecycle.

## Notes

`h5wasm` added to devDependencies. No keys required.

title: feat(wind): keyless NOAA GFS wind layer with animated particles
body:
## What

Adds a **Wind** data layer animating the global 10 m wind field from NOAA GFS, with nullschool-style animated particles over the Cesium globe.

## How

- `server/providers/wind/` — cycle selection, `.idx` parsing, byte-range fetch, ecCodes (WASM) decoding, and resampling.
- `server/providers/wind.js` — `/api/wind/manifest`, `/api/wind/grid/<id>.bin` (Float32 U then V), `/api/wind/status`. Selects the latest available 0.25° cycle, byte-range fetches only `UGRD`/`VGRD` 10 m messages (~1 MB each instead of the whole ~500 MB file), resamples to a compact grid (1° default), and caches per cycle for an hour (single-flight, last-good on failure). Keyless.
- `src/layers/wind/` + `src/data/wind.js` — particle overlay: bilinear field sampling with longitude wrap, per-frame advection, Cesium camera projection, and globe-occlusion culling via `EllipsoidalOccluder`. Registered as `wind` (token `k`).

## Validation

Run end-to-end against the **real 2026-09-14 06z cycle** on Node 25: 180×91 grid at 2°, exact 131,040-byte payload, plausible mean |u| ≈ 4.3 m/s and |v| ≈ 4.0 m/s. The ecCodes WASM decoder requires **Node ≥24**, which `package.json` already requires.

## Honest limits

This is a **forecast, not an observation** — particles show model flow, not measured wind. The particle rendering is a 2D canvas overlay projected through the camera, not a 3D primitive, so it is a visual approximation. No visual browser QA was run in this environment (Node 22 here); the rendering is covered by unit tests with fakes.

## Verification

- `npm test` — 3412 pass, 0 fail (1 skipped; allocation microbenchmarks skip on non-Node-24).
- `npm run check:boundaries` — pass.

ECMWF IFS as a second wind model (keyless ECMWF Open Data, `10u`/`10v`) is the intended next PR on top of this one.

title: feat (cctv): live video feeds, starting with DelDOT
body:
Title: cctv: live video feeds, starting with DelDOT

What this is

CCTV cameras that publish a video stream now play as continuous live video instead of refreshed stills. The video projects onto the monitor plane in the scene and plays in the panel card at the same time, from one decoder. Delaware ships as the first agency: a statewide DelDOT loader registers every active camera from their public catalog (about 290 cameras), so the feature is demonstrable out of the box.

This is a re-port of #189 onto the current architecture. That PR predated the CCTV reorg (vite.config.js proxies into server/providers/cctv/, ui.js into src/ui/), so it targeted files that no longer exist. I closed it and rebuilt the same reviewed code on the new structure. The pipeline itself has weeks of soak testing behind it against DelDOT's streams.

How it works

The server owns the upstream session. Two strategies, picked by URL:

.m3u8 upstreams: a Node puller polls the chunklist, re-resolves the master playlist when a session expires, and serves a proxy-owned playlist. No new dependencies.
RTMP and everything else: ffmpeg remuxes with -c copy (no re-encode) into local segments, respawning instantly when the agency drops the session. ffmpeg is optional; without it those cameras fall back to the stills path and nothing else changes.

The client plays the proxy playlist through hls.js. All media requests stay origin-pinned: sub-paths resolve only against the registered camera's origin, and a playlist reference that would resolve elsewhere is refused. Segments live in a short rolling window under the OS temp dir and get reaped when idle.

Why the playback-rate governor exists

DelDOT's encoders deliver roughly 52 seconds of content per 60 seconds of wall time, so no transport can play them continuously at 1x. The client holds playbackRate slightly under 1.0 based on buffer depth and eases back to 1.0 when the buffer is healthy. Cameras with honest clocks sit at 1.0 and never leave it. The stream ends up 20 to 30 seconds behind live, which is the tradeoff for never starving.

Testing

10 minute uninterrupted soak on a DelDOT camera (scenario now in TESTING.md section 6)
Camera switching, projection toggle, and stills/video coexistence all covered in that scenario
Session death and recovery exercised heavily: DelDOT restarts every stream on a 60 second timer, which turned out to be a good adversarial test bed

Known limitations

DelDOT rate limits per IP. Bursts of rapid camera switching can bring on 404s and faster drains until it cools off. Normal use does not hit this.
The roughly once a minute stream restart shows as a brief hitch. That is the agency's publish cycle, not a pipeline bug.

Not in this PR

More agencies. Caltrans exposes a streamingVideoURL field in the same catalog the existing loader already reads, so that is the natural next one. I would rather land this and follow up than grow the diff.
A WebGL render path for the panel card (sharper video at small sizes).

title: feat(vessels): add keyless APRS-IS live vessel source
body:
Adds an optional APRS-IS provider for the existing vessel layer. It reuses the
current vessel ingestion, selection, cards and tracking path; it does not add a
second visual layer.

## Why APRS-IS, not APRS.fi

APRS.fi does not expose a public WebSocket and its REST API requires a private
API key, so it cannot back a keyless live feed. APRS-IS is the documented,
receive-only amateur-radio network and is the correct source for a continuous
stream. No APRS.fi endpoint is called and nothing is scraped.

## What changed

- `server/providers/vessels/aprs-live.js`: server-side, receive-only TCP/TLS
  client with line framing, bounded record cache (2,000 records, 30-minute
  expiry), and reconnect with exponential backoff.
- `server/providers/vessels/aprs-parser.js`: dependency-free parser for AIS
  `!AIVDM` position reports (Class A types 1/2/3 and Class B type 18), maritime
  APRS position packets (`!`, `=`, `/`, `@`), and APRS telemetry.
- `/api/aprs-live` and `/api/aprs-live/track`: same-origin JSON endpoints.
  Returns 503 with `configured:false` when the source is not enabled;
  credentials never reach the browser.
- `src/sources/live/standalone.js`: `createAprsIsSource()` implementing the
  existing provider-neutral vessel contract, exported from
  `src/sources/live/index.js`.
- `src/data/aisLiveVessels.js`: env-driven provider selection
  (`VITE_VESSEL_SOURCE=aprs-is`); AISStream remains the default.
- Attribution in `src/data/dataCredits.js` and `DATA_SOURCES.md`, plus
  `docs/APRS-IS.md`.

## Viewport filter

Snapshot requests carry the camera's visible bounds, which the server converts
to an APRS-IS area filter (`a/latN/lonW/latS/lonE`). Antimeridian crossings are
split into two boxes. Updates are applied to the live connection without
reconnecting and are coalesced (change check plus a 5-second minimum interval),
so camera movement cannot flood APRS-IS. `APRS_IS_FILTER` remains the fallback
before the first viewport and whenever the viewport is absent or degenerate.

## Tracking

Positions accumulate in a bounded per-reference history (64 samples per vessel,
5,000 vessels). Selecting a vessel backfills its recent path through
`/api/aprs-live/track?reference=...`, reusing the existing trail path. The
reference is validated before lookup and is never interpolated into an APRS-IS
filter.

## Vessel telemetry

APRS telemetry reports (`T#sss,a1,a2,a3,a4,a5,bbbbbbbb`) are parsed and kept per
source callsign: latest sample plus a bounded recent history (32 samples).
Analog channels are exposed raw because their units live in the station's
separate `PARM`/`UNIT`/`EQNS` messages; no unit is invented.

The latest reading is rendered through the existing vessel card detail-line
contract rather than a dedicated renderer:

- selected card — a `TLM #n · A: … · D: …` detail line, alongside the existing
  type/speed/heading, destination and identity lines;
- ambient card — a compact `TLM #n` summary, only when the card has no other
  metrics to show, so decluttered labels stay small;
- vessel HUD — a monospace telemetry line below the identity row.

Telemetry is carried through the store on both create and in-place update, so a
refresh without a report keeps the last known reading. APRS rows are labelled
`APRS`/`CALL` while AIS rows keep `AIS`/`MMSI`, and callsign-only beacons use
the callsign as their identity.

## Configuration

`APRS_IS_ENABLED=1` (or `APRS_IS_HOST`), `APRS_IS_HOST`, `APRS_IS_PORT`,
`APRS_IS_CALLSIGN`, `APRS_IS_PASSCODE` (`-1` is receive-only) and
`APRS_IS_FILTER`. Credentials stay on the server.

## Verification

- `node --test server/providers/vessels/aprs-parser.test.mjs server/providers/vessels/aprs-live.test.mjs src/sources/live/aprsIs.test.mjs src/sources/live/contract.test.mjs` — 24/24, including an independent spec-based AIS encoder that decodes Class A and Class B position reports, viewport/antimeridian filter construction, history caps, telemetry parsing, and the endpoint contract.
- `node --test src/data/aisLiveVessels.test.mjs` — 84/84, covering telemetry formatting, APRS/AIS labelling, HUD output, and in-place telemetry propagation across refreshes.
- `npm test` — 3407 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
- `npm run check:boundaries` — passed.
- `npm run build` — passed (the worktree logs an unrelated Cesium asset-copy warning because `node_modules` resolves from the parent checkout).
- `prettier --check` on the changed files — clean.

## Limitations

- AIS multipart (type 5 static data) and long-range type 27 reports are not
  decoded.
- APRS beacons have no MMSI, so their identifier is the callsign.
- Telemetry analog channels are shown as raw values; resolving them to physical
  units would require consuming each station's `PARM`/`UNIT`/`EQNS` messages.

title: feat(firms): keyless NOAA GOES ABI fire detections
body:
Makes the Active Fires layer work **without any API key**, by reading the NOAA GOES-R ABI fire/hot-spot product straight from the public GOES S3 buckets.

## Why GOES

The layer currently merges three VIIRS NRT sources through `/api/firms`, which needs a free `FIRMS_MAP_KEY`; without it the layer is empty. Keyless MODIS/VIIRS is not an option: `MOD14`/`MYD14` and `VNP14IMG` are distributed through NASA LAADS/LP DAAC and require an Earthdata Login token for programmatic download, even though the data are public. There is no AWS Open Data bucket for them.

GOES is different. `ABI-L2-FDCF` lives in `noaa-goes18`/`noaa-goes19`, which are AWS Open Data: anonymous access, `us-east-1`, not requester-pays. I verified against the live buckets while building this — the product is still produced, with granules landing every 10 minutes (`Last-Modified` of the newest granule was minutes old when I checked). GOES-16 and GOES-17 are decommissioned and produce no 2026 data, so only 18/19 are used.

The trade-off is geometric and worth stating: GOES is geostationary, so it images the full disk every ~10 minutes and catches fires far sooner than a twice-daily polar overpass — but at ~2 km at the sub-satellite point (coarser toward the limb) and only over the Americas and adjacent oceans. VIIRS is ~375 m. The providers are complementary, so **FIRMS still wins whenever its key is configured**.

## Data path

```
noaa-goes19.s3.amazonaws.com/ABI-L2-FDCF/YYYY/DDD/HH/OR_ABI-L2-FDCF-M6_G19_s…_e…_c….nc
        │  anonymous HTTPS, ~1.8 MB HDF5
        ▼
server/providers/goes-fires.js     list newest key → download → cache (10 min)
        ▼
server/providers/goes/fireGrid.js  HDF5 decode + ABI projection + detection
        ▼
GET /api/goes-fires                FIRMS-shaped rows
        ▼
src/layers/firms/source.js         keyless fallback on 503 no_key
        ▼
existing fire layer                adapt → cards → render (unchanged)
```

## Finding the newest granule

The `s<timestamp>` segment is the scan start and does **not** land on the 10-minute boundary (e.g. `s20262570000215` = 00:00:21.5Z), so the key cannot be derived by rounding the clock. The provider lists the current hour prefix and takes the last key, walking back an hour at a time when the prefix is empty.

## Decoding and detection

The granule is NetCDF-4/HDF5, read with `h5wasm` (WASM HDF5 — no native toolchain). Scale factors, offsets and fill values are read from the file rather than hardcoded.

Detection is `Power > 0`, and that criterion is **checkable against the granule's own aggregates**: on the 2026-09-14 00:00Z GOES-19 granule, `Power > 0` selects 83 pixels and filtering `DQF == 0` leaves exactly 79 — the value of the file's `total_number_of_pixels_with_fire_radiative_power`. Valid `Temp` pixels (59) match `total_number_of_pixels_with_fire_temperature` the same way.

`Mask` is a scene-classification bit field. Its class semantics are deliberately **not** reimplemented — the raw value is passed through, because guessing the bit meanings would silently mislabel detections.

The product ships no `Lat`/`Lon` variables, so the ABI fixed grid is inverted using `perspective_point_height`, the two axes and `longitude_of_projection_origin`. Note that the latter is in **degrees** while the formula works in radians; mixing them yields longitudes near −4300°.

Confidence: FDCF has no FIRMS-style confidence category. `DQF` maps to the vocabulary the layer already understands (`h`/`n`/`l`), documented as a DQF-derived tier. The string form matters — `src/data/firmsAdapt.js` interprets numeric confidence as the MODIS 0–100 scale and would divide a 0–1 value by 100.

## Client wiring

`createFirmsSource` falls back to `/api/goes-fires` **only** when `/api/firms` answers `503 no_key`, so a genuine FIRMS outage (500/502) is never masked by the fallback. Both providers return the same `fires` row shape, so the adapter, cards, viewport and rendering path are untouched. `getStats()` reports which backend answered via `provider`, and the layer's source label names both.

## Verification

- `node --test src/data/goesFireGrid.test.mjs src/data/goesFiresProxy.test.mjs` — 8/8. The grid test builds a **real HDF5 granule** with `h5wasm` and decodes it end to end, covering fill-vs-value scaling, DQF/mask passthrough, day/night and the scan-angle indexing; the proxy test drives the middleware through list → download → decode → JSON and covers cache hits, partial satellite failure and the 502 path.
- **Live smoke test**: listed and decoded an actual GOES-19 granule (1.78 MB) — **162 detections**, 155 with `DQF == 0`, coordinates landing in southern Brazil/Uruguay. 
- `npm test` — 3430 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
- `npm run check:boundaries` — passed.
- `npm run build` — passed.
- `prettier --check` on the changed files — clean.

## Note on the boundary checker

`h5wasm` must be imported as `h5wasm/node` (the root entry is a browser/MEMFS build that cannot open a real path, and neither build exposes `FS`). The checker required every `external` entry to be an exact dependency name, so it rejected the subpath. It now accepts a declared dependency **or a subpath of one** — the exact specifier still has to be listed so the bundler externalizes it, and the dependency it belongs to must still be declared for that runtime.

## Limitations

- Only the full-disk `FDCF` product; `FDCC` (CONUS) and the mesoscale products are unused.
- GOES coverage stops at the limb — no fires outside the Americas and adjacent oceans.
- Only the newest granule per satellite; no multi-scan temporal compositing or persistence filter.
- `Mask` class semantics are passed through undecoded.

title: feat(air-quality): add the Air quality layer to the Weather group
body:
## What

Adds a keyless **Air quality** layer to the Weather group, with Environment and Climate Change
Canada's AQHI as the first registered provider. Around 134 stations across ECCC's five
administrative zones, on the published 1–10+ health-risk bands, plus a WEATHER panel card showing
the band legend and the worst readings currently in view.

**Coverage is Canada only**, and the provider descriptor, the layer row and the card all say so.

## Why readings aren't just a number

Readings are carried as `{ provider, scale, value, band }`.

Air-quality indices aren't interchangeable. Canada's AQHI runs 1 to 10+ on health risk; the US AQI
runs 0 to 500 on concentration breakpoints; Europe's EAQI is a five-step category. There's no
shared numeric meaning to collapse them into, so a reading names the index it belongs to and the
band it falls in. `AIR_QUALITY_PROVIDERS` is the seam a second network registers against without
anything having to be retrofitted.

## The details worth reviewing

**AQHI is a published index, not a measurement.** ECCC reports whole numbers from 1, with anything
above ten as the open-ended "10+". The API hands you the underlying decimal — 1.08, 2.32 — and
publishing that as-is would invent a precision the index doesn't claim. Writing the rounding
surfaced a related trap: `Number(null)` and `Number('')` are both `0`, which floors to a confident
**AQHI 1** for a station that reported nothing at all. The empty forms are guarded before any
coercion, with a test.

**The station catalog is load-bearing.** It's the only thing that supplies a reading its
coordinates, so observations are joined against it rather than trusted to be placeable. That also
sets the cadence: the catalog changes a few times a year and is cached twelve hours, while readings
poll every twenty minutes against an hourly publication. The observations query uses `latest=true`
— without it the collection returns the full history, roughly 2,000 rows nationally. An empty
catalog refresh can't blank a good one, and readings older than six hours are dropped rather than
shown as current.

**Late responses can't redraw.** `update()` aborts any in-flight request, passes the signal to the
source, and refuses to touch the scene if the request was superseded, aborted, or the layer was
disabled while it was outstanding.

## Coverage caveat

**Quebec is thinly represented, and that's upstream rather than anything this layer does.** The
province runs its own Info-Smog program, so only a handful of Quebec stations appear in ECCC's
national feed. The reporting count also drifts hour to hour as stations report or fall silent — a
live run returned 123 across four of the five zones. Documented in `DATA_SOURCES.md` so the gap
doesn't read as a bug.

## Verification and budgets

- `npm test` green on Node 24.14.0 and 26.8.2 (allocation gate enforced on 24.14.0)
- `npm run build`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries` all clean
- `npm run test:track` 109 passed, 0 failed
- `node scripts/qa-air-quality.mjs` — 6 passed, 0 failed live: 123 stations, four ECCC zones,
  provider-shaped records, and the readout list populated with the camera over Canada
- 33 unit tests across the model and the layer's ownership/lifecycle

The station cohort is registered in the overlay allocation gate, re-measured against the current
worker: median 3,900 B/frame, max 4,114, and 85.7 B/candidate at the ceiling — inside the shared
154 B/candidate bound, so no per-source exception. The 5,200 frame budget leaves 26% headroom.
Measured standalone rather than stacked on the Phase-5 host, following the submarine-cable
precedent.

## Licensing

ECCC Data Servers End-use Licence — open, attribution required, no endorsement implied. Registered
in `dataCredits.js` and documented in `DATA_SOURCES.md`.

The share-link token is `0`, which is what `layer-token:next` allocates against the current
ledger. Taking it moves the ledger fixtures that had hard-coded `0` as the free digit and `3` as
the one after; those shift to `3` and `4`. The pinned equality between the reservation ledger and
`LEGACY_LAYER_STATE_TOKENS` becomes "the closed legacy set plus `air-quality`", since that set is
documented as never growing. Happy to re-pin it differently if the fixtures should instead derive
their provisional digits from `nextLayerStateToken()`.

Freshness is judged on observation time rather than receipt time: `getStats()` reports `observedAt`
and `stale` alongside `lastUpdate`, so `layerFeedState()` reports the layer stale past two missed
hourly publications instead of letting the HUD and voice describe hours-old readings as live.

title: Google Earth Pro EOL opportunity: evolve God's Eye View into a native, local-first geospatial workstation
body:
## Context

Google has announced that **Google Earth Pro will no longer be available for new downloads beginning June 25, 2027**. Existing installations may continue to run, but the desktop product is now clearly entering a legacy/distribution-sunset phase while Google directs users toward Earth on web and mobile.

That creates a concrete opportunity for God's Eye View.

God's Eye View already has the hard part that makes this interesting: a capable globe, live/public data layers, real-time feeds, AI/voice interaction, and an open-source codebase that can be extended instead of waiting on a vendor roadmap.

This issue proposes treating the Google Earth Pro sunset as a strategic feature opportunity: evolve God's Eye View toward a **native/local-first desktop geospatial workstation**, rather than merely another browser-based globe.

## Problem

Google Earth Pro historically behaved like a workstation tool: installed locally, launched from the OS, worked directly with user files, preserved local places/projects, and could remain in use independently of a constantly changing hosted UI.

A browser-first geospatial application inherits different constraints:

- the browser remains the primary runtime and UX container;
- local files and persistent workspaces are secondary to web application state;
- large local datasets, long-lived caches, filesystem integration and offline workflows are awkward;
- browser lifecycle and security boundaries dictate application behavior;
- the user cannot easily preserve a known-good application version as a durable workstation tool;
- serious Earth/GIS workflows remain fragmented across browser tabs, GIS programs and local utilities.

The opportunity is not to recreate Google Earth Pro line-for-line. The opportunity is to reclaim the **desktop geospatial workstation model** and combine it with the live/intelligence capabilities that already differentiate God's Eye View.

## Proposal

Make **local-first desktop operation** a first-class architectural target.

A future workstation-oriented God's Eye View should aim for:

- an installable desktop application that launches directly from the operating system;
- persistent local projects/workspaces under user control;
- first-class KML/KMZ import/export;
- Earth-style placemarks, folders/layers, paths, polygons and measurement workflows;
- local imagery, terrain, raster, vector and 3D datasets where licensing permits;
- a provider abstraction for remote imagery, terrain, tiles, feeds and APIs instead of hard-wiring the application to one vendor;
- interoperability with open geospatial formats/services such as GeoJSON, GeoTIFF, GeoPackage, WMS/WMTS/TMS and 3D Tiles where practical;
- durable local caches and explicitly supported disconnected/offline operation for user-owned datasets;
- direct filesystem integration and a portable project format;
- existing God's Eye View live layers and future AI/agent/local-model capabilities running on top of the same globe;
- remote/cloud services as optional providers, not as the authority for the user's project state.

## This is not "rewrite Google Earth"

The implementation strategy should be aggressive integration and refactoring, not a ground-up clone.

Mature open components already solve much of the low-level work. Candidates worth evaluating include:

- **Cesium Native** for native geospatial/3D Tiles runtime components;
- **osgEarth** for native terrain/globe/geospatial rendering;
- **GDAL/OGR** for raster/vector interoperability;
- **libkml** or equivalent KML/KMZ support;
- **Open Google Earth Enterprise (OpenGEE)** as an Apache-licensed reference/source for private globe serving, portable datasets and legacy Earth-style backend concepts.

Google open-sourced the Earth Enterprise Fusion/Server/Portable Server stack, but **not** the proprietary Google Earth desktop client. Useful OpenGEE pieces should therefore be mined selectively rather than treated as a codebase that must be inherited wholesale.

## Important boundary

This proposal does **not** mean copying, scraping or redistributing Google's proprietary imagery, historical imagery, Street View data, private protocols or closed-source Earth Pro client code.

The target is the **workstation architecture and workflow**, implemented independently on properly licensed/open components and data providers.

## Suggested phased path

### Phase 1 — Desktop shell and preservation of current functionality

Package the existing application as a self-contained desktop program while preserving the current globe, layers, live feeds and AI functionality.

### Phase 2 — Separate application state from browser state

Move projects, settings, caches, provider configuration and local data behind explicit runtime interfaces so the browser is no longer the architectural authority.

### Phase 3 — Local geospatial workflows

Add persistent projects, KML/KMZ, local raster/vector datasets, folders/layers, paths, polygons, measurement and local cache management.

### Phase 4 — Provider abstraction

Define stable interfaces for imagery, terrain, vector, 3D content and live feeds so remote and local sources are interchangeable providers rather than hard-coded dependencies.

### Phase 5 — Native-core evaluation

Run a focused spike on Cesium Native/osgEarth/GDAL/OpenGEE and determine whether the existing renderer should remain, be wrapped behind an abstraction, or gradually yield to a native geospatial core.

### Phase 6 — God's Eye View differentiation

Keep and expand the features that make this project more than an Earth replacement: live aircraft, ships, satellites, cameras, fires, earthquakes, traffic, voice, AI tools, event streams, agent-generated layers and local-model integrations.

## Research spike before any large rewrite

Before committing to a deep refactor, build a thin prototype and answer:

- Can the current CesiumJS application state/data model be separated cleanly from its browser UI/runtime?
- What percentage of the existing globe/layer model can survive behind a renderer abstraction?
- Can Cesium Native and/or osgEarth reproduce the required camera, terrain, imagery, KML and 3D Tiles behavior without reimplementing fundamentals?
- Which local formats can be supported cheaply through GDAL/OGR?
- What should a portable God's Eye View project/workspace format contain?
- Which parts of OpenGEE are genuinely useful versus archaeological overhead?
- What belongs in the desktop host versus renderer versus server/provider processes?

The output should be an architecture decision record plus a thin working prototype, not a speculative multi-year rewrite plan.

## Initial success criteria

A first workstation milestone is successful when a user can install God's Eye View, launch it without a development toolchain, create and reopen a persistent local project, load a KML/KMZ plus at least one local raster/vector dataset, navigate the globe, use the existing live layers, and retain useful functionality when optional remote providers are unavailable.

The user's project state should remain readable/exportable without requiring a hosted God's Eye View account.

## Why now

Google Earth Pro's June 25, 2027 distribution cutoff creates a clear deadline and a visible user population that still values a serious desktop Earth workflow.

God's Eye View does not need to become a Google Earth clone. It can become the **native, local-first geospatial workstation that Google no longer appears interested in building**.

title: fix(providers): bound the remaining upstream body reads
body:
Six proxied fetches still buffered upstream bodies with no size limit: FIRMS CSV, CelesTrak TLE groups, adsb.lol `/v2/mil` (both the OK and relayed-status paths), TomTom flow tiles, OpenSky `states/all` and adsbdb enrichment lookups. This routes each through the shared capped readers in `src/sources/httpBody.js`, following the pattern #180 established for GBFS.

`readResponseBytesCapped` gains the same optional `signal` as `readResponseTextCapped`, with the same cancel-on-abort plumbing and reader release, so the TomTom tile path can share its route deadline instead of reading `arrayBuffer()` unbounded; the existing GTFS-Realtime caller is unchanged. Caps are bounds sized well above measured payloads, not budgets (FIRMS 64 MiB per source, CelesTrak 16 MiB, OpenSky/adsb.lol/TomTom 8 MiB, adsbdb 1 MiB). Where a route already had a deadline, the same signal now covers the body read; for OpenSky `states/all` that is each 10-second attempt in `fetchOpenSkyStates`. The adsb.lol military poll had no deadline and gains a 12-second one, missing into its existing STALE path.

Deliberately left alone: FIRMS map-key status, the OpenSky token exchange and CCTV media (#26/#28). `traffic-provider` and `firms-provider` now declare `common/http.js` and `src/sources/httpBody.js` in package-boundaries, matching the other groups; the new test is adopted into format-scope in a separate mechanical commit.

Validation: focused reader tests in `src/sources/httpBody.test.mjs` (exact bytes, chunk order, Content-Length rejection without pulling, streaming cap with cancel, exactly-at-cap, abort mid-stream never returns a partial body, pre-aborted signal, non-stream fallback); full unit suite (4,143 tests, 0 failures), formatting, import directions, package boundaries and production build. Run on Node 24.13.1, one patch below the declared `>=24.14.0` engine, so CI on the pinned runtime is the authoritative check.

Noticed while building a similar CesiumJS globe (a weather/storm tracker) and converging on the same capped-read design for its own proxies; this seemed like the useful piece to bring back.

title: Keep your target in view: smooth camera controls and organized data layers
body:
## Explore the map without losing your target
Tilt and north-up used to stop tracking an aircraft or satellite. Both controls now keep the selected target centered while easing into the new angle over 650 ms, preserving camera range. Tilt switches between top-down and oblique views; north-up takes the shortest rotation. Rapid presses reverse a pending tilt, and pressing north-up during a tilt completes both changes.

New navigation, target selection, map gestures, and teardown cancel the transition. Cockpit keeps its existing camera guard.

## A data panel that follows how you explore
The panel now has five clearly labeled sections:

| Section | Layer order |
| --- | --- |
| Movement | Satellites → Live Flights → Military Flights → Live Vessels → Street Traffic → Bike Share |
| Cameras | Cameras → Mapped ALPR Cameras |
| Infrastructure | Mapped Installations → Data Centers → Submarine Cables → Dams |
| Events | Space Missions → Earthquakes → Active Fires |
| Utilities | Directions → Radio |

Readable panel labels replace CCTV, Bikeshare, Datacenters, and provider-heavy names. Source attribution remains in the subtitles, and toggle accessibility labels match the visible names. Presentation order is independent of layer registration; hidden layers stay hidden and unlisted layers remain available under Other layers.

## Validation
- Camera changes: full Node 24 suite, including allocation gates — 3,699 passing and one skipped.
- Final panel changes: 42 focused tests passed; browser inspection confirmed all sections, ordering, and labels.
- Real Cesium Camera/EntityView tests cover moving aircraft, low/high satellites, cancellation, navigation ownership, and rapid button presses.
- Live browser: UITMSAT-2 remained centered and selected through tilt and north-up, including combined commands.
- Final formatting, package-boundary checks, and production build pass.
- GitHub CI verifies the final head on Node 24, Node 26, and Windows onboarding before merge.

title: feat: Nebraska 511 camera pack and an agency-agnostic message-sign layer
body:
## What this is

Two separable contributions from Nebraska 511 (NDOT), on one branch because they share an upstream and an attribution story. Both are **opt-in**: neither loads unless its env flag is set to `1`.

| Commit | What |
|---|---|
| `d69b21a` | Nebraska 511 camera pack, a keyless CCTV pack |
| `8520272` | `message-signs` layer, NDOT as its first pack |
| `49548aa` | Sign-face images served from the app origin |
| `7069d83` | Per-sign attribution; no agency named in the layer |
| `f3cead1` | Format-scope adoption — mechanical only, per CODE-BOUNDARIES |
| `f95ad16` | Token-ledger fixtures carried across the reserved digit |
| `856b7bb` | Bounded proxy reads; media type from the body, not the extension |
| `c611bd6` | A sign retired upstream clears; a failed refresh keeps the last good list |
| `f928bbd` | Merge of upstream `8b8ccc9` |
| `d5f378f` | Merge of upstream `713285b`; share-link token `5`, i18n for the sign layer, pins re-derived |
| `677a20d` | Road headings keyed by camera position; `loadRoadHeadings()` reads from `sourceRoot` |
| `279806d` | Both packs opt-in (`CCTV_NE511_ENABLED`, `SIGNS_NE511_ENABLED`) |
| `2f95dc3` | `dataCredits` entries; changelog moved to `changelog.d/584-nebraska-511.md` |
| `2ab3c1f` | Merge of upstream `2dca762`; zh-CN strings; voice entry fitted to the prompt budget |
| `d7a9611` | Merge of upstream `a7fcb3c` |
| `1060dbc` | Merge of upstream `0d1a681`; share-link token `6`; sign-layer strings for the new locales |

### 1. Nebraska 511 camera pack

NDOT highway cameras statewide, enabled with `CCTV_NE511_ENABLED=1`. One keyless POST to the CARS-X GraphQL endpoint behind the 511 site (`mapFeaturesQuery`, `layerSlugs: ["normalCameras"]`), at a zoom past the server's clustering threshold — at the site's own statewide zoom, dense areas collapse into `Cluster` entries that carry no camera.

- A mast may expose several angles sharing one position; the first usable view wins, as with Ontario 511.
- Frame URLs are validated against `dot511.nebraska.gov/images/` rather than trusted from the payload, and stripped of their `?<epoch-ms>` cache-buster so each camera registers one stable URL.
- The catalog POST refuses redirects, so the list host cannot be steered, and the response body is read under a cap.
- Anchors are spaced along the I-80 corridor rather than on metro cores. Anchors only *order* a pack and `cap.js` thins from the end of that order, so corridor spacing keeps a thinned catalog statewide instead of collapsing onto Omaha.

**Headings.** NDOT publishes no camera bearing, and the titles are positional ("I-80: Scale E of Lincoln" is where the camera sits, not where it looks), so a title-derived facing would aim most cones wrongly.

`scripts/precompute-ne511-headings.mjs` resolves each camera position against OSM road geometry offline and writes the road axis there to a table keyed by position (lat/lon to 5 decimals), so it survives NDOT renumbering its camera ids. `server/providers/cctv/headings.js` joins it at load from `sourceRoot` and resolves which way along the axis each camera looks: a travel bearing in the title picks that end, otherwise the id-hash prior picks the nearer one, so co-sited masts still fan apart. The committed table holds 341 positions and matches **330 of the 335 live cameras**; the other five keep their id-hash prior until the table is regenerated.

A road axis fixes the line a camera looks along but not which way down it, so `headingConfidence` stays `low`, and the camera keeps the HUD `(ESTIMATED)` tag and dashed coverage wireframe.

The table is OSM-derived and therefore **ODbL**; it is listed in `DATA_SOURCES.md` under the existing share-alike section alongside the datacenter/dam extracts and the Warendorf pack's OSM-derived pose.

### 2. `message-signs` layer

Live electronic message signs rendered as readable board faces rather than markers. Agency-agnostic in the shape the CCTV provider uses: one layer, N packs under `server/providers/messageSigns.js`, each opt-in through its own env flag. Nebraska 511 is the first pack (`SIGNS_NE511_ENABLED=1`). With no pack enabled, `/api/signs` answers `503 {code: 'no-packs'}` and the layer row says no sign packs are enabled, pointing at `.env.example`. The layer names no agency in its labels, errors or links — each record carries the provider and licence of the agency that published it, and the readout and entity context attribute that.

The route is server-side by necessity: the upstream POST answers `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, but its JSON content type forces a CORS preflight, and the OPTIONS request is served by the SPA's S3 host as HTML with no CORS headers, so the browser cannot call it directly. `/api/signs` caches 60 s and reads the upstream body under a cap. Each pack reports success or failure explicitly rather than through an empty list: a pack that answers replaces its own signs, including with none, so a sign retired upstream leaves the board; a pack that fails keeps its last good list; a pack that fails with no prior list contributes nothing.

Sign-face images are proxied too. The vendor bucket sends no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` and labels the PNG `application/octet-stream`, so a cross-origin texture load fails and the board renders blank. `/api/signs/image` resolves the upstream from the cached catalog by sign id and page index — only registered URLs are fetched — and the vendor URL never reaches the browser.

The served media type comes from the response body's leading bytes rather than from the registered URL's extension: a body matching no image signature returns 502 instead of being relabelled as a sign face. The read is bounded as it happens — a declared `Content-Length` over the cap is refused before the body is touched, and a chunked body is cancelled once it crosses the cap.

**Orientation is the part worth reviewing.** Sign titles carry a true travel bearing, so unlike the camera titles these are high-confidence. The board's *face* points the **reverse** of that bearing: a sign addresses oncoming traffic, so facing it along the direction of travel would show its back to every driver reading it. The face is a plane rather than a billboard so it cannot swivel to the camera and be read from the wrong side; Cesium planes are double-sided and render the text mirrored from behind, so an opaque housing panel occludes it. `fromDegrees` takes an ellipsoidal height, so the board stands at the resolved ground floor plus its mount height, and the face stays hidden until that floor is warm while a board glyph carries the sign.

Layer id `message-signs`, grouped under **Utilities** beside `directions` in the layer panel, with its name in `LAYER_NAME_KEYS` and its UI strings marked for translation (de, es, fr, it, ja, pt, ru, uk, zh-CN, zh-Hant). Its share-link token `6` was allocated with `npm run layer-token:next` against current `main` and recorded in the reservation ledger; `npm run layer-token:check -- --base-ref upstream/main` reports `32 published, 1 new`. The layer-state and catalog layer-count guards move 32 → 33 and 33 → 34.

The layer is registered in `CATALOG_SOURCE_CONTRACTS`, so with no signs source configured it reports unavailable like any other optional source. Its voice manifest entry is context-only: voice reads a selected or pointed-at sign through `get_entity_context`, and the layer is toggled from the panel. That keeps the Realtime prompt at 51,982 characters, under the 52,000 budget in `pointAndAsk.test.mjs`; the only change to the tool definitions is `message-signs` in the `get_entity_context` layer enum, and the voice tool-schema pins are re-derived for it.

## Note on the catalog cap

`main` already exceeds the 4,000 CCTV ceiling without this pack, so with `CCTV_NE511_ENABLED=1` round-robin thinning applies to Nebraska as well; observed on a dev server on `1060dbc`, it served 242 of 335. This PR leaves `DEFAULT_CCTV_MAX_SOURCES` unchanged; `CCTV_MAX_SOURCES` raises the ceiling.

## Verification

On `1060dbc`, against upstream `0d1a681`:

- `npm test`: **9,192 tests, 9,191 pass, 0 fail, 1 skip.**
- `npm run test:track`: **109 passed, 0 failed.**
- `npm run build`, `npm run format:check` (1,541 files), `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run i18n` (all ten locales complete), `npm run layer-token:check` — all green.

Live, on a dev server on `1060dbc`:

- Defaults: the Nebraska pack does not load; `/api/signs` answers 503.
- Both flags set to `1`: 16 signs; Nebraska serves 242 of 335 cameras under the shared cap.

From `c611bd6` (code paths unchanged since):

- **Frames through the proxy**: Nebraska frames return real `image/jpeg`. The sign face returns `200 image/png`, 336×96, media type derived from the body's signature; unknown sign id and out-of-range page both 404.
- **Bounded reads** carry regression cases for both oversize shapes the proxy can meet: a declared `Content-Length` over the cap, asserting the body is cancelled rather than buffered, and a chunked body with no declared length, asserting the read stops near the cap. Signature detection is covered including an HTML error page served from a `.png` URL.
- **Sign cache** regressions: a cached sign disappears when the pack returns a valid empty response, survives an upstream failure, and a failing pack keeps only its own signs while a second pack updates beside it.
- **Browser**: message signs verified head-on and from behind (face readable in front, opaque housing behind), in a top-down view, and via click-to-read. No console errors.

## Terms

NDOT asserts no redistribution licence; its [Policies and Disclaimers](https://dot.nebraska.gov/policies-and-disclaimers/), which the 511 app links as its Terms of Use, carries only a use-at-your-own-risk disclaimer. Its Highway Camera Policy says the images "are for transportation purposes only, unless otherwise approved" and "are not archived". That is why both packs are opt-in, as with the NYC, Lithuania and Florida packs. The frame proxy streams on demand and stores none. `DATA_SOURCES.md` records this and the ODbL heading table, and `dataCredits` credits both packs.

title: Add a Global Meteor Network observatory with 3D trajectories and replay
body:
## Summary

Add an opt-in meteor observatory using Global Meteor Network's public trajectory summaries. Enabling **Events → Meteors · latest batch** opens the observation date, time distribution and bright events to explore. Selecting an event frames its atmospheric path with direction and endpoint-altitude labels, an altitude profile, camera-station evidence and a six-second replay with pause/resume and scrubbing. Other trajectories can be shown as context.

![Meteor observatory and an annotated passage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RyZenoKelb/gods-eye-view/6981cb3fec001ed9e95989a28f083ce28dd626e7/docs/media/meteor-observatory.png)

## Data and integration

- [GMN high-level data](https://globalmeteornetwork.org/data/) is CC BY 4.0. Attribution and source semantics are included in the UI and docs; the parser fixture contains one attributed source row.
- These are processed observations from the latest published batch, with incomplete coverage. Endpoint heights are above the WGS84 ellipsoid. The fitted path and illustrative constant-speed replay do not infer a ground impact or reproduce camera footage. Vertical guides indicate altitude relative to the ellipsoid.
- A keyless, fixed-upstream provider serves development and built preview, with bounded downloads, shared refreshes, six-hour caching and stale-data retention. Initial outages keep the observatory visible with retry instructions; malformed empty batches are rejected. Rendering is capped at 2,000 trajectories.
- The layer starts disabled. Visibility is shareable; the two existing voice layer menus accept `meteors`. Schema pins and catalog counts are updated for that addition. No new voice tool or tracking target kind is introduced.

Details and manual exploration instructions: [`docs/METEORS.md`](https://github.com/RyZenoKelb/gods-eye-view/blob/f4cf3ad67d1fdbc66d9bdae8b327ffb2e70d21bc/docs/METEORS.md).

## Validation

Tested locally on macOS with Node 26.8.2:

- `npm run doctor -- --json`
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries`
- `npm test`: 3,912 passed, 1 skipped. The runner also excludes two Node-24-calibrated allocation microbenchmarks on Node 26; CI's Node 24 job remains responsible for that gate.
- `npm run build`
- `npm run test:track -- --url http://127.0.0.1:4173 --headful`: 109 passed, no failures or skips with the Mac GPU. The headless SwiftShader run completed with 105 passed and four frame-window timeout assertions (23/30 and 27/30 frames); the unchanged suite passes with hardware acceleration.
- `node scripts/qa-meteors.mjs`: loaded 148 real GMN observations; checked overview, endpoint heights, click selection, isolated/context visibility, altitude guides, midpoint scrubbing, playback completion/render-hold release, disable/re-enable cleanup, mobile layout/collapse, first-load failure with visible feedback and successful retry, failed-refresh retention and an empty batch. No page errors.

title: feat(transit): live public-transit vehicles from open GTFS-Realtime feeds
body:
Supersedes #218 by @spcpza, ported onto the current component layout with fixes from review.

Verified before merge: format, package boundaries, unit suite, build, and the browser tracking suite; a browser harness for the change where one applies; adversarial review applied.

Contributor: @spcpza. His original commit is the base of this branch, and his own re-port onto main (2026-09-15, `5b69011`) was consulted while finishing the height work. That port reads every vehicle's surface from the app's shared ground-floor system (`cachedGroundFloor` / `warmGroundFloor` / `GROUND_FLOOR_LIFT_M`) rather than sampling the scene per layer, keeps a vehicle hidden until its cell answers, warms a bounded batch per poll on a timer instead of per frame, and renders at the ellipsoid above the altitude gate. That is the sounder primitive — one floor system for the app, with the rooftop-versus-street question already settled against a datum-correct DEM prior — and this branch's height work was rebuilt on it, replacing a bespoke cell cache, ground prior and rooftop rule written here. Credit for that direction is his.

Future work (not in this PR), both written up in docs/CURRENT-STATE.md:

- Readable route names. The realtime feeds carry only `route_id`; `route_short_name` / `route_long_name` live in each operator's static GTFS `routes.txt`, and headsigns in `trips.txt`. Doing it properly wants a server-side metadata loader beside the transit proxy with fixed registered static sources, bounded indexes built once and persisted, a slow conditional refresh, and a versioned route dictionary the browser caches. Shipped here: ids are never rewritten, and a cut one carries an ellipsis instead of reading as a typo.
- Below-ground rendering. Subway vehicles are drawn on the surface directly above themselves, because the feeds carry no depth and a train nobody can see is not worth drawing; the card says so plainly. Real treatment wants OSM tunnel geometry per city and a ghosted sprite tethered to the surface. The owner recorded it and left it.

Round four and after (2026-09-15). The owner tested round three under FLIR and NVG, and then asked for the design to be taken further: elegant in performance, beautiful on camera, trails with a cache for public transport, Cesium-native, and a core other moving layers can adopt. Codex Astra reviewed the plan (it confirmed the speed fault: a glide started from the drawn position at receipt time but spanned the gap between report times, so with MBTA reporting every ~10 s against a 15 s poll every second glide ran at 1.5x; it rejected a queued-segment patch), then wrote the design, then implemented it in commit-sized passes with adversarial review between them and real-browser harness runs by the integrator.

What this PR now contains beyond the contributor's original port:

- Delayed playback in a contact-agnostic core (`src/data/contactPlayback.js`): each vehicle keeps a typed, bounded fix history and a display clock that runs at one second per second through it, a feed-derived lag behind real time, holding at its newest fix rather than extrapolating and never sprinting to catch up. Marker, course, motion word, card and trail all read the same displayed sample. The clock has an explicit time-offset and seek API so a rewind is a later feature, not a rewrite; flights and vessels are untouched.
- A selected-vehicle trail (`src/data/contactTrailRenderer.js`, `src/layers/transit/trails.js`): the retained history drawn with batched Cesium primitives, clipped at display time so the head is exactly the sprite, faded by age, in the mode colour (white under sensor presets), on the same surface path as the marker.
- Bounded proxy-side history (`server/providers/transitHistory.js`): fifteen minutes and at most 128 fixes per vehicle with hard byte ceilings, MBTA only for now (opt-in per feed), served by a small endpoint that never fetches upstream, so a selected trail survives a browser reload while the server keeps running.
- Scene work bounded to what is visible and moving, an occluder, cached DETECT candidates, holds on the render loop only while something visible moves.
- Sensor presets: white-hot haloed sprites under NVG/FLIR/noir (black-hot inverts), saturated mode colours under CRT, per-mode bracket tiers in every theme, the selected card keeping its mode colour.
- A discriminating browser harness (`scripts/qa-transit.mjs`) that samples postRender frames, reads the real card anchor, and measures fleet budgets at 800 and 3,000 vehicles.

Not built, recorded as follow-ups: curated route display names (lowest priority per the owner), fleet-wide tails, route snapping, a rewind UI, adoption of the playback core by flights and vessels.

Verified at merge (2026-09-15 morning): unit suite 3,896 passing, build clean, format and boundary gates clean, tracking regression 109/109, browser harness keyless 200 pass / 0 fail (13 sensor checks unexercised because the live view offered fewer than six isolated sprites; every judged sprite passed), keyed on Google 3D tiles 198 pass with the per-frame allocation gate as the only failure. Follow-ups recorded: the keyed build's playback sampler still allocates per frame (CPU and frame time stay within budget; the 3,000-vehicle metro view sits at a 27.6 ms frame interval against a 25 ms budget), the shared detection overlay's per-paint allocation, friendlier route names, fleet-wide tails, a rewind UI, and adopting the playback core for vessels and flights.

title: fix(terrain): bound the client terrain-height cache with LRU eviction
body:
## Intent

Bound the in-memory cache in the client terrain-height resolver. It deliberately leaves the **proxy's disk cache** alone — the file header's point 2 discusses that one, and it is a separate concern with its own eviction story.

Reported as #327. That issue names `src/data/terrainHeights.js`, which is now a 10-line re-export shim, so the defect it describes actually lives at `src/services/terrainHeights.js`. That is presumably why it is still open.

## The defect

`src/services/terrainHeights.js` held a module-scoped `Map` with no eviction, so a session retained every coordinate it ever resolved for the lifetime of the page.

The 5-decimal rounding the file header documents makes *repeated visits to one place* share a key, which is why this has not been noticeable — but it does nothing to bound *how many distinct places* a session visits. `groundFloor.js` snapping to its ~111 m grid slows the growth further. Neither bounds it.

Being straightforward about severity: this is slow growth, roughly one ~100-byte entry per distinct cell ever visited, not a dramatic leak. It is unbounded, which is the part worth fixing.

## The change

- `CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES`, defaulting to 20 000 and overridable per instance via `createTerrainHeights({ maxCacheEntries })` — the same injectable-limit shape as `maxBytes` on the GBFS reader, so the bound is testable without minting twenty thousand coordinates.
- Eviction is **least-recently-used**, not insertion-ordered: consumer reads promote their entry. Revisits here are spatial, so the cell the camera is parked on must not be dropped merely for having been resolved early. Plain FIFO would evict exactly the wrong entry.
- Batch results are assembled from what the call resolved, so eviction *during* a large batch cannot report a just-resolved point as `unresolved`. This guards a hazard the bound itself introduces.

The cap is a bound, not a budget: it sits far above a city-scale session, so normal use never evicts and issues no additional proxy requests. Re:Earth vs. geoid-fallback entry semantics, the fallback cooldown, and the abort-time flush are all unchanged.

## Verification

Every gate `CONTRIBUTING.md` names, re-run on the candidate rebased onto `2746ec7` (the original run was on `a8125ad`; `main` moved and the CHANGELOG conflicted, so this is the combined candidate, not just my original head):

```
$ npm run format:check
Checked 851 source files.

$ npm run check:boundaries
Checked transit-service: 1 exports, 8 owned modules.          (all groups pass)

$ npm test
ℹ tests 4029
ℹ pass 4019
ℹ fail 0
ℹ skipped 10

$ npm run build
✓ built in 9.05s

$ npm run test:track        # against npm run dev on :4173
RESULT: 109 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped
```

`test:track` is the one I most wanted green here, since its `display-floor` and corridor groups exercise this resolver directly — including `no console errors across the FULL run` and `no HTTP 5xx responses across the FULL run`.

**The new tests fail on the old implementation.** Three of the four behavioural ones, checked by reverting the source and re-running them:

```
✖ the in-memory cache stops growing once it reaches its entry bound
✖ a coordinate a consumer keeps reading outlives an equally old one it ignores
✖ a batch larger than the cache bound still reports every point it resolved
✔ an out-of-range cache bound falls back to the default instead of disabling the cache
```

The fourth is a guard on the new option rather than a regression test, so it passes either way.

**Declared, not waived:** `npm test` skips 2 allocation microbenchmarks because I am on Node 26.5.0 and the budgets are calibrated for Node 24 — the harness says so itself and it is unrelated to this change. The build's chunk-size warning is pre-existing (#40).

## Out of scope

- The proxy's unbounded **disk** cache, per the intent above.
- While reading neighbouring code I noticed the OpenSky `states/all` fetch (`server/providers/aircraft/opensky.js:473`, and the Basic-auth retry at `:488`) carries no `signal` at all, so a hung connection stalls that poll indefinitely. Left alone here: it is a different defect in a file #581 is already editing, and I have raised it there instead.

> 🤖 Claude Code helped

title: feat(cctv): add the Open Catalonia camera pack
body:
Catalonia (Servei Català de Trànsit) as a keyless CCTV source pack: 135 cameras from one WFS/GML feed (`https://www.gencat.cat/transit/opendata/cameres.xml`) that aggregates SCT's own highway cameras (103) with hotlinked Barcelona (25) and Terrassa (7) municipal cameras. Each partner is named as a `credit` beside the shared provider, under the Llicència oberta d'ús d'informació – Catalunya (attribution required).

SCT's own frame link needed a workaround: `RenderService` 302s to a hardcoded-http `Location` even over https, and separately `mct.gencat.cat`'s TLS fails the handshake with Node's fetch (`ERR_SSL_WRONG_SIGNATURE_TYPE`). The loader therefore builds the working `TransitCamera` URL itself instead of registering the broken upstream link.

### Outbound hosts (server-side only)

| Host | Use | Transport |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `www.gencat.cat` | camera catalog | https, redirects refused, 1 MiB body cap |
| `mct.gencat.cat` | SCT frames | **plain http** (only transport the host serves to Node, see above) |
| `www.bcn.cat` | Barcelona frames | https |
| `emap.terrassa.cat` | Terrassa frames | https |

Frame URLs come only from the catalog and are checked against this host allowlist; links carrying `user:pass@` userinfo are rejected even on an allowed host. Frames are fetched at request time and never stored. `CCTV_CATALONIA_ENABLED=0` disables the pack and `CCTV_CATALONIA_MAX_SOURCES` caps it.

### Known limitation

The feed has no camera status field, so an offline camera stays registered and shows its publisher's own "image unavailable" still (SCT and Barcelona both answer HTTP 200 with one). On 2026-10-12, 42 of 135 cameras were serving that still. This matches the other packs that have no status field, and it is documented in DATA_SOURCES.md.

### Validation (head `492ecb4`, Node 24, macOS)

- `npm run doctor -- --json` ready · `npm run format:check` · `npm run check:boundaries`: pass
- `npm test`: 6251 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped (includes `src/data/cctvCataloniaSource.test.mjs`, fixture-based and keyless)
- `npm run build`: pass
- `npm run test:track` against a dev server of this branch: 109/109
- Feature gate `node scripts/qa-cctv-v2.mjs`: 52 passed, 0 failed, 1 inconclusive (headless GL geometry-load drain: needs headful evidence, independent of this pack)
- Live check through the dev proxy: `/api/cctv/sources` returns 135 Catalonia cameras, and all 135 `/api/cctv/frame/<id>` requests return `200 image/*` (93 live frames plus the 42 publisher stills above)

Docs: `CHANGELOG.md` (Unreleased), `DATA_SOURCES.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`, README CCTV row, `.env.example`.
