title: fix(traffic): say which upstream declined a road load
body:
Refs #661 — deliberately not `Fixes`. This addresses the reporting half of that issue and leaves the fallback half open, so the issue should stay open after this merges.

## Changes

Street Traffic has two upstreams: OpenStreetMap for road geometry and TomTom for flow. When the road load failed, the row said `Road data temporarily unavailable` no matter what happened, so there was nothing in it to tell the two apart. The reporter of #661 checked their TomTom status endpoint and a live flow tile, both healthy, while the actual failure was the public Overpass mirrors declining their network with HTTP 406 — a status the code already had in hand and threw away at `src/layers/traffic/ingestion.js:70`.

- `roadRequestError(status)` in `src/layers/traffic/source.js` maps a refusal to the line the panel prints: `Overpass rate-limited` (429), `Overpass timed out` (504), or `Overpass refused the road query (HTTP <status>)`. A refusal whose code is unreadable — the layer takes its source by injection, so an adapter may not supply one — says `Overpass temporarily unavailable` rather than printing `HTTP undefined`. The first two are the words `alpr`'s Overpass source already uses — this is the existing vocabulary, not a new one. What the status adds is *which* upstream declined and *how*, which a single-source layer never needs to say.
- The thrown error is a `RoadRequestError` carrying `status` beside the message, following `LiveSourceError` in `src/sources/live/contract.js`, so a caller can branch on the code without parsing English.
- The catch in `loadRoadsForBounds` promotes a classified refusal and keeps `Road data temporarily unavailable` for everything else. That branch is on the error type, not on the text: a dropped socket throws whatever the platform felt like saying, and `Failed to fetch` on a panel row helps nobody.

Nothing about retries, backoff, caching or the mirror rotation changes. The proxy already rotates all four mirrors and only surfaces a refusal once none of them answered, so a status arriving in the browser means the proxy had nothing better to offer.

## How it was verified

Same fault, same instrument, once per side. The 406 is injected at the network boundary rather than waited for: the mirrors that refused my network on 18 September answer it again today, and a transient upstream ban is not something a reviewer can reproduce on demand. Everything below the injection point is the real stack — proxy, source, ingestion, controls, panel.

| | row rendered in the browser |
|---|---|
| before | `UNAVAILABLE · OpenStreetMap · Road data temporarily unavailable` |
| after | `UNAVAILABLE · OpenStreetMap · Overpass refused the road query (HTTP 406)` |

Read out of the DOM, not out of `getStats()`, because the claim is about what a person sees. At 420px the row wraps and the page does not scroll horizontally.

Before injecting anything I checked the premise the issue rests on: `overpass-api.de` and `lz4.overpass-api.de` returned 406 to this network for the application's User-Agent, for curl's default, and for a browser User-Agent alike, while `overpass.kumi.systems` and `overpass.private.coffee` timed out. So the refusal is not something the `OVERPASS_USER_AGENT` header provokes, and there was no header fix hiding here.

Tests:

- `navigation.test.mjs` drives the assembled layer with a source returning `{ok: false, status}` and asserts the row text for 406 and 429, plus a companion test that a plain thrown `Error` still yields the general line. Reinstating the old assignment turns the first red and leaves the second green, so it is the behaviour that is pinned and not the presence of a string.
- `source.test.mjs` covers the mapping, that `status` survives on the error object, and that an absent or unreadable code never reaches a row as `HTTP undefined`.

Gates on Node 24.14.0: `npm run build`, `npm test` (4148 tests, 0 failures, 1 pre-existing skip), `npm run test:track`, plus `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries`. The diff adds no console calls: the existing `[Data:Traffic] Fetch error:` warning still carries the underlying error object, unchanged.

## What this does not do

#661 also asks for a cached or local road snapshot so valid TomTom flow can still be drawn when Overpass is unreachable. That is a feature with its own design questions — which snapshot, how stale is too stale, what the row says while it is being used — and I have left it alone rather than smuggle it in behind a message change. This PR only makes the failure legible.

title: fix(cctv): aim the Street View fallback at the registered camera and meter it
body: Fixes #20. ## Changes `/api/cctv/frame/:id` degrades upstream snapshot → Street View → synthetic card. Only the middle step leaves the machine on a metered account: Street View Static bills the operator's own Google key per image. That step read `lat`/`lon` off the query string, ran for any camera id whether or not the catalog served it, and nothing counted the calls. Two things followed from that, both reproducible in one request: - an id the catalog never served still bought a lookup — `GET /api/cctv/frame/no-such-camera?lat=…&lon=…` returned a Street View frame; - a *registered* id could be aimed anywhere. `/api/cctv/frame/tln-103?lat=48.8584&lon=2.2945` asked Google for the Eiffel Tower while `tln-103` is a Tallinn camera at `59.436563, 24.752702`. That makes a registered camera a general-purpose geocoding lookup on someone else's key. Neither path had a ceiling. SECURITY.md already states the invariant this sits under — *"the CCTV frame proxy fetches only server-registered camera/frame URLs — clients cannot pass an upstream URL to fetch"* — and CONTRIBUTING repeats it for source packs. The Street View branch honoured it for the *URL* and not for the *destination*: the URL was fixed, but the client chose which place on Earth it returned a photograph of. This change makes the documented guarantee true for that branch too. I have left SECURITY.md's wording alone rather than edit a file thirteen open PRs are touching; say the word if you would like the bullet extended. - `resolveStreetViewTarget(source)` in the new `server/providers/cctv/streetview.js` resolves the billable target from the **registered record**. The browser still sends `lat`/`lon` on every frame, but `frameUrlFor` in `src/layers/cctv/source.js` copies them off the camera record it got from `/api/cctv/sources`, so they were always a restatement of what the server already holds — which is what makes them safe to stop honouring. An unregistered id resolves to nothing, and so does a pose that is absent, non-numeric or off-globe. `Number(null)` is `0`, so "absent" is checked before coercion rather than after; otherwise a catalog row with no position buys a frame of the Gulf of Guinea. - Admission is metered per client with `makeRateLimiter` and `clientKey`, the same primitives `military-installations` and `places/routes` use. The cap is 240/min per IP with a 720 aggregate backstop, sized from the layer's own demand rather than from a round number: the ambient card drain is capped at 16 cameras (`CCTV_AMBIENT_CARD_DRAIN_CAP`) and an active card re-requests every `ACTIVE_FRAME_REFRESH_MS` (10s), so one viewer whose cameras have all lost their upstreams legitimately sits at 96 fallback frames a minute. The 90/min used by the Overpass-backed routes would have cut into normal use here. - `heading` now wraps into `[0, 360)` beside the existing `fov` and `pitch` clamps, because a bearing is periodic — 400 is 40, not "too far north". A refused lookup returns the synthetic card the route already serves when no frame is available, not a 429: the response goes into an ``, which has no way to render a status code. The upstream-snapshot and synthetic steps are untouched, and a frame for a registered camera is byte-for-byte what it was. A refusal is deliberately not logged. The one situation that reaches the cap in volume is the abuse loop, so a line per refusal would turn a flood into log spam on the operator's own terminal; the health map already reports the camera as `degraded`, which is the signal the panel reads. Happy to add a rate-limited warning line if you would rather have it. ## How it was verified Same probe, same instrument, once per side, driving the real exported `cctvProxy()` handler — the catalog, the fallback chain and the SVG exit are the shipped code. Only `globalThis.fetch` is intercepted, at the network boundary, so the probe never spends a real lookup; `GOOGLE_MAPS_SERVER_API_KEY` is set to a dummy value so the fallback is reached at all. | | `before` (`0d41b6b`) | `after` | |---|---|---| | unknown id + client coordinates | served `streetview`, **1** billable call | served `synthetic`, **0** | | 300 such requests | **300** billable calls | **0** | | registered `tln-103`, upstream down, request carrying `lat=48.8584&lon=2.2945` | served `streetview`, Google asked for **`48.8584,2.2945`** | served `streetview`, Google asked for **`59.436563,24.752702`** | The third row is the regression check that mattered most: the fallback still works for a real camera, and it is the catalog's coordinates that reach Google. `src/data/cctvStreetViewQuota.test.mjs` covers the decision surface — unregistered id, absent/non-numeric/off-globe pose, the `Number(null) === 0` case, bearing wrap, the per-IP window, the global backstop, and that a capped caller does not consume another caller's quota. Mutation-checked rather than assumed: removing the unregistered-camera guard, removing the coordinate bounds, and lowering the cap to 90 each turn exactly one test red, and restoring each returns 11/11. One thing worth stating plainly, because it shaped the verification: an early revision used `normalizeHeadingDeg` in `cctv.js` without adding it to the import. Every unit test stayed green — they exercise `streetview.js` directly — and `streetViewFallback`'s `catch` swallowed the `ReferenceError` into a `null`, silently demoting every registered camera to the synthetic card. Only the route-level probe caught it. The committed tests cover the pure decision surface, matching how this repo already tests `media.js`; the integration claim rests on the probe above. Gates on Node 24.14.0 with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1`: `npm run doctor`, `npm run format:check` (918 files), `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`, `npm test` (4170 tests, 0 failures, 1 pre-existing Windows-only skip; both allocation microbenchmarks ran), and `npm run test:track`. Per CONTRIBUTING rule 3, `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` both record the behaviour change; the `CURRENT-STATE` paragraph sits in **Places and CCTV request bounds**, beside the existing note that Places rejects out-of-range coordinates before its limiter. `scripts/qa-cctv-v2.mjs`, the CCTV v2 subsystem harness, run on this branch and on `0d41b6b` for comparison: **48 passed / 0 failed** here against **47 passed / 1 failed** on main. The five `INCONCLUSIVE` results are identical on both sides — they need an on-screen gizmo arrow this GL stack does not produce, headless or headful — and main's one failure is the tiles-load-timing ground-sample check, which is network-dependent; I am not claiming this PR fixed it. Its "no console errors during CCTV v2 exercise" check reports clean, which is the rule-2 requirement. ## What this does not do `heading`, `fov` and `pitch` are still taken from the query string. That is deliberate, and it is the one part of the issue's first bullet this PR does not close literally. They are a genuine refinement rather than a restatement — `src/layers/cctv/source.js` sends `camera.pitchDeg || -10`, so a catalog row with no pitch gets a sensible default from the client — and pinning them to the catalog would change what real frames look like. They cannot choose a location, cannot change what a call costs, and are each bounded before the request. If you would rather the pose came from the catalog too, say so and I will follow up; I did not want to change rendered output inside a security fix. #29 and #22, from the same review, are untouched: SSRF hardening for server-registered CCTV URLs and preview-server exposure of key-bearing routes are separate problems in separate code paths, and folding them in here would make one change impossible to review. --- **Re-validated after updating the branch.** Merged `main` (`81eb443`) in at `8c495132` — clean, nothing to hand-resolve. The validation above predates that merge, so on the merged tree (Node 24.20.0, Linux aarch64): `doctor` · `format:check` · `check:boundaries` · `build` all exit 0 · `npm test` with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1` **5,086 pass / 1 skipped / 0 fail** of 5,087, and the 1 and 13 allocation budgets green. `npm run layer-token:check -- --base-ref main` → `28 published, 0 new`. That one is new: #744 added it to CI after the checks recorded above this line, so this is the first time the branch has been measured against it. The branch shares no source file with #744 — the overlap is documentation and `scripts/format-scope.json`, which merged cleanly. Browser-driven gates were not re-run for the merge itself, since what the merge brings in is confined to the share-link token ledger.

title: feat(overpass): support self-hosted endpoints via OVERPASS_EXTRA_UPSTREAMS (#648)
body:
> **Draft:** the code, tests and docs are complete, but I have not yet confirmed dots on screen end to end against a freshly imported local instance. Marking ready once that passes.

## Why

Closes the operator half of #648. The overpass-api.de maintainers report this app consuming ~20,000 CPU-seconds in 24h against a fair share of ~300, and asked heavy consumers to run their own instance rather than rotate through the remaining free ones. Today there is no way to do that short of editing `server/providers/overpass/constants.js`, so a user's practical options are "keep hammering a shared mirror" or "the Overpass-backed layers are broken". Every one of them — Street Traffic, Mapped Installations, the OSM webcam pack — needs Overpass geometry before it can render anything, so this is not a niche path.

This does not itself solve #648 (that wants planet dumps / vector tiles). It gives the people who are ready to self-host today a supported way to, and it makes the recommendation in that thread actionable.

## What

**`OVERPASS_EXTRA_UPSTREAMS`** — one or more endpoints, whitespace- or comma-separated, tried **before** the built-in list. Built-ins remain as fallback.

Extras go first deliberately: an endpoint someone configured is a better first try than one that just timed out for them, and each dead built-in costs a full `OVERPASS_TIMEOUT_MS` before the chain advances. Resolution is lazy and memoised on the raw env string — module evaluation happens before the dev server copies `.env` into `process.env`, so reading it at module scope always sees `undefined`.

Structural URL validation only. A localhost or RFC1918 address is *allowed* here, unlike `osmWebcamStillUrl` whose input is a world-editable OSM tag; this value comes from the operator's own environment, where a private instance is the entire point.

**The regional-extract hazard.** This is the part worth reviewing closely. An instance built from a state or country extract answers HTTP 200 quickly for queries anywhere on Earth, returning an empty element list outside its own region. Left alone the proxy caches that as a valid answer for 7 days, silently pinning every Overpass-backed layer to "no roads here" over regions that have plenty — it fails quietly, which is the worst shape. So an empty answer from a *configured* endpoint is treated as that endpoint declining: rotate to the next, and if nothing answers, surface a visible failure. Built-in planet mirrors keep the original semantics, where empty can legitimately be the truth.

The emptiness check is substring-first so multi-MB payloads are never parsed just to learn they are non-empty, and an unparseable body is explicitly *not* called empty — an unknown shape is the caller's problem, not grounds for rotating off a healthy endpoint.

**Test fix.** `coalesced outage callers both receive last-good data` asserted `fetches === 4`, a hardcoded mirror count that any operator with their own endpoint would fail. It now counts the resolved chain; the invariant under test is one shared sequence per outage, not how many mirrors exist.

## Ships with

- **`docker-compose.overpass.yml`** — parameterised by `OVERPASS_PLANET_URL`, defaulting to a single US state: small enough to prove the setup works before committing to a continent. Note `OVERPASS_PLANET_PREPROCESS`: Geofabrik no longer publishes `.osm.bz2` for US extracts and this image expects bz2, so the `.pbf` is converted in place with `osmium cat`. That line is load-bearing, not boilerplate.
- **`docs/SELF-HOSTED-OVERPASS.md`** — prerequisites, verification, region-switching, troubleshooting, and measured disk/time per region:

| Region | Download | Disk after import | Import time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Washington state | 0.3 GB | ~2 GB | ~15 min |
| California | 1.2 GB | ~7 GB | ~45 min |
| Great Britain | 2.0 GB | ~12 GB | ~1 hr |
| United States | 11.3 GB | ~60 GB | ~6 hr |
| North America | 18.1 GB | ~85 GB | ~8–12 hr |
| Europe | 32.6 GB | ~150 GB | ~16–24 hr |
| Planet | 88.3 GB | ~400 GB | multiple days |

Downloads are measured from Geofabrik/planet.osm.org; disk and time are estimates that scale with storage speed, and assume `OVERPASS_META: 'no'` as shipped. Because traffic only activates below `ACTIVATION_ALTITUDE` (8 km), coverage only needs to include the places a user actually descends into — starting regional and re-importing larger later costs one extra download and nothing else.

## Credit

The `OVERPASS_EXTRA_UPSTREAMS` idea and its parser are from @Schnix84's #104, which was closed pending a maintainer batch. That PR predates the `vite.config.js` → `server/providers/overpass/` split, so this is a port to the current layout rather than a rebase, plus the regional-extract handling and the compose/docs.

## Testing

- 7 new tests in `src/data/overpassUpstreams.test.mjs`: parsing, ordering, dedup, private-address allowance, empty-rotates-for-extras, and empty-is-still-data for built-ins
- `src/overpassProxy.test.mjs` 11/11
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries` clean
- No behaviour change when `OVERPASS_EXTRA_UPSTREAMS` is unset: the resolved chain is exactly the current built-in list

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: feat: vessel voyage intelligence (history, screening, reckoning, narrative) + local LLM support
body:
Two independent features. They share no code, so if only one is wanted the other can be dropped — happy to split into separate PRs on request.

Everything below was measured against the live AISStream feed, not assumed.

---

## 1. Vessel intelligence

The AIS pipeline was discarding most of what the feed already carried, and kept nothing across restarts. A vessel was a position, a name and a speed; the moment it stopped transmitting it vanished.

**Extraction.** `ShipStaticData` was parsed for four fields and the rest thrown away. Now also draught, ETA, call sign, hull dimensions and navigational status. On a live 6,250-vessel sample: nav status on 3,618, dimensions on 859, draught on 624, ETA on 540.

**Durable history** (`ais-history.js`, opt-in via `GEV_AIS_HISTORY`, default off). SQLite through `node:sqlite` — no new dependency. Batched transactions; voyage rows written only when intent changes rather than on every rebroadcast. It also seeds a cold cache: static reports arrive only every few minutes, so after a restart thousands of hulls were known by position alone while the database already described them.

**Load state.** Draught is the only cargo signal AIS carries, and it only speaks once the same hull has been seen both deep and shallow. `LADEN`/`BALLAST` stays `UNKNOWN` until the observed range exceeds 0.5 m.

**Sanctions screening** (`ais-sanctions.js`). OFAC SDN — public domain, keyless, 1,540 vessel entries, cached to disk and refreshed daily. `sanctioned` requires identity-grade evidence: a checksum-valid IMO or a call sign. An early build matched on name and flagged **40 of 3,213 vessels, every one a false positive** — a German pleasure craft named LISBOA matched a Panamanian tanker on the Iran list. Name collisions now surface as `possibleNameMatch` for a human to judge, never as a verdict.

**Identity** (`ais-identity.js`). Flag state from the ITU MID table and IMO check digits, both computed offline, so every contact carries them. Prefix rules are respected — an aid-to-navigation MMSI carries its MID at digits 3–5, not 0–2.

**Dead reckoning** (`ais-reckoning.js`). Hulls persist across AIS gaps instead of vanishing, projected along a great circle with confidence decaying to zero at 12 h. Moored, anchored and sub-0.5 kt vessels hold position. The live feed doubles as a coverage map: silence in a cell still delivering other traffic is `DARK`; silence where nothing reports is a coverage `GAP`.

**Plain-language narrative** (`ais-narrative.js`, `ais-cargo.js`, `ais-locode.js`, `ais-origin.js`). Every clause is graded. Cargo separates what the ship *declares* (IMO hazard category in the AIS type code — 661 vessels live) from what a single-commodity terminal *implies* from what only the hull class supports. Origin is reconstructed from the app's own track and says plainly when it observed nothing.

**Also:** search across the whole server cache with a fallback to persisted identities; durable trails replacing the process-local ring buffer; camera follow on `F` (vessels are billboard primitives, so this pins an invisible entity to the hull's live position and tracks that).

**Optional partner feeds** (`ais-partners.js`): Global Fishing Watch (AIS-off events) and BarentsWatch. Both inert without credentials; neither can degrade the vessel feed. GFW is non-commercial-use-only per their terms.

### Bugs the tests caught while being written

- `Number(null)` is `0`, so a course-less hull was projected **due north**, and a speed-less position report read as a vessel sitting still — inventing port calls out of missing data.
- `readTrack(limit: 1)` orders ascending for path drawing, so it returned the **oldest** fix where "last seen" was meant.
- An absent ship type was reported as *"not a cargo-carrying type, so nothing to carry"* — an assertion the evidence did not support.

---

## 2. Local LLM (Ollama / llama.cpp)

Every AI feature required an OpenAI key and metered spend. `GEV_LLM_PROVIDER` selects `openai` (default, unchanged), `ollama` or `llamacpp`. Both local options speak the OpenAI-compatible chat-completions dialect, so this is base-URL/model/auth indirection rather than a second client. Leaving the variable unset preserves today's behaviour exactly.

`/api/llm/status` reports the configured provider, reachability and available models (Ollama `/api/tags`, llama.cpp `/v1/models`). It only probes loopback, RFC-1918, link-local, ULA or `.local` hosts — anything else is refused rather than turned into a request from the server's network.

Configured in **POWER UP → Provider Settings → TEXT MODEL**. Only changed fields are submitted, so a default never becomes an explicit override.

The HUD summary — the only non-voice LLM consumer in the repo — routes through the abstraction. Local providers are sent **no `Authorization` header**, so an OpenAI key cannot leak to a local server. An unreachable model returns the existing keyless response shape, which the HUD already treats as "show the deterministic line".

**Voice does not work locally, and the UI says so.** GEV MIC uses OpenAI's Realtime *speech* API — an ephemeral secret from `api.openai.com` and a WebRTC session against its calls endpoint. Neither local runtime implements that protocol, so no base-URL swap would make it work and none was added. The 28 voice tools ride the same session.

---

## Verification

Run on a **clean clone of this branch**, not the working directory:

```
npm test                          4,177 passing, 0 failing
node --test server/**/*.test.mjs    141 passing, 0 failing
npm run check:boundaries            PASS
npm run format:check                clean (936 files)
boots keyless with no .env          HTTP 200
```

168 new tests. All network-dependent tests use mocked fetch and pass with nothing running.

New modules are registered in `scripts/package-boundaries.json`. `.env.example`, `README.md` and the docs are updated.

## Things worth pushing back on

Flagging these rather than letting a reviewer find them:

- **`node:sqlite` is experimental** in Node 24 and prints a warning on start. History is opt-in and off by default, so a default install never sees it.
- **Runtime fetch of the OFAC list** adds an external dependency and a `data/` write. It is disable-able via `GEV_SANCTIONS=0`, fails soft, and the cache is gitignored.
- **Hand-curated reference data** — ~150 UN/LOCODE ports, the ITU MID table, port-commodity mappings. Correct as far as tested, but it is data you would be trusting. Unlisted codes degrade to a country rather than a guess.

title: docs(attribution): credit adsbdb and carry its route-data terms
body:
Fixes #256.

## Changes

`api.adsbdb.com` is a live, user-visible source — it supplies the aircraft type, model name and registration on enriched flights, and the airline and origin/destination pair behind the tracked contact's `FROM → TO` strip — and it was registered in neither attribution surface. On `0d41b6b`, `DATA_SOURCES.md` and `src/data/dataCredits.js` each contain **zero** occurrences of `adsbdb`, which is what both files and CONTRIBUTING's fourth pull-request item say must not happen. `adsb.lol` is a different operator; its ODbL credit does not cover this data.

@jsawyerdev left the patch off #256 on purpose — *"I could not verify adsbdb's license or terms, and inventing the required attribution string is precisely the claim that should not be guessed."* That was the right call, so this PR takes the terms from the source instead of inventing them. From the [adsbdb README](https://github.com/mrjackwills/adsbdb):

- aircraft data comes from **PlaneBase**;
- the ICAO-to-N-number conversion is **Guillaume Michel**'s;
- the flight route data *"is the work of David Taylor, Edinburgh and Jim Mason, Glasgow, and may not be copied, published, or incorporated into other databases without the explicit permission of David J Taylor, Edinburgh."*

No licence and no rate limit are published for the service itself, so neither is claimed here.

- **`DATA_SOURCES.md`** — one row in the live-sources table, and a bullet in *Notes on the live sources*. The note records the politeness posture the issue observed was written down nowhere: at most 4 requests in flight, dispatches dripped to roughly 5/s, each key asked at most once per session, route lookups reserved for the tracked aircraft, and a 24-hour per-key disk cache including negative answers. It also records why that cache is safe to keep — `.gev-cache/` is gitignored, so the route data stays on the operator's machine and is never bundled or redistributed, which is what its terms require.
- **`src/data/dataCredits.js`** — the matching `DATA_CREDITS` entry, so the credit reaches the in-app **Data attribution** popover, and the `adsbdb` name added to the enumeration in *In-app attribution* that had listed every other credited source.
- **`src/data/dataCredits.test.mjs`** — new. Pins the adsbdb credit and the route-data restriction, plus a structural check that every entry has a unique key and something to render.
- **`CHANGELOG.md`** — one entry, following #511, the closest precedent here: a documentation-only attribution change that still earned a changelog line.

The test is the part worth arguing for. This attribution is a requirement, not a preference: if a later refactor drops the two names or the restriction, that should fail a gate rather than go unnoticed until someone reads the popover.

## How it was verified

The claim is that the source *surfaces in the app*, so that is what was measured — the real page, not the module.

Loaded the app in Chromium, expanded the **Data attribution** popover and read the rendered line back out of the DOM. It is one of 42 credit lines, and reads:

> Aircraft type, registration & flight routes: adsbdb · aircraft data from PlaneBase · route data is the work of David Taylor, Edinburgh, and Jim Mason, Glasgow, and may not be copied, published, or incorporated into other databases without the explicit permission of David J Taylor, Edinburgh

The `before` side needs no browser: the registry held no `adsbdb` entry at all, so there was nothing for the popover to render.

The new test is mutation-checked rather than assumed green — stripping the restriction from the credit, and renaming the entry's key, each turn it red; restoring returns 2/2.

Gates on Node 24.14.0 with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1`: `npm run doctor`, `npm run format:check` (917 files), `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`, `npm test` (4161 tests, 0 failures, 1 pre-existing Windows-only skip; both allocation microbenchmarks ran) and `npm run test:track`.

## Notes for review

Five judgement calls worth your eye:

- The note says the disk cache holds each key for **24 hours**, which is `TTL_MS = 24 * 3600_000` in `server/providers/aircraft/enrichment.js:11`. `src/layers/flights/policy.js:216` describes that same cache as keeping entries "on disk forever" — the comment predates the TTL. I took the number from the constant and left the comment alone rather than widen this PR into the flights layer, but it is worth a one-line fix by someone.
- This does not collide with #308, which bounds the same cache. That PR adds an entry ceiling and a server-side limiter *on top of* the 24-hour TTL; it does not change the TTL, the 4-concurrent fan-out or the 200 ms drip, so every number written here stays true whichever merges first. Nothing in this PR touches the proxy.
- `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` is deliberately untouched. It already describes the adsbdb middleware, its caching, and the cockpit `FROM → TO` strip in five places; no runtime capability changes here, only the attribution surface. #511 — the documentation-only attribution change this most resembles — touched `CHANGELOG.md` and not `CURRENT-STATE.md`, and that is the shape followed.
- The table row is not padded to the column widths of its neighbours. The table already mixes padded and unpadded rows, and re-aligning it would bury a one-line addition in a whole-table diff.
- `scripts/qa-l9-matrix.mjs`'s C12 credit expectations are untouched. adsbdb enriches the flights layer rather than being a layer of its own, so `flights: /OpenSky/i` still describes that layer's required credit correctly; the adsbdb credit is registered statically and is present regardless of which layers are on.

title: feat: add zh-TW desktop app and Taiwan CCTV
feat: make CCTV discovery follow the map view
body:
## Problem

When the map is centered on Cape Town, the CCTV panel can still show a Vancouver feed and an unsearchable dropdown containing the worldwide catalog. Finding cameras near the area being explored is difficult.

## Changes

- Default to cameras inside the map's geographic view bounds and refresh after map movement ends.
- Add city, camera and provider search, plus an explicit **All cameras** scope.
- Sort results by distance from the map center and show approximate distances.
- Keep panel enable and Previous/Next within the filtered results. Explicit Nearest uses the filtered results when available; when the view contains no cameras it finds the closest camera worldwide by map-center distance, ignoring search, so an empty area can reach coverage.
- Hide an out-of-view active camera's panel preview in local scope and explain missing coverage. Map movement and searching alone do not select a camera or move the globe.
- Translate discovery copy into Spanish and Russian with plural-aware counts and localized numbers.
- Reuse option nodes on distance changes and reordering, including the 4,000-camera worldwide catalog.

Includes date-line handling, listener cleanup, regression coverage, and runtime/changelog documentation. Merged upstream main (`8ed1bbbd`) in `961c878d`, preserving the shared form-field/action-button components alongside map-relative discovery and all Spanish/Russian translations. The shared-control browser fixtures now provide geographic camera records and exercise filtered selection.

Discovery uses the loaded catalog; it does not add sources. Geographic view bounds approximate the visible area rather than testing terrain occlusion. Filters apply to panel controls; voice navigation and layer auto-hop retain their existing catalog-wide contracts, explained in the scope tooltip and documentation. #991 is still open and adds layer-level screen-center nearest selection, navigation history, live playback changes, and an enable-time focus guard. This PR handles panel discovery and empty-view fallback. Both use the viewed location; whichever lands second must reconcile the shared panel bindings/presentation and application-shell changes, preserving #991's focus guard/history alongside this filtered selection and fallback.

## Validation

All passed locally on Node 24.14.0:

- Full unit suite: 8,188 passed, one skipped; both allocation gates passed (1 and 14 checks)
- `npm run build`
- `npm run test:track -- --headful --offline-imagery`: 109 passed, no failures
- `npm run i18n`
- `npm run format:check`
- `npm run check:boundaries`
- `node scripts/qa-cctv-discovery.mjs` — search, scope, local navigation, map changes, empty-view Nearest fallback, Spanish/Russian rendering, and 4,000-option node reuse
- `node scripts/qa-camera-controls.mjs` — existing panel/calibration/frame/navigation regressions, explicitly using worldwide scope


- `node scripts/qa-form-fields.mjs`: passed in an isolated browser run, including keyboard, calibration, disposal and responsive layouts. Panel measurements wait for the field to become visible.
- Published layer-token and changelog checks passed.

Additional baseline comparison: `qa-action-buttons.mjs` passes its CCTV dispatch, focus, disabled-state and disposal assertions, but reports two Scene-panel layout failures at 1440px and 390px. Both failures also reproduce on an unmodified checkout of upstream `8ed1bbbd`; no unrelated Scene runtime changes are included here.

This PR contains CCTV changes only. The separate air-quality contribution remains in #1291.

title: feat: water quality data layer
body: ## What Adds a keyless **Water Quality** layer backed by the [Water Quality Portal](https://www.waterqualitydata.us/) — the joint USGS / EPA / NWQMC service aggregating 400+ state, tribal and local agencies. Monitoring sites load per viewport; clicking one loads that site's measurements. No API key, no new dependency. ## How it works Two endpoints behind a new `/api/water-quality` proxy: - `…/sites` — viewport-bounded site search, returns GeoJSON - `…/results` — one site's measurements, loaded **only on selection** The split is deliberate: the site query is cheap and runs on every camera settle, while result queries are heavy and are spent only on a site someone actually opened. They use separate abort controllers, so a camera move cannot cancel a card fetch in progress. Five analyte families (nutrients, metals, PFAS, microbiological, radiochemical), one active at a time. Each resolves to a *list* of upstream vocabulary values — a single value silently loses sites, because the portal indexes Cape Fear PFAS under `PFAS,Perfluorinated Alkyl Substance` and returns nothing for `Organics, PFAS`. The proxy validates the family against an allow-list rather than forwarding client strings, bounds the viewport, caps responses, snaps requests onto a shared cache grid, coalesces in-flight work, and serves stale data when the upstream fails. **The 2° viewport bound is measured, not guessed.** Against the live upstream: 1° answers in 11 s, 2° in 20 s, 3° times out. The 10° bound used by the Overpass-backed layers turns every regional view into an empty map here. A test pins it. ## Structure Follows the existing layer-family shape (`src/layers/installations/` as the template): `policy / source / state / model / viewport / ingestion / rendering / selection / controls / lifecycle / index`, plus a Cesium-free `measurements.js` for card formatting. Server side mirrors `server/providers/military-installations/`, reusing `common/http.js`, `common/rate-limit.js` and `common/query.js`. Registered in `package.json` exports, `package-boundaries.json`, `layerState.js` (token `k`), `constructCatalog.js`, `layerSources.js` and `local.js`. Attribution added to `DATA_SOURCES.md` and `dataCredits.js`; `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` updated. ## Verification `npm test` (4164 pass), `npm run test:track` (109 passed), `npm run build`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries` — all green. 23 new unit tests across three Cesium-free modules covering viewport admission, family allow-listing, cancellation, malformed payloads, and card formatting. Exercised against the live upstream: 7 sites and 39 PFAS measurements over the Cape Fear river; 90 sites over Austin; clicking a site returns its analytes. ## Known limitations - **No analyte-family selector in the UI yet** — `setAnalyteFamily()` exists and works, but nothing calls it, so the layer is nutrients-only until a control is added. `disposition: 'enabled-only'`, so the family does not travel in a share link. - **Cache is memory-only** — no disk tier, so a restart re-fetches. The long TTL makes that acceptable for now. - **No `scripts/qa-water-quality.mjs`** harness yet.

title: [Proposal] Canonical provenance/freshness hash for live data snapshots
body:
I reviewed God's Eye View at `0d41b6be5490db1f10a171f238be75db4d4ec3b4`, including the recent work distinguishing partial vessel snapshots from stale data.

I implemented a reference contract for carrying that same data-quality idea across the full live world state.

### Proposal

For every provider snapshot, expose a small normalized provenance envelope:

- provider/source identity
- observation timestamp
- freshness window
- full / partial / stale / unavailable state
- normalized-content hash
- geographic/time scope
- source/terms identifier
- uncertainty or contradiction state

Then deterministically hash the current set of envelopes into one `world_state_root`.

That gives other parts of the application a stable answer to: **exactly which live-data state produced this view or analysis?** It also makes stale/partial-source changes explicit instead of implicit.

### Executed reference proof

God's Eye View is pinned as the perception/source input in a single Supreme Computation source lineage. The contract is merged and the full reference suite is green on Python 3.11 and 3.12.

- Proof: https://github.com/KnowledgeeKZA3224/scqos-reference-implementation/blob/main/proofs/ABSOLUTE_SOURCE_TOTALITY_2026-09-19.md

feat: Scouts — a community reporting layer for God's Eye
body:
### Problem

God's Eye is read-only. You can observe live aircraft, vessels, satellites, and events, but there is no way to record what you saw, when you saw it, or what you think it means. Close the tab and everything you were looking at is gone. There is no persistence, no annotations, no community discussion attached to a physical location.

### Proposal

I built a feature layer that plugs into God's Eye and adds persistent scout reports — numbered pins on the globe with observations, evidence, and threads attached to real coordinates.

What it adds:
- Numbered markers on the globe at every report coordinate
- A Scout Places drawer listing every location with place name, report count, recency, and nearby report count
- Click a list item → globe flies there. Click a marker → drawer opens to that report
- Threads attached to any coordinate: observations, evidence, hypotheses, disputes
- SHA-256 hashed evidence cards (timestamped, source-labeled)
- AI analyst tab (BYOK — Ollama, OpenAI, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek)
- Reverse-geocoded place names via Nominatim (free, no API key)

It is not a fork. It is src/scouts/ plus five import lines added to the top of main.js.

Repo: https://github.com/vanshannonideamine/gods-eye-scouts

Two questions:
1. Do you want this as a PR upstream?
2. Or does it make sense as a standalone companion repo?

MIT licensed. Credited in the README and LICENSE. Happy to change the structure to fit how you'd want it contributed.

### Data source, license, and attribution

No new data sources introduced. This layer consumes the existing God's Eye View provider stack (USGS, OpenSky, ADSB.lol, Celestrak, NASA FIRMS, TomTom, etc.) through the same local API proxies God's Eye already exposes. No additional API keys or credentials are required beyond what God's Eye already needs.

Reverse geocoding (place names like "Austin, Texas") uses the public Nominatim API from OpenStreetMap:
- License: ODbL (Open Database License)
- Attribution: © OpenStreetMap contributors
- Rate limit: 1 request per second (handled by serializing the queue)
- No API key required

All scout reports, threads, and evidence are stored client-side in the browser's localStorage under the key `ges.scouts.v1`. Nothing is transmitted to any server. No telemetry. No analytics. No third-party storage.

SHA-256 hashing for evidence cards uses the browser's native Web Crypto API (crypto.subtle.digest). No external crypto library.

The code itself is MIT licensed, same as God's Eye View.

If the maintainers prefer the Nominatim calls be routed through an existing God's Eye proxy endpoint rather than called directly from the client, I'm happy to change that — the request pattern is a single GET per unique coordinate.

### Will you build it?

Yes, I plan to open a PR

title: fix(tomtom): size the daily tile budget to the real free allowance
body:
## Problem

`TOMTOM_DAILY_TILE_BUDGET` defaults to **40,000 per day**, but TomTom's free allowance is granted **per month, not per day**: 200,000 Traffic Flow & Incidents tile requests per month ([pricing](https://docs.tomtom.com/pricing/)).

At the current default a user exhausts their entire monthly allowance in **five days**, and the traffic layer then falls back to stale/no tiles for the remaining ~25 days of the billing period.

The docs also contradict each other on this figure:

- `server/providers/traffic.js` describes the free tier as `~50k/day`
- `.env.example` cites the correct `200K tile requests/month` two lines below quoting the `40000` default
- `DATA_SOURCES.md` repeats `default 40,000`

`~50k/day` would be ~1.5M/month, about 7.5x the actual allowance.

## Changes

- `DEFAULT_DAILY_BUDGET` 40,000 -> 6,000. A 31-day month lands at 186,000, inside the 200K allowance with headroom.
- Corrects the stale free-tier figures in `server/providers/traffic.js`, `.env.example` and `DATA_SOURCES.md`.
- Updates `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` per CONTRIBUTING.

This stays an **application-side safety ceiling, not a billing cap**, and the surrounding text still says so. TomTom's free tier needs no card, so an overrun cuts the layer off rather than generating a charge — but a layer that dies three weeks into every month is worth avoiding by default. Anyone who wants the old behavior can still set `TOMTOM_DAILY_TILE_BUDGET=40000`.

## Verification

Run on Windows 11, Node 24.19.0, with a real TomTom key configured.

- `npm test` — 4,149 passed, 0 failed
- `npm run build` — clean, only the pre-existing chunk-size warnings
- `npm run test:track` — **109 passed, 0 failed**, no console errors, no HTTP 5xx
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries` — clean
- Live check: `/api/tomtom/status` reports `{"hasKey":true,"dailyCount":0,"budget":6000,...}` with the default, and still honors an explicit `TOMTOM_DAILY_TILE_BUDGET` override.

## Note

I checked open PRs before filing and found none touching the tile budget or the free-tier figures. Happy to adjust the number if you'd rather target a different safety margin.

title: fix(security): ignore the whole dotenv ladder, not just .env
body:
## Problem

`.gitignore` lists only the bare filename `.env`, but the app reads **four** credential files, not one:

- `scripts/setup-doctor.mjs:92` walks ``['.env', '.env.local', `.env.${mode}`, `.env.${mode}.local`]``
- `server/standalone/vite.config.js:11` calls Vite's `loadEnv(mode, root, '')`, which reads the same ladder

gitignore matches literally, so three of those four are committable today. Verified on a clean checkout of `main`:

```
.env                    ignored
.env.local              COMMITTABLE
.env.production         COMMITTABLE
.env.production.local   COMMITTABLE
```

A key placed in `.env.local` is **fully live** for the app. `npm run doctor` reports it as configured, the provider proxies use it, and the browser-exposed defines pick it up. It is also staged by `git add -A`:

```
$ printf 'OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-proj-…\n' > .env.local
$ git add -A --dry-run
add '.env.local'
```

Two things make this sharper than a generic hygiene nit:

1. The in-app **Provider Settings** panel deliberately trains people to keep real keys inside the checkout rather than in a shell profile, so the odds of a key landing in a dotenv file here are high by design.
2. The repository has ~7.7k forks, all of which inherit the gap.

## Changes

Replaces the single `.env` entry with:

```gitignore
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
```

The negation keeps the tracked `.env.example` template exactly as-is — confirmed still tracked and still not ignored after the change.

Deliberately scoped to the dotenv ladder only. Other credential-bearing artifacts (a repo-local `OPENSKY_CREDENTIALS_FILE`, `*.pem` / `*.key`) are a separate judgement call and are left for a follow-up rather than widened into this PR.

## Verification

Windows 11, Node 24.19.0.

- Repro above no longer stages: `.env.local` is ignored after the change
- All of `.env.local`, `.env.production`, `.env.production.local`, `.env.development.local`, `.env.test` now ignored
- `.env.example` still tracked and not ignored (`git ls-files --error-unmatch .env.example` passes)
- `npm test` — 4,145 passed, 0 failed
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm run test:track` — **109 passed, 0 failed**
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries` — clean

## Note

I checked open and closed PRs and issues before filing and found nothing covering this. No behavior changes, so no `CHANGELOG.md` / `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` entry — happy to add one if you'd prefer it recorded.

title: feat: add the Operations Console and a Render deployment blueprint
body:
Two additions, neither of which changes how the existing interface behaves.

## Operations Console

Structural chrome layered over the globe: a command bar with live camera telemetry (lat/lon/elevation/heading/tilt/MGRS, frame rate, UTC clock), a telemetry strip of active feed chips, a module rail, an intelligence dossier and a ⌘K command palette.

It is additive by construction. The console registers no layer, owns no camera and holds no scene state — every action delegates to the control that already owns it: the layer lifecycle for feeds, the style manager for visual presets, and a panel's own disclosure button for panels, so a console command and the equivalent click settle in the same state. A MutationObserver follows panel state, so the rail stays correct when a panel moves for any other reason. Standing the console down removes one body class and leaves the original floating-panel interface untouched; it also stands aside for clean view and the first-person cockpit.

The bottom band is left alone on purpose. The Cesium attribution, the command dock, the mic pill and the toast live there and the credit must stay visible, so no console surface is anchored to it — src/tooling/consoleMarkup.test.mjs pins that, alongside the existing clearance model in creditAttribution.

## Scene analyst

/api/openai/analyst, brokered by the provider that already issues the realtime voice token. The browser sends a question plus a snapshot of what the console can see; the credential never leaves the server. GET reports only whether a key is configured, so the panel can show ANALYST OFFLINE without spending a request. Every request is bounded before it reaches OpenAI, and the existing opt-in GEV_RATELIMIT_OPENAI_PER_MIN throttle covers it.

## Render blueprint

render.yaml plus server/standalone/render.config.js: `vite build` for the bundle, `vite preview` for the server, which runs the same provider middleware as the dev server because every provider declares configurePreviewServer. The in-app credential editor does not attach outside development, so a public deployment cannot be talked into writing keys to disk. The config adds only what a managed host dictates — assigned port, routed hostname, security headers, immutable caching for hashed assets. Keys are prompted for at deploy time, never stored in the repository, and the blueprint sets the per-IP spend guards rather than leaving them unlimited.

Verified with `npm run qa:console` (18 browser checks: telemetry, palette ranking and execution, rail/panel round trip in both directions, dossier feed toggle through the lifecycle, analyst availability, stand-down and restore) plus 45 new unit tests. Full suite: 4188 passing.

title: feat(perf): opt-in render-quality presets for weak GPUs
body:
Follow-up to [the profiling I posted on #8](https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view/issues/8#issuecomment-5748116872). You asked there for current-main profiling and a measured frame-time comparison before taking perf changes; this implements only the part that measured.

## Problem

The viewer is constructed at `msaaSamples: 4` and never sets `resolutionScale`, so it renders at full device pixel ratio with 4x MSAA. On a discrete GPU that's the right default and this PR leaves it alone. On integrated graphics it's the difference between a usable globe and a slideshow.

## Change

`src/app/renderQuality.js` — a pure preset table plus a resolver over `location.search`, following the existing query-flag convention (`?detectDebug=1`, `?trafficDebug=1`). `?quality=balanced` and `?quality=performance` set `scene.msaaSamples` and `viewer.resolutionScale` together. Both are runtime-settable in Cesium, so the preset is applied just after construction and the WebGL context is never rebuilt.

**The default is unchanged.** `high` reproduces the construction values exactly, so nothing moves unless a user opts in. A test asserts that equivalence so the guarantee can't silently rot.

| `?quality=` | msaa | scale | measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| *(none)* / `high` | 4 | 1.00 | 17.9 fps |
| `balanced` | 2 | 0.85 | 22.6 fps |
| `performance` | 1 | 0.60 | 35.1 fps |

## Measurement

Intel UHD 770 (ANGLE/D3D11, i7-12700T), 1264x705 canvas, keyless Esri basemap, no layers enabled, parked camera, warm tile cache.

Frames are counted from `scene.postRender` and every arm asserts the canvas dimensions are unchanged. Worth stating why: an earlier unverified pass of mine reported a clean 60 fps for one arm — rendering had silently stopped and rAF was just free-running. Any perf number not tied to a verified render count and canvas size shouldn't be trusted, including mine.

End-to-end verification drove the real app at each `?quality=` value and asserted the viewer actually adopted the preset:

```
PASS  no param (default)       msaa 4 scale 1     canvas 1264x705  16.5 fps
PASS  ?quality=high            msaa 4 scale 1     canvas 1264x705  15.6 fps
PASS  ?quality=balanced        msaa 2 scale 0.85  canvas 1074x599  22.6 fps
PASS  ?quality=performance     msaa 1 scale 0.6   canvas  758x423  35.1 fps
PASS  ?quality=nonsense        msaa 4 scale 1     canvas 1264x705  15.7 fps
```

## What is deliberately NOT here

Two items ranked above MSAA in #8 measured as noise on this hardware, so I left them out rather than bundle unmeasured changes into a perf PR:

- **`preserveDrawingBuffer`** — flipped to `false` and re-ran the full matrix: 17.9 → 18.2 fps with overlapping samples, across two independent runs. The reasoning is sound in general; on this driver path it isn't costing anything measurable.
- **`backdrop-filter`** — +6% in one run, −1% in the next. Also tested hiding overlay containers one at a time; no single element moved the needle.

Also worth recording: frame time fits roughly **22 ms fixed + 40 ms per megapixel** across scales 1.0/0.75/0.5/0.35/0.25. That fixed term is outside JS (main thread idle ~72%, Cesium render phase ~11 ms) and bounds this machine near ~44 fps regardless of preset. The presets buy back the resolution-dependent half; I could not reduce the rest.

## Robustness

Resolution is total and fails soft. Unknown, empty or malformed values fall back to `high`; prototype keys (`__proto__`, `constructor`) can't smuggle a non-preset through the lookup (`Object.hasOwn`, not `in`); a viewer without a scene is left alone rather than taking down startup over a display preference. 12 tests cover these.

## Verification

Windows 11, Node 24.19.0.

- `npm test` — 4,157 passed, 0 failed (12 new)
- `npm run build` — clean
- `npm run test:track` — **109 passed, 0 failed**
- `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries` — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` updated per CONTRIBUTING

New module registered in both `package-boundaries.json` groups that own `src/app/viewer.js`, and the new test in `format-scope.json` (test files are excluded from runtime auto-discovery).

## Notes

n=1 machine, so the fixed-cost floor in particular may not generalise — the preset *values* are a judgement call and I'd happily take different numbers. A DISPLAY-rail control is the obvious follow-up; I kept this to the mechanism plus the evidence rather than also touching the shell, share-link state and the structural invariant tests in one go. Happy to do that next if you want it.

title: feat: convergence (rendezvous) detection
body:
# feat: convergence (rendezvous) detection

Adds a derived-intelligence layer, sibling to Pattern Watch: it reports where
two independently tracked entities closed to the same place and time, held
proximity, then separated — computed over the track history already sitting
client-side, rendering nothing itself.

## Scope

- `src/data/convergenceDetection.js` — pure engine. `detectConvergences(tracks)`
  and a `createConvergenceEngine({ getTracks })` factory mirroring
  `analystEngine`'s injected-provider shape. Exports `metersBetween`,
  `resampleTrack`, `analyzePair`, `CONVERGENCE_DEFAULTS`.
- `src/data/convergenceDetection.test.mjs` — `node:test`, colocated. 17 tests:
  geometry, fly-by rejection, parallel rejection, gap-not-interpolated, a
  synthetic scene with ground truth (total recall; planted rendezvous rank
  above coincidences), the rendezvous-signature separation, recurring-rendezvous
  scoring, engine factory, and a **source-level assertion that the event shape
  carries no intent field**.
- `docs/convergence-detection.md` — method, the rendezvous signature, and the
  limitations: what it observes vs. what it deliberately does not infer.

## Rendezvous signature — the part that makes this useful

Proximity + dwell alone cannot separate a deliberate meet from two entities that
happen to drift within range for a few minutes. Each event therefore carries a
**rendezvous signature** built from additional observed geometry: distance
closed on approach (`closedFromM`), per-entity hold-vs-transit speed
(`loiterRatio`, `stationKeeping`), and co-motion — combined into a
`signatureStrength` that events are ranked by.

On the fixtures the gap is wide where raw proximity is not: a scripted meet
(came 8 km, held station, parted) scores `signatureStrength ≈ 0.90`
(`stationKeeping: true`); a coincidental slow hold (drifted within 130 m for
15 min, never slowed) scores `≈ 0.32` — while its raw proximity `score` is
`0.67`, high enough to mislead on its own. The signature is what lets an
operator gate the coincidences out.

Still observed behaviour, not intent: a strong signature means the motion
matched a deliberate-meet profile, nothing more.

## Recurring rendezvous — the strongest signal

`detectRecurringRendezvous(events)` groups events by the unordered pair and
surfaces pairs that meet repeatedly — the same two entities, same place, regular
cadence. Recurrence is the strongest observed pattern here: three meets at one
spot on a weekly cadence score `recurrenceStrength ≈ 0.84`; three scattered,
irregular meets score `≈ 0.39`; a single meet is never recurring. It folds in
events from prior windows/days, so it catches a pattern no single run shows.
Same restraint: it measures repetition, it does not name a reason.

No surface/Cesium wiring is included in this PR — the engine is framework-free
and node-tested. Wiring it to the trail-history store and drawing the closest-
approach marker is a focused follow-up, kept out so this reviews cleanly.

## Observed, not inferred

The engine reports geometry — closest approach, dwell, approach/departure — and
a coincidence score. It never labels an event a meeting, transfer, or
relationship; the event object has no field for intent, and a test fails the
build if one is added. That interpretation is the operator's. This carries the
same observed-vs-inferred line Pattern Watch draws.

## Checks

- `npm test` — the new suite is auto-discovered by
  `scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs`; 17/17 green on Node 22 and 24.
- Formatted with the repo Prettier config.
- No new data sources; nothing fetched at runtime; no `DATA_SOURCES.md` change.

title: docs: test edit from Tanvir
fix(server): throttle the cost-bearing proxies by default
body:
Refs #16.

## Changes

The per-IP caps on the endpoints that spend a server-held key were opt-in, so an unconfigured server ran them unlimited. This turns them on, using the caps the Pinokio build already ships.

What made this worth doing is not the issue text but what the rest of the server already does. An always-on per-IP cap is the established pattern here — six modules apply one with no env var involved, and every one of them fronts a free upstream:

| Route | Upstream cost | Per-IP cap on `de2a419` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/api/overpass` | free | 90/min |
| `/api/military-installations` | free | 90/min |
| `/api/route` (OSRM) | free | 60/min |
| `/api/weather-effects` | free | 45/min |
| `/api/geocode` (Nominatim) | free | 30/min |
| `/api/regional-brief` | free | 30/min |
| `/api/openai/hud-summary` | **billed — OpenAI** | opt-in, off by default |
| `/api/realtime/token` | **billed — OpenAI** | opt-in, off by default |
| `/api/google/nearby-places` | **billed — Places** | opt-in, off by default |
| `/api/google/text-search` | **billed — Places** | opt-in, off by default |

To be precise about what this table does and does not say: plenty of other free routes carry no per-IP cap either, and several bound themselves by other means instead — `/api/tomtom` keeps a persistent daily tile budget, `/api/adsbdb` a disk cache and a bounded fan-out, `/api/opensky` request coalescing. The claim is narrower than "everything else is capped": it is that an unconditional per-IP cap is an existing, repeatedly-used pattern in this server, and the four routes that bill the operator were the ones not following it. This makes them follow it rather than invent a policy.

- **The caps are yours, not mine — and they are the ones already shipping.** `pinokio/_ENVIRONMENT` sets `GEV_RATELIMIT_OPENAI_PER_MIN=30` and `GEV_RATELIMIT_GOOGLE_PER_MIN=120`, so every Pinokio install already runs with exactly these numbers. Adopting them as the code defaults leaves the packaged app's behaviour untouched and changes only unconfigured servers — from unlimited to what the product already runs with.
- **A drift this PR also closes.** `.env.example` had come to suggest `60` for Google while the shipped build used `120`. The file now states the defaults and keeps `60` as the tightening it recommends when `HOST` is not localhost, and a test reads `pinokio/_ENVIRONMENT` and pins the code defaults to it, so the two cannot separate again unnoticed.
- **Measured against real demand, not guessed.** An open tab asks for a HUD summary every 15s (`HUD_SUMMARY_INTERVAL_MS`) — 4/min — and a voice session mints one token. 30/min clears that more than seven times over. Places calls are user-driven rather than polled — a search, a nearby lookup, an installation probe — so 120/min is far above anything the app generates.
- **A typo no longer disarms the guard.** Unset or blank takes the default; a positive integer overrides it; exactly `0` disables the limiter. A value that cannot be read as a number — `3O`, `60/min`, a negative — now takes the default instead of meaning unlimited. Opting out stays possible, but only by saying `0`, which nobody types by accident.
- **Keyless paths are untouched.** Keyless HUD summary and keyless Places still resolve before the limiter, so a server with no key spends no budget on them.
- **Two renames.** `makeOptInRateLimiter` → `makeCostRateLimiter`, `enforceOptInRateLimit` → `enforceRateLimit`. After this change the old names state the opposite of what the functions do, and a name that lies is the same defect as a stale comment.
- Docs follow the behaviour: `.env.example`, `SECURITY.md` ("opt-in" → on by default, with both values), `README.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`.

## How it was verified

**Before and after, on the real exported handler.** One LAN peer (`198.51.100.7`), 40 requests to `/api/realtime/token`, upstream `fetch` stubbed so the run costs nothing — everything else is the shipped code path:

| | `upstream/main` | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tokens minted | **40** | 30 |
| requests refused `429` | 0 | **10** |
| calls that actually reached OpenAI | **41** | 30 |
| first refusal at | never | request **31** |
| `Retry-After` | — | `5` |

The pristine side was measured in a detached `git worktree` at `de2a419`, not by reverting in place.

**Tests.** Eight new cases in `src/costEndpointThrottle.test.mjs`, including two that drive the real route handlers — the realtime token route to its 31st request, and the Places route to its 121st — and assert that the refusal is a `429` with `Retry-After: 5`, that it never reaches the provider, that it does not leak the server-held key, and that the Places refusal keeps the `places: []` shape every other error on that route carries. They are mutation-checked rather than assumed green: restoring "unset means unlimited" turns three red, letting an unreadable value disable the guard turns one red, and reverting returns 8/8. title: feat: add Fire Perimeters layer (NIFC WFIGS) with InciWeb incident links
body:
## What this adds

A new **Fire Perimeters** data layer (Events group, beside Active Fires): live NIFC WFIGS interagency wildfire incident perimeters rendered as ground-clamped polygons with a containment-colored fire line (red uncontained → orange → amber → green contained). The official incident picture to complement the FIRMS hotspot layer — FIRMS shows where satellites see heat right now; this shows what each managed incident *is*: its mapped boundary, containment, and response.

- **Source:** the public, keyless WFIGS Current Interagency Perimeters ArcGIS feature service, refreshed every 5 minutes with geometry simplified to ~100 m (`maxAllowableOffset`) and `exceededTransferLimit` paging past the service's 2,000-record cap. Individually invalid features (e.g. ArcGIS `geometry: null` for generalized-away polygons) are skipped so one bad incident can never blank the layer.
- **Incident cards:** clicking a perimeter shows a card at the incident's centroid — acreage, containment %, cause, behavior, complexity, personnel, county, cost to date, complex membership, and discovery/update ages — with every fact omitted when the incident doesn't report it.
- **InciWeb links:** when an incident has an InciWeb page, the card gains an "InciWeb ↗" line and clicking it opens the official page (narratives, evacuation/closure notices). Matching is deliberately conservative: InciWeb's publication catalog is matched by normalized title, corroborated by the dispatch unit's state, resolved through complex membership (`attr_CpxName`) for member fires, and verified against the publication's created/changed timestamps — so a current fire never links to an archived same-name incident. Links use the stable `/node/{id}` redirect (InciWeb soft-404s guessed slugs). The catalog is fetched off the render path at most every 6 hours per session.
- **Integration:** layer catalog + share-link state (token `k`), Events panel group, Realtime voice tool enums and spoken aliases ("turn on fire perimeters"), the analyst query engine (acres/containment/personnel/cost with spatial scoping), package exports and boundary groups. Perimeter picks deliberately stay out of the shared pick-ownership registry so sibling layers' overlay cards keep working over perimeter polygons.
- **Docs & attribution:** DATA_SOURCES.md rows for both sources (U.S. government public data, with access-cadence notes), an always-on `DATA_CREDITS` entry rendering in the Data attribution popover, CHANGELOG and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` updates, and the layer's runtime + test files adopted into `scripts/format-scope.json`.

## How it was verified

- `npm test`: 4,193 passing, including 52 new colocated unit tests for the layer (feed normalization, paging, card model, selection lifecycle, InciWeb matching/verification, outage tolerance)
- `npm run build` clean; `npm run test:track`: 109 passed, 0 failed, no console errors across the full run
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries` clean
- Live visual verification over the current fire season feed (190 incidents): layer toggle and counts, perimeter rendering at globe and regional zoom, containment coloring, card selection and clearing, InciWeb click-through on state- and recency-verified matches (e.g. Frijoles/NM, Second Flat/OR, and the Rowe Creek Complex member-fire fallback)
- Link matching was validated against both live feeds: earlier iterations were measured producing 7 wrong-state and 8 stale-archive links out of 109 resolved; the shipped matcher produces none of either, at ~103 verified links of 190 current incidents (the remainder genuinely have no InciWeb page)

Happy to split anything out or adjust to taste — the InciWeb linking is separable from the base layer if you'd prefer it as a follow-up.

title: fix(server): stop track backfill from spending the OpenSky credit budget
body:
Fixes #259.

## Changes

`/api/opensky-track` spends 4 OpenSky credits per call against the same account as `/api/opensky` — the file's own doc comment says so. But it participates in none of the credit governor that proxy maintains, and its only throttle is a 60-second per-`icao24` result cache. That cache bounds **memory, not spend**: `icao24` is six hex digits, so a caller varying it produces a fresh key and a fresh live call every time.

The governor this route was missing is not something I invented. `server/providers/aircraft/opensky.js:28-39` records the incident that produced it:

> The global `/states/all` this proxy fetches costs 4 CREDITS per call against OpenSky's ~4000/day authenticated budget — a day with the app open burned the whole quota in ~8h and the layer then hard-died until the daily reset ("rate limited for 48h" owner report; auth itself was fine).

Three levers were added there. This route had none of them, while spending the same budget.

- **A per-client limiter, always on.** 30 requests/minute/client, 90 global, on both track routes. That is the band `/api/geocode` and `/api/regional-brief` already use, and it is sized against real demand rather than guessed: a backfill is issued once per aircraft the operator *selects* (`_backfillTrail`, reached from the tracked-contact path in the flights, military and vessels layers), and re-selecting the same aircraft inside a minute is served from cache. 30/min is a target switch every two seconds, sustained.
- **The cooldown is now shared.** `opensky.js` exports `openSkyCooldownRemainingMs()` — a read-only view of the existing `_openskyCooldownUntil`; only that module still writes it. While the account is cooling, `/api/opensky-track` does not mint a token and does not call upstream: it serves any cached track (lever 3, serve-stale — a cached body costs nothing further) and otherwise answers `429` carrying the remaining cooldown.
- **adsb.lol gets the limiter but not the governor.** It is free and unmetered, so there is no credit budget to protect; the limiter is there for the operator's IP reputation with a community service, the same reason `/api/overpass` carries one. Saying this explicitly because the two routes now look asymmetric on purpose.

Client behaviour is unchanged. `_backfillTrail` is fire-and-forget and already treats any non-OK response as "keep the locally accumulated trail" — a `429` is a path it has always had.

## How it was verified

**Six cases in `src/openSkyTrackGovernor.test.mjs`**, driving the real exported route handlers with `fetch` stubbed per test and restored after, so a case that reaches upstream fails loudly rather than making a request:

- 30 lookups with a **different `icao24` each time** pass; the 31st is refused with `429` + `Retry-After`, and upstream saw exactly 30 calls. This is the issue's core claim — that varying the key walks past the cache — asserted directly.
- A second client address still has its own quota, so one noisy host cannot take the layer away from everyone.
- `/api/adsblol/trace` is metered too.
- A malformed `icao24` is still rejected with `400` before any upstream call.
- `openSkyCooldownRemainingMs()` reads 0 until armed, and a past cooldown never reads as active.
- **End-to-end across both modules:** a stubbed `429` from OpenSky's `/states/all` arms the real governor through the real `/api/opensky` handler; a subsequent cold `/api/opensky-track` is then refused with the remaining cooldown and **zero** upstream calls.

**Mutation-checked rather than assumed green.** Disabling the limiter turns 3 of 6 red; keying the limiter globally instead of per-client turns 1 red; ignoring the cooldown turns 1 red. Reverting each returns 6/6.

**Gates** on Node 24.14.0 with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1`: `npm run format:check` (919 files), `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`, `npm test` (4167 tests, 0 failures, 1 pre-existing skip, all 13 allocation microbenchmarks ran), and `npm run test:track` (109 passed, 0 failed).

The limiter does not throttle the project's own harness: `test:track` is 109/109 with it on.

## Notes for review

- **`scripts/package-boundaries.json` needed two lines.** `check:boundaries` refused the first build because the `live-providers` package does not own `server/providers/common/rate-limit.js` or `src/sources/rateLimit.js`. I declared both, copying exactly what `place-providers` already declares. Flagging it because it widens a package's surface, which is your call rather than an implementation detail.
- **The issue's line references have gone stale.** It cites `vite.config.js:4956-5043`; that code now lives in `server/providers/aircraft/tracks.js`, and the governor it compares against is in `server/providers/aircraft/opensky.js`. The finding itself reproduced exactly as described.
- **What this does and does not bound.** A per-minute cap slows a determined abuser; it does not by itself make the daily credit budget unreachable. The cooldown is what actually protects the budget, because it engages the moment OpenSky says the account is out. I would rather state that plainly than imply the limiter alone closes the issue.
- **`globalMax` is 3× the per-IP cap here** (90), matching the always-on limiters in this repo rather than the 20× the opt-in helper uses.

title: fix(server): bound the terrain-heights cache and its request rate
body:
Fixes #260.

## Changes

The shape of this endpoint is what makes it worth bounding: **every distinct 5-decimal point is its own cache key, its own permanent line in `.gev-cache/terrain-heights.json`, and its own upstream call.** Nothing limited the request rate, and coordinates were validated for being *finite* rather than for being *on Earth* — so `0,999` was a perfectly good cache key.

Four bounds, each following a pattern already in this repo rather than a new invention:

| Bound | Precedent followed |
| --- | --- |
| WGS-84 range rejected with `400` at parse | — (the gap itself) |
| Point cache ≤ 50,000 entries, oldest-first eviction | `trackBackfillProxies`'s `TRACK_CACHE_MAX` |
| Cache file above 24 MB not read back | `rocketLaunchesProxy`'s `maxDiskCacheBytes` |
| 90 requests/min/client, 270 global | `/api/overpass`, `/api/military-installations` |

**Both numbers are measured, not guessed.**

- The entry ceiling: this checkout's `.gev-cache/terrain-heights.json` held **6,189 entries in 1,039,666 bytes** after ordinary use — ~168 bytes/entry. 50,000 entries is eight times that working set and ~8 MB on disk, comfortably inside the 24 MB file ceiling.
- The rate cap: I instrumented the route and ran the full `npm run test:track` suite, the heaviest exercise this app has. It served **10 requests, peaking at 8/min**. 90/min is an order of magnitude above that.

Eviction is safe here in a way it would not be for a live feed: terrain does not move, so dropping an old point costs one refetch and never a wrong answer.

Range is enforced in `parseTerrainPoints` — at the edge, so no later stage has to repeat it. The poles and the antimeridian still parse; a batch containing one out-of-range point is rejected whole rather than silently trimmed.

## How it was verified

**Seven cases in `src/terrainHeightsBounds.test.mjs`**, driving the real exported route handler with `fetch` stubbed per test and restored after. Each of the four bounds is gated as *behaviour*, not asserted as a constant:

- Off-globe coordinates (`0,91`, `181,0`, `1e9,1e9`, `0,90.00001`) do not parse; the poles, the antimeridian and an ordinary point still do.
- An out-of-range point returns `400` with **zero** upstream calls, and one hidden inside a valid batch rejects that batch.
- **Eviction is proven by refetch:** with the ceiling set to 3, four distinct points cost four lookups; the newest is then served from cache at no cost, while the oldest has been evicted and costs exactly one refetch.
- **The disk ceiling is proven both ways:** the same cache file is skipped under a ceiling that excludes it (so the point is a miss) and *used* under one that admits it — which is what shows the first result came from the size guard rather than a broken path.
- The 91st request in a minute is refused, and a second client still has its own quota.

The ceilings are constructor options precisely so they can be driven like this; production constructs the proxy with no arguments.

**Mutation-checked.** Removing the range check reds 3 of 7; disabling eviction reds 1; removing the disk ceiling reds 1; disabling the limiter reds 2. Restoring each returns 7/7.

**Gates** on Node 24.14.0 with `GEV_REQUIRE_ALLOCATION_GATE=1`: `npm run format:check` (919 files), `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`, `npm test` (4168 tests, 0 failures, 1 pre-existing skip, all 13 allocation microbenchmarks ran), `npm run test:track` (109 passed, 0 failed).

## Notes for review

Three things I want your eye on, two of which are changes to *your* test files that I would rather flag than bury.

- **`src/proxyErrorResponses.test.mjs` needed two lines.** That harness evaluates the extracted proxy source in a `new Function` scope, so a new import in the production file is an undefined identifier there. I added `makeRateLimiter` and `clientKey` to its `deps` — the real ones, so a fixture request is throttled exactly as production would be. The file is not in `format-scope.json`, so I edited it by hand and did not run the formatter over it.
- **The same harness dictated a signature.** It slices each proxy to the first closing brace in column zero, so a multi-line destructured parameter list cuts the function in half. The options are therefore destructured in the body, with a comment saying why — otherwise the next person will "tidy" it back and get a confusing `SyntaxError`.
- **One bug found by running the full suite, not by the new tests.** My first version called `fsp.stat` unconditionally before `readFile`. `environmentProviders.test.mjs` mocks `readFile` but not `stat`, so a missing file made `stat` throw and silently skipped the legacy-cache migration entirely. Fixed by treating "cannot measure it" as distinct from "too large": without stat, `readFile` decides, exactly as before. Worth knowing that path had no direct coverage of its own.
- **What the rate cap does and does not do.** 90/min still permits a lot of distinct points over a day. The entry ceiling is what actually bounds memory and disk; the limiter bounds the burst and the load on Re:Earth. I would rather say that than imply the limiter alone closes the growth issue.
- **The issue's line references have gone stale** (`vite.config.js:2242-2250` etc.); this code now lives in `server/providers/terrain.js` and `src/data/terrainHeightsProxy.js`. Every finding reproduced.
