title: Architecture: authoritative scientific data providers and POWER UP auth boundary
body:
## Summary

America.gov's launch exposed a useful architectural shift for God's Eye View: use government-wide conversational discovery to find authoritative scientific and geospatial sources, but keep the application itself wired directly to the first-party agency APIs, catalogs, archives, and tile services.

This is not a proposal to make America.gov a runtime dependency.

It is a proposal to make **authoritative first-party scientific data** the preferred data plane, and to put optional authenticated capabilities behind the existing **POWER UP** boundary.

## Why this matters

God's Eye View already does part of this well:

- Recent Imagery already uses **NASA GIBS** for display-ready imagery and **NASA CMR** for granule discovery.
- Weather already uses **NOAA GFS**, **NOAA nowCOAST**, and **NHC/CPHC** sources.
- The existing **POWER UP** surface already owns optional provider credentials and capability unlocks.

A discovery session through America.gov made it much easier to descend from a vague user intent ("what scientific data does the government expose?") into the actual machine-readable infrastructure: GIBS, CMR/STAC, Harmony, Earthdata Login, NWS APIs/GIS services, USGS event feeds, EPA services, MAST/Roman archives, and other agency-native sources.

That suggests we should treat this as an architectural pattern rather than adding one-off layers.

## Proposed architectural direction

### 1. Prefer authoritative first-party providers

For scientific, environmental, infrastructure, and government-derived layers, prefer the agency or archive that owns the source data when it exposes a usable machine-readable interface.

Examples:

- NASA: GIBS, CMR/CMR-STAC, Harmony, MAST
- NOAA/NWS: weather.gov API, NWS GIS/MapServer/WMS/WMTS services, NHC/CPHC, GFS
- USGS: FDSN/ComCat, GeoJSON feeds, science catalogs, hydrology/hazard networks
- EPA: AQS, Envirofacts, ArcGIS services, RadNet
- Census / FEMA / USDA / DOE / FAA and other agencies where equivalent first-party sources exist

Third-party providers still make sense when they add unique value, fill a real coverage gap, normalize difficult sources, or materially improve reliability. The point is to stop choosing a downstream source merely because it was easier to discover.

### 2. Treat POWER UP as the authentication boundary

The base globe should remain useful without credentials.

Public/keyless sources should stay public and keyless. Authenticated agency capabilities should be enabled through **POWER UP**, not spread through unrelated layer UI or global application state.

Example: NASA Earthdata.

- GIBS and public CMR discovery can remain available without requiring a user to sign in.
- Deeper operations such as protected granule downloads, Harmony processing, or other Earthdata-gated services can be unlocked through an Earthdata capability in POWER UP.
- A local/developer deployment can use an Earthdata bearer token.
- A future multi-user deployment should prefer Earthdata Login/OAuth rather than asking users to paste long-lived passwords into the application.

The same boundary can generalize to other agency credentials or user-authorized data providers later.

### 3. Separate visualization, discovery, transformation, and source assets

Not every provider is "a layer."

NASA is a good example of the separation:

- **GIBS**: visualization / tile plane
- **CMR / STAC**: discovery / metadata plane
- **Harmony**: transformation / subsetting plane
- **DAAC-hosted files**: underlying scientific asset plane

God's Eye View should be able to show a fast visual representation first, then let a selected location/time resolve into the actual observation, granule, instrument, acquisition time, processing level, and source product when the provider supports it.

That moves the application from "pretty overlay" toward an inspectable scientific record.

### 4. Audit existing subsystems before rewriting them

This proposal is **not** "rewrite everything because a new source exists."

Instead, audit each major subsystem against the authoritative source landscape:

- What source do we use today?
- Is it the authoritative upstream source?
- What resolution, cadence, history, provenance, or coverage are we losing?
- Are we reimplementing transformations the source already provides?
- Is the current provider still the best operational choice?
- Does a richer provider belong beside the existing one rather than replacing it?

NOAA/weather is an obvious first audit because the federal stack exposes multiple first-party forecast, observation, radar, GIS, precipitation, and climate products. Existing GFS/nowCOAST work should be treated as a strong starting point, not discarded automatically.

A rewrite should be justified by a measurable improvement in fidelity, latency, coverage, provenance, inspectability, or maintainability.

## America.gov's role

America.gov should be treated as a **discovery and reconnaissance tool**, not a runtime backend.

Its value is that a developer can ask broad questions such as:

- "What federal scientific data could be visualized on a globe?"
- "What raw geomagnetic measurements are publicly available?"
- "What NASA Roman data is available now versus after science operations?"
- "What machine-readable wildfire, hydrology, radiation, aviation, or space-weather data exists?"

and get routed toward the responsible agencies and their technical entry points.

Once a useful source is identified, God's Eye View should integrate the **original agency endpoint directly** and document the provenance in `DATA_SOURCES.md`.

That keeps the runtime architecture stable even if America.gov changes.

## Relationship to existing work

This issue is intended as an architectural umbrella for deeper scientific-data work such as #850 (expanded JPSS satellite layers).

#850 asks for specific NASA/NOAA products. This proposal defines where those products should sit:

- first-party source where practical,
- explicit source/provenance metadata,
- keyless core where possible,
- POWER UP for optional authenticated capabilities,
- and a clean distinction between rendered imagery and underlying scientific observations.

The existing Recent Imagery implementation already demonstrates much of this pattern with GIBS + CMR.

## Candidate next work

The next useful step is an **authoritative-source audit**, not a mass rewrite.

Start with a small set of existing or adjacent subsystems:

1. Weather / atmospheric data
2. Recent imagery / Earth observation
3. Wildfire / hazards
4. Seismic / geological observations
5. Space / astronomy data

For each, document the current provider, authoritative upstream alternatives, update cadence, spatial/temporal resolution, authentication requirements, and whether a provider change would materially improve the product.

From there, generalize only the seams that repeat across multiple domains.

## Non-goals

- Do not make America.gov a production dependency.
- Do not require authentication for data that is already public.
- Do not replace a stable provider solely because a government endpoint exists.
- Do not collapse every scientific source into one universal schema before we have evidence that the abstraction is useful.
- Do not turn POWER UP into a general settings drawer; keep it focused on capability/provider activation and credentials.
- Do not hide provenance. A user should be able to tell what agency, product, timestamp, and processing level produced the data they are viewing.

## Design principle

**God's Eye View should make authoritative data easy to see, inspect, and deepen into—without requiring users to understand the agency topology that produced it.**

America.gov made the source landscape easier to discover. The application should take advantage of that discovery without inheriting America.gov as a runtime dependency.

title: refactor(qa): extract scripts/qa-browser.mjs for unified browser resolution (#770)
body:
### Summary
Follow-up to #402 addressing the ownership and deduplication problem identified in #770.

This extracts a centralized browser resolution module (`scripts/qa-browser.mjs`) to replace duplicated browser path resolution logic across QA harnesses.

### Resolution Hierarchy
Follows the exact priority order outlined in the review:
1. `PUPPETEER_EXECUTABLE_PATH` environment variable (if set and exists on disk).
2. Puppeteer's pinned Chrome-for-Testing binary, wrapped with a safe sync/async/throw handler around `puppeteer.executablePath()`.
3. Cross-platform system fallbacks for macOS (`darwin`), Linux (`linux`), and Windows (`win32`).

### Exports
- `resolveChromeExecutable(puppeteer?, options?)`: Returns the first existing browser executable path.
- `getPuppeteerPinnedPath(puppeteer)`: Safe sync/throw wrapper around `puppeteer.executablePath()`.
- `getSystemChromeCandidates(platform?)`: Cross-platform fallback paths.
- `launchQaBrowser(puppeteer, launchOptions?, resolveOptions?)`: Convenience launcher injecting the resolved `executablePath`.
- `findChromeExecutable`: Alias for backward compatibility across existing harnesses.

### Testing & Verification
- Added test suite in `src/tooling/qaBrowser.test.mjs` (**13/13 tests passing**).
- Tests cover sync/async `executablePath`, throwing/rejection error safety, cross-platform candidate lists, and priority order resolution.
- Code formatted and verified via `npm run format:check` (1128 files clean).

Closes #770

title: fix(ais): ignore unavailable positions and stop scanning the cache per message
body:
## What

Two fixes in the AISStream store (`server/providers/vessels/ais-store.js`).

### 1. "Position not available" reports were placed near the pole

ITU-R M.1371 reports a missing position as latitude 91 / longitude 181. Both are finite, so `ingestAisStreamEnvelope` accepted them. The store already rejects the equivalent sentinels for speed (102.3), course (360) and heading (511); lat/lon was the one left out.

Effect: a Class A transponder without a GPS fix was stored, served, drawn at `Cartesian3.fromDegrees(181, 91)` and seeded its track ring buffer with that point. When the fix returned, the trail drew a line from the pole.

Now such a report is treated as positionless. It still returns `true` because it still proves the feed is live. The vessel layer (`normalizeVessel`, `hasUsableVesselCoordinates`) also refuses any row outside ±90° / ±180°, as a second line of defense.

### 2. Cache pruning scanned every stored vessel on every message

`pruneAisStreamCache()` runs at the end of every position message. It iterated the whole live cache (up to `AISSTREAM_CACHE_MAX` = 50,000) plus the pending-fix map. When the cache was over the cap, it also copied and sorted the entire map. With the default whole-globe subscription (hundreds of messages/s), this ran on the dev server's event loop that serves every other `/api/*` proxy.

The live and static maps are now kept in update order (`delete` + `set` on write). Stale and over-cap eviction then stop at the first surviving entry, so each prune is O(evicted). The pending first-fix sweep, which still needs a full walk, runs at most once a minute.

`_aisStreamStatic` was never evicted and grew by one entry per MMSI ever seen. It is now capped at twice the live cache, since static reports also arrive for MMSIs that never send a position.

Local micro-benchmark (Node 24, 40,000 cached vessels, 5,000 updates to existing MMSIs):

| | per message | max throughput |
|---|---|---|
| before | ~967 µs | ~1,000 msg/s |
| after | ~4 µs | ~250,000 msg/s |

## Tests

- `src/data/aisStreamSentinels.test.mjs`: two new cases.
  - A 91/181 report is not stored, adds no track, and still counts as liveness.
  - A real fix after a 91/181 report starts a clean trail.
  - Both fail on `main`.
- `src/data/aisStreamPruning.test.mjs` (new), using mocked `Date`.
  - It pins the eviction contract that the update ordering has to preserve: stale eviction removes the least recently updated vessel (and its track) even when an earlier-inserted vessel keeps reporting.
  - Over the cap, the least recently updated vessel is evicted, not the first inserted.
- `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` are updated.

## Validation

- `npm test`: 5,373 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped, plus the allocation and frame-budget batches green.
- `npm run build`: OK. The only warning is the existing large-chunk one.
- `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`: clean.
- `npm run test:track`: 109 passed, 0 failed (dev server run keyless; with my local Google key the only failures were console 401s from `tile.googleapis.com`, which is a key problem unrelated to this change)
- `node scripts/qa-vessel-cards.mjs --data synthetic`: 2 passed (Rotterdam, Houston); vessels and cards render

title: docs(security): drop the HTTP referrer restriction from the browser Google key
body:
## Summary

`SECURITY.md` and `.env.example` both told operators to restrict the client-exposed `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` by **HTTP referrer**. Following that advice silently breaks place search, so this takes the option-3 fix from #363: correct the guidance instead of moving the call.

The browser calls the **Geocoding web service** endpoint directly — `src/search/defaults.js:49` (forward) and `src/search/http.js:56` (reverse) — and Google rejects referrer-restricted keys on every web service endpoint:

```json
{ "status": "REQUEST_DENIED",
  "error_message": "API keys with referer restrictions cannot be used with this API." }
```

Referrer restrictions apply to the Maps JavaScript API and client SDKs, not to web services. Photorealistic 3D Tiles *are* fetched client-side and would honour one, which is what made the guidance look right; geocoding is the endpoint that cannot. So the documented restriction has to be API scope only.

Related Issue: #363 (option 3 — the minimum that resolves the contradiction; option 1, a server-side geocode proxy, is left as the code follow-up)

## Changes

- **`SECURITY.md`** — the browser-key entry now says "Restrict its **API scope**" instead of "Restrict it (HTTP referrer + API restriction)", and gains a blockquote naming why the referrer restriction is unavailable, quoting the verbatim Google error so it is recognisable in the console, and pointing at provider-side quotas/budget alerts for the geocoding spend.
- **`SECURITY.md`** — the `#33` split paragraph no longer claims the browser key is "referrer-restricted".
- **`SECURITY.md`** — new note that IP-restricting `GOOGLE_MAPS_SERVER_API_KEY` needs **both the IPv4 and IPv6 address** of a dual-stack host, or it fails with `API_KEY_IP_ADDRESS_BLOCKED`. That reads like a broken key rather than a missing second entry.
- **`.env.example`** — same correction on the `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` entry (the text an operator reads while filling in the file, so it cannot live only in `SECURITY.md`), plus the dual-stack caveat on `GOOGLE_MAPS_SERVER_API_KEY`.
- **`src/googleBrowserKeyRestrictions.test.mjs`** (new) — a doc sentence is the entire fix here, so nothing in the suite would notice it drifting back. Five pins cover both directions.

Unchanged on purpose: no code, no `.env` parsing, no proxy behaviour, and no server-key restriction semantics.

## Testing

- `node --test src/googleBrowserKeyRestrictions.test.mjs` — **5/5 pass**. Verified as a real regression pin: against the unmodified `SECURITY.md` / `.env.example` the same file reports **3 of 5 failing**, then passes again once the fix is restored.
- `npm test` — **2255 tests, 238 fail both with and without this branch** (baseline 2250/238). Every failure is `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` for uninstalled dependencies (`cesium`, `vite`, `pbf`, `sharp`, `egm96-universal`) — `node_modules` was never installed in this environment. So: **+5 tests, +0 failures, no regressions.** `src/googleServerKey.test.mjs` and `src/googlePlacesKeyless.test.mjs` fail identically on and off this branch for the same reason.
- `prettier --check src/googleBrowserKeyRestrictions.test.mjs` — clean against the repo's `.prettierrc.json`.
- `node scripts/check-import-directions.mjs` / `check-package-boundaries.mjs` — unchanged (the new test imports only `node:*` and two sibling modules, no new direction).

Not run, and why: `npm run build`, `npm run test:track` and the `qa-*.mjs` gates need a full `npm install` and a live dev server; the disk on this box is at 99% (2.1 GB free), so `npm install` (Cesium + Puppeteer's Chromium) was not attempted. **This change touches only two documentation files and adds one test file, so it cannot affect the production build** — but flagging it explicitly rather than implying a green build I did not observe.

## Checklist

- [x] Conventional Commits subject, signed off (`Refs #363`)
- [x] Docs-only change to `SECURITY.md` / `.env.example`
- [x] New test added, verified to fail before the fix and pass after
- [x] Prettier clean
- [x] No secrets committed
- [ ] `npm run build` / `npm run test:track` — see *Testing*; not runnable here

title: fix(server): bound upstream requests that relied on fetch's 300 s defaults
body:
## What

Node's `fetch` only gives up on a silent upstream after undici's 300 s header and body timeouts. The calls below passed no `signal`, so a single stalled connection held its caller for five minutes. This PR adds `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, following the inline idiom already used in `tracks.js`, `celestrak.js` and `realtime.js`.

| Call | Budget | Why it mattered |
|---|---|---|
| OpenSky OAuth token (`aircraft/opensky.js`) | 10 s | A stalled token request kept the shared `_openskyTokenPromise` pending, so every `/api/opensky` and `/api/opensky-track` caller awaiting it hung too |
| OpenSky `/states/all` and its Basic-auth retry | 20 s | The global snapshot is several MB, so it gets a longer budget |
| adsb.lol `/v2/mil` (`aircraft/adsb-lol.js`) | 15 s | Military poll |
| Google Places nearby and text search (`places/google.js`) | 10 s | Search box |
| OpenAI HUD summary (`openai/hud-summary.js`) | 15 s | Five-word summary |

A timeout does not add a new failure mode. It takes each route's existing failure path: the last-good cache, the adsb.lol regional fallback, or its 502.

Not in this PR (kept small on purpose): coalescing concurrent `/states/all` fetches after the TTL, and `no-store` on Places error responses. Happy to follow up on either.

## Tests

The new `src/tooling/upstreamTimeouts.test.mjs` drives each route against an upstream that never answers, with `AbortSignal.timeout` mocked to expire immediately. It checks two things:
- the route still answers through its failure path;
- every requested budget is bounded.

All 5 cases fail on `main` and pass here, and the file runs in milliseconds.

## Validation

- `npm test`: 5,374 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped, plus the allocation and frame-budget batches green.
- `npm run build`: OK. The only warning is the existing large-chunk one.
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries`: clean.

title: perf(flights): skip dead-reckoning contacts that stay behind the horizon
body:
## What

`_fleetTick` in `src/layers/flights/rendering.js` handles every aircraft on every ~80 ms tick: dead-reckoning, ground floor, then the horizon test. Only after all that does it hide the aircraft that are behind the horizon. The worldwide OpenSky feed carries ~13k aircraft, and with the camera zoomed in well under 1% of them are on screen. So almost all of that work only produces a hidden billboard.

With this change, an aircraft that **is already hidden** and **is still behind the horizon at its last position** is re-reckoned only on its turn. The turns form a staggered rotation, one tick in every `HIDDEN_CONTACT_DR_TICKS` (12), which is about once a second. The slot comes from the id, so no single tick handles the whole fleet.

What stays the same:
- An aircraft whose last position puts it in view takes the full pass immediately, as does any aircraft with a fleet 3D model. On-screen behaviour does not change.
- The tracked aircraft is still skipped entirely, as before.
- `getNearby({ includeHidden })` and `getAllPositions` still read hidden aircraft positions. Those positions are now at most about 1 s old (~250 m for an airliner), well inside the 30 s poll's own uncertainty.

## Measurements

Chrome, Radeon 780M, 1024×768. Same view (Colombia at 4 km, ~12.9k aircraft, 56 on screen), measured before and after by timing the `scene.preRender` listeners:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| `_fleetTick` per frame | 7.66 ms | **2.03 ms** |
| longest single tick | 50.9 ms | **~16 ms** |
| frame time | 20.6 ms | **14.0 ms** |
| FPS | 42.9 | **57.8** |

Behaviour checks in the same session:
- **Teleport:** after moving the camera to Madrid, 975 aircraft were on screen within 100 ms. There was no pop-in delay.
- **Update rates:** over 5 s, hidden aircraft updated about once a second (largest gap 1.17 s). Visible aircraft kept updating on every tick.

## Tests

`src/layers/flights/hiddenContactRotation.test.mjs` checks three properties of the rotation:
- its period is about 1 s;
- slots are stable per id;
- a 13k fleet spreads evenly across the ticks.

The skip itself is exercised end to end by `test:track`.

## Validation

- `npm test`: 5,372 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped, plus the allocation and frame-budget batches green.
- `npm run build`: OK. The only warning is the existing large-chunk one.
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries`: clean.
- `npm run test:track`: 109 passed, 0 failed. It ran on a keyless dev server with its own Vite `cacheDir`, because a second dev server sharing `node_modules/.vite` gets `504 Outdated Optimize Dep`.

The military layer has the same `_fleetTick` shape, but it carries hundreds of aircraft, not thousands, so I left it out of this PR.

title: perf(vessels): let the scene idle with AIS vessels enabled
body:
## What

AIS vessels move only when a poll lands. There is no per-frame interpolation in `src/layers/vessels`. Even so, enabling the layer held the continuous render loop (`holdContinuousRender('ais-vessels')`) for as long as it stayed on. A parked vessels-only scene therefore rendered every frame. This PR contains two changes.

### 1. The layer no longer holds the loop

The two passes stay in `preRender`. In idle mode `preRender` only fires on rendered frames, so the layer now asks for frames when it needs them:
- **Forced pass** (new data, selection): the pass asks for its own frame (`governorRequestRender`).
- **Trailing frame:** when the camera moved inside the 800 ms visibility cadence, one timer-driven frame is scheduled, so the view the camera stopped on is always evaluated.
  - It is keyed to camera motion alone. The pass publishes labels, and that publication requests a frame. A first version scheduled on any skipped pass and looped at ~1.2 Hz; the headless check below caught it.
- **Hold:** `ais-vessels` is held only while focus emphasis is animating (`activeCount > 0` or a transition in progress).

### 2. Cheaper focus pass while anything is tracked

The 80 ms focus pass advanced focus state for every vessel. A new `spriteFocusAtRest(sprite)` in `focusDeemphasis.js` lets it skip hidden sprites that meet two conditions:
- they hold no pending focus state;
- their alpha is already 1.

Advancing such a sprite with no screen position changes neither its state nor its alpha. The existing "restores a hidden sprite before releasing" test still passes.

## Measurements

**Parked, vessels only** (headless Chrome with SwiftShader, 1280×800). The same script ran before and after:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| governor mode | `continuous` (`ais-vessels`) | **`idle`** |
| frames in 5 s at rest | 28 | **0** |
| horizon visibility mismatches after moving the camera and settling | 0 | **0** |

**Focus pass**, measured in Chrome on a Radeon 780M with 12,000 vessels (11,353 hidden) and a real focus rect:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| time per pass | ~4.0 ms | **~1.2 ms** |

## Tests

- New in `src/data/aisLiveVessels.test.mjs`: with a target tracked, only the on-screen sprite is projected and measured, and hidden sprites at rest are left untouched. On `main` the same test sees 102 projections instead of 2.
- The `ownership.test.mjs` render double gains the governor functions the layer now uses.

## Validation

- `npm test`: 5,370 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped, plus the allocation and frame-budget batches green.
- `npm run build`: OK. The only warning is the existing large-chunk one.
- `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries`: clean.
- `node scripts/qa-perf.mjs`: 24 passed, 0 failed.
- `npm run test:track`: 109 passed, 0 failed.
- `node scripts/qa-vessel-cards.mjs --data synthetic`: 2 passed.

title: perf: byte-bound Recent Imagery thumbnail residency
body:
## TL;DR

Decoded Recent Imagery thumbnail residency now has an explicit **byte ceiling** in addition to the existing LRU entry-count ceiling.

Default behavior is unchanged:
- current `maxDecoded` remains authoritative;
- default byte budget is derived from `maxDecoded × thumbnailWidth × thumbnailHeight × 4`.

Low-memory/mobile profiles may provide a tighter `maxDecodedBytes` without changing probe or freshness semantics.

## Behavior

Evicting decoded pixels does **not** forget source knowledge:
- `present / empty / error` status remains;
- acquisition time remains;
- an evicted known-present thumbnail can be fetched again on demand.

`memoryStats()` exposes current decoded bytes, the configured byte budget, and estimated decoded bytes per image.

## Tests

Adds focused coverage proving the byte ceiling evicts the least-recently-used decoded image even when the entry-count ceiling would still allow it.

This is independent of the motion-safe imagery work and can be reviewed separately.

title: fix(server): declare Allow on every 405 response (#809)
body:
Fixes #809.

Every local route that answers `405 Method Not Allowed` now declares the methods it accepts in an `Allow` header (RFC 9110 §15.5.6). Status codes and response bodies are unchanged.

## What changed

- **One formatter:** `allowedMethods()` in a new dependency-free module, `server/providers/common/methods.js`. It keeps the route's order, drops repeats and rejects malformed methods. It sits apart from `common/http.js` so `openai-provider`, `standalone-key-setup` and `mapillary-provider` can own it without the browser-shared body readers; `scripts/package-boundaries.json` registers it with each package that uses it.
- **Each 405 site keeps its own reply style:** `writeHead` headers, `setHeader`, or a `status === 405` branch in the local `json`/`send`/`sendJson`/`refuse` helper.
- **Declared methods match each guard:**
  - `GET, HEAD`: local receivers
  - `GET, DELETE`: CCTV media
  - `GET, POST`: Realtime token, and `/api/overpass/status`
  - `POST`: Overpass queries, HUD summary, debug log, setup keys, ChatGPT OAuth login
  - `GET`: everything else, including Mapillary, the Google geocode and reverse-geocode routes, ChatGPT OAuth status, and transit
- `/api/transit` lives in `src/sources/transitService.js`, which can't import server modules, so it sets `Allow: GET` directly, like the MCP route in `src/tools/mcp/http.js`.
- The radio catalog and Fire Perimeters values, which already declared `Allow`, now use the same formatter.
- Docs: `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` (Proxy/Security Baseline) and `changelog.d/883-allow-on-405.md`.
- **Out of scope:**
  - The three read-only proxies in #794. Whichever PR lands second switches their hand-written `Allow: 'GET'` to `allowedMethods('GET')`.
  - HEAD policy, unchanged as the issue scopes.

## Verification (merged with `main` at a868cebe)

- **Regression tests:** assertions on representative GET, POST, GET+HEAD and GET+POST routes and on the formatter, in `localServices`, `localReceiversProxy`, `environmentProviders`, `spaceProviders`, `placeProviders`, `mapillaryProvider`, `googleGeocodeProxy`, `transitProvider` and `proxyErrorResponses`. The new assertions fail without the change.
- **Full suite:** `npm test` 7,714 tests with 0 failures; `npm run build`, `format:check` and `check:boundaries` pass; `npm run test:track` against `npm run dev` gives 109 passed, 0 failed, 0 skipped.
- **Live on `npm run dev`:** wrong-method requests return `405` with the expected `Allow`, e.g. POST `/api/transit/feeds` gets `GET`, HEAD `/api/overpass/status` gets `GET, POST`, DELETE `/api/overpass` gets `POST`, and POST `/api/setup/status` gets `GET`.

Thanks to @daikaginza for the site census on the issue, and to @quanticsoul4772 for validating the PR across 43 routes and catching the transit, geocode and Overpass-status gaps.

title: feat(cctv): show the hardware maker for Austin cameras
body:
> **Stacked on #645.** This reuses #645's `manufacturer` passthrough (normalize → `/api/cctv/sources` → browser catalog), so until #645 merges the diff below also shows its commits. The change itself is the last commit, `b0274ab`.

## What

Austin is the reference camera city, and its dataset ([b4k4-adkb](https://data.austintexas.gov/resource/b4k4-adkb.json)) names each camera's **maker or product line** in `camera_mfg`. Among the live (`TURNED_ON`) cameras today: Wisenet 503, Advidia 311, Axis 2, Sarix 2, Spectra Enhanced 2. The Austin pack now serves it as `manufacturer`, mapped to the full name (`Hanwha Wisenet`, `Pelco Sarix`, `Pelco Spectra Enhanced`, …). A blank value is omitted, and an unknown maker passes through trimmed.

- **HUD:** `HW HANWHA WISENET` after the FOV token.
- **Camera panel:** the label after the provider and credit.
- **Public camera state:** `hardwareLabel`.

## What it deliberately does not do

`camera_mfg` is a maker, never a model, so it says nothing about the optics. **Pose and the FOV estimate are unchanged.** There's no spec lookup and no `(DATASHEET)` FOV; that stays model-only, as in #452.

The one inference is **PTZ for Pelco Spectra**. Spectra is a PTZ-only line: all 160 Spectra models in the [CCTV Camera Database](https://github.com/ch-bas/cctv-camera-database) (CC0) are PTZ domes. Those cameras read `HW PELCO SPECTRA ENHANCED (PTZ)`, because their listed facing is at best a home position. Lines that mix fixed and PTZ hardware are labelled only. For example, the Sarix line includes one PTZ model and some Bosch AUTODOME models are fixed.

This is the same provenance principle as #639/#643 (heading) and #452 (FOV): say what the source actually tells us, and nothing more.

## Tests

`src/data/cctvAustinManufacturer.test.mjs`:
- `camera_mfg` mapping: known values, an unknown maker passes through, blank/missing gives `''`.
- The Austin loader carries `manufacturer`, omits it when blank, and leaves the pose untouched.
- **End to end through the real `/api/cctv/sources` middleware into the browser catalog**, the boundary #645's review asked to pin.
- The PTZ flag fires only for PTZ-only lines.

Checks: `npm test` 5,378 pass / 0 fail on a clean `npm ci` (two runs) · `check-package-boundaries` and `check-import-directions` green (`hardware.js` registered) · Prettier clean on all changed code. `CHANGELOG.md` and `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` are updated.

title: feat(weather): add a NOAA SWPC OVATION aurora forecast layer
body:
## What this adds

A keyless global aurora forecast layer, `weather-aurora`, from NOAA SWPC's
OVATION product. Both hemispheres, not just the northern one.

It is the rare layer that is genuinely better on a globe than on a map: an
auroral oval only reads as an oval on a sphere, and it needs altitude to read
at all.

## Source, rights and delivery

`https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/ovation_aurora_latest.json`

Verified against the live endpoint while preparing this PR: HTTP 200,
~918 KB, `Content-Type: application/json`, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`,
`Cache-Control: max-age=60`, and exactly 65,160 coordinates — 360 × 181 on a
1° grid spanning −90° to +90°.

U.S. public-domain NOAA federal information, with no contrary product
annotation. Credited as "NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) · OVATION
aurora forecast", courtesy credit, no endorsement implied. `DATA_SOURCES.md`
carries the full entry. **Nothing is vendored** — the data is fetched at
runtime.

Wildcard CORS means a browser *could* fetch it directly, so the proxy earns
its place on other grounds: `/api/aurora` validates the grid shape, bounds it,
coalesces concurrent callers, caches one ~5-minute generation, and exposes a
bounded stale last-good result explicitly flagged `stale`. It also hands the
client ~131 KB instead of ~918 KB. Without it every open tab independently
re-downloads an unchanged generation.

## It is a forecast, and says so

The layer never presents modelled probability as observation:

- Labelled `FORECAST` throughout.
- Valid time and issue/input time shown **separately**.
- The variable 30–90 minute horizon is stated, not averaged away.
- Copy says modelled probability is not guaranteed visibility; darkness,
  cloud and light pollution are not modelled.
- A low probability is not rendered as an all-clear.

## Rendering: a curtain, not a decal

The field is drawn as **nine raised shells from 95 km to 320 km**, on every
map source — globe imagery and photorealistic 3D Tiles alike.

This is the part worth reviewing. Auroral emission is in the thermosphere: the
green 557.7 nm line peaks near 100–120 km, the red 630 nm line reaches
200–400 km and is much fainter. Draping the field on the surface — which is
all an imagery layer can do, since imagery has no altitude — puts the aurora
on the ground. A single raised sheet is not much better: right height, no
body, still a decal seen edge-on.

Three properties make the stack work, each one a fix for the version before:

- **Per-shell alphas are small.** Compositing is `1 − Π(1 − a)`, so the nine
  together come to about the opacity one shell carried. The view from above is
  as bright as a single sheet rather than saturating.
- **They are closely spaced.** Spent as a few strong shells, the limb read as
  venetian blinds instead of a curtain.
- **Meshes coarsen with altitude**, since a facet 300 km up subtends less
  against the limb. The stack totals **~208k cells against ~259k for one
  0.5° shell** — the curtain costs *less* geometry than the sheet it replaced.

`createShellSurface` gains an optional `granularityDegrees` (default 0.5,
unchanged for existing callers) to make that possible.

## Share token

`5`, provisionally: the next free digit `npm run layer-token:next` reports
against current `main` (`3` and `4` went to `gnss-integrity` and `air-quality`
while this was open). Per CONTRIBUTING.md the token is assigned against the
merge-time base, and several open PRs (#887, #1089, #1090, #1091, #1143, #1175,
#1188) hold the same provisional `5`. Whichever merges first keeps it; I'll
rerun the helper and take the next one if this isn't first.

The ledger fixtures in `layerStateTokenLedger.test.mjs` that used `5` as their
"next free" token shift accordingly. **`LEGACY_LAYER_STATE_TOKENS` is
deliberately left frozen**: it records what is already in the wild, and a new
layer earns a fresh reservation rather than joining it.

## Gates

Run locally on this branch, rebased onto `main`:

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run doctor -- --json` | pass |
| `npm run format:check` | pass |
| `npm run check:boundaries` | pass |
| `npm run layer-token:check -- --base-ref origin/main` | pass — 29 published, 1 new |
| `npm test` | pass — 6021/6022, 0 failures (1 skipped) |
| `npm run build` | pass |

Feature gates, per CONTRIBUTING, for the shared weather-shell code this
touches:

- **`qa-layer-token-twochar.mjs`** — 10 passed, 0 failed.
- **`qa-weather-journey.mjs`** — all 19 steps; wind, radar, satellite,
  lightning and cyclones all report `error: null`. It emits some
  `chip ... missing or disabled` warnings; a pristine `main` worktree emits a
  strict superset of them (10 distinct against 6 here), so this branch adds
  none.
- **`qa-weather-teardown.mjs`** — reports
  `{"listeners.moveEnd": [5, 8], "windCells": [null, 0]}`. **This is
  pre-existing**: the same gate on a pristine `main` worktree produces a
  byte-identical verdict. Not introduced here, and not fixed here either.

**Not run:** `npm run test:track`, and the `qa-*.mjs` gates unrelated to
weather. `test:track` is a 3D tracking harness this change does not touch.

## Verification

Driven in a headless browser on **both** imagery hosts, because the two take
different render paths:

- Globe imagery (keyless default): the shells install, `imageryLayers`
  untouched.
- Photorealistic 3D Tiles: `primitives` 2 → 3+ as the stack is added.

On both: the layer registers, enables to a `nominal` feed, and draws a
continuous curtain standing off the limb with no console errors.

Against live data the field is correctly near-invisible right now — the
current forecast peaks at 14% with no cell above 25%. Rendering was confirmed
by driving the same code path with a synthetic high-probability grid, which is
also how the limb gradient and the brightness-from-above were tuned.

title: Feat/view angles
Add a Magnetosphere layer: IGRF-14 filaments, Tsyganenko T89c/T96 external field, and a live magnetopause
body:
## What this adds

A `magnetosphere` layer: Earth's magnetic field drawn as filaments in 3D, with
a magnetopause boundary that follows the live solar wind.

The field is not fetched. IGRF-14 ships as a derived table and the field lines
are traced in the browser, so the geometry needs no network at all — only the
solar wind state crosses the wire, through `/api/magnetosphere`, in a few
hundred bytes.

Like the aurora, this is a layer that only works on a globe. A magnetotail is a
three-dimensional object; there is no useful 2-D projection of it.

## The honest version of what is drawn

IGRF models the field generated *inside* the Earth. Past a few Earth radii the
external magnetospheric currents dominate, and with IGRF alone the lines
balloon out on the dayside and never form a tail. So the trace adds an external
field from a Tsyganenko model — whichever the live feed supports:

| Model | Needs | Gives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **T96** | Pdyn, Dst, IMF By and Bz | Explicit magnetopause, interconnection field, so southward IMF erodes the dayside |
| **T89c** | Kp only | Seven disturbance bands, no boundary, no IMF — but it needs one number |
| neither | — | Internal field only, visibly wrong past a few Re |

When the feed supports neither, the filaments stay internal-only and the row
says so. There is deliberately **no fallback to a guessed storm state**: a
magnetosphere modelled as calm during a storm looks entirely plausible and is
entirely false. The row's meta line names the model that drew the lines on
screen, and says when either is being run outside the parameter range it was
fitted within.

Both models are empirical fits, not physics, and both stop at 70 Re — their
stated limit of validity — rather than extrapolating into a region they were
never fitted for.

## Sources and rights

Everything here is public domain U.S. federal data or an IAGA model distributed
as such. `DATA_SOURCES.md` carries the full entries.

- **IAGA IGRF-14** — *vendored*, not fetched. `scripts/build-igrf-coefficients.mjs`
  derives an 8.8 KB table from IAGA's 42 KB distribution, so the field model
  ships with the app. It is the only vendored piece.
- **NOAA SWPC propagated solar wind** — speed, density, IMF By/Bz, already
  time-shifted from L1 to Earth, which is what a magnetopause model wants.
- **NOAA SWPC planetary K index** — Kp, T89's only input.
- **Kyoto Dst via NOAA SWPC** — hourly Dst, T96's ring-current input.

The three live feeds are keyless and send wildcard CORS, so the proxy earns its
place on other grounds: it validates shape, bounds the body, coalesces
concurrent callers, caches one generation per minute, and serves a bounded
last-good result explicitly flagged `stale`. Each auxiliary feed has its own
cache and fails soft — losing Dst costs T96 and nothing else; losing Kp costs
T89 and nothing else; neither touches the boundary.

## The magnetopause is a model surface

Shue et al. (1998), driven by live dynamic pressure and IMF Bz. It is drawn as
a cage rather than a solid shell for exactly that reason, it reports when it is
driven inside geosynchronous orbit, and it says when the solar wind has left
the range the fit was published for.

## Validation

The two Tsyganenko models are mechanical transliterations of the MIT-licensed
Python `geopack` translation of Tsyganenko's Fortran. That is the only
defensible way to add 3,000 lines of dense empirical arithmetic: a transcription
slip anywhere still produces a smooth field that looks like a magnetosphere, so
agreeing with ourselves would prove nothing.

Each layer is checked against something that is not itself:

- **IGRF** — 105 points against Python `geopack`, agreeing to 0.0002%. This
  caught a real bug: Schmidt semi-normalisation seeds the sectoral recursion at
  *n* = 1 and only applies `sqrt((2n-1)/2n)` from *n* = 2 up. Getting that wrong
  left every sectoral term short by √2 — a field that was smooth,
  self-consistent and about 10% wrong at the equator.
- **T89c** — 420 points across bands, tilts and positions.
- **T96** — 61,488 points over seven solar wind states, six dipole tilts and
  positions from 2.5 to 60 Re. Worst absolute error **9.7e-11 nT**, worst
  relative **1.4e-11**, half the points bit-identical. The committed fixture is
  a stratified sample covering all fourteen reachable combinations of the three
  magnetopause cases, four region-1 zones and five region-2 branches, and a test
  asserts every branch is actually exercised.
- **Bessel J0/J1** — T96's cylindrical harmonics need them and nothing in the
  tree had them. Ascending series crossed over to the Hankel asymptotic
  expansion at 12, which is measured rather than guessed: worst absolute error
  over 0–60 is 8.6e-13 there, against 5.8e-11 at a crossover of 10 and 2.3e-11
  at 16. Checked against a spectrally-accurate quadrature of the integral
  representation, which shares no coefficients or truncation rule with it.

Beyond the fixtures there are property tests that would catch a sign or index
slip the fixtures might not: outside the magnetopause the external field must
cancel the geodipole *exactly*; the subsolar standoff must follow `pdyn^-0.14`
to round-off; and reflecting the equator (`z → -z`, `ps → -ps`) must flip the
field as a pseudovector.

## Note on the layer-state token

This claims `5`, provisionally: it's what `npm run layer-token:next` hands out
against current `main` (`3` and `4` went to `gnss-integrity` and `air-quality`
while this was open), and what `layer-token:check` enforces.

It is shared with my aurora PR #885 and with #1089, #1090, #1091, #1143, #1175
and #1188. That is the ledger working as designed: CONTRIBUTING.md assigns the
token against the merge-time base, so whichever merges first keeps `5` and the
rest rerun the helper. I'll do the one-line bump here if this isn't first.

## Gates

`npm run build`, `npm test` (**6068 pass, 0 fail**, rebased onto `7cbe04f`) are green, as are `doctor`, `format:check`,
`check:boundaries` and `layer-token:check`.

`scripts/qa-magnetosphere.mjs` is the layer's own gate — **16 passed, 0 failed**.
It measures the drawn polylines rather than trusting the row label, because the
one failure mode the unit tests cannot see is a layer that names an external
model while the filaments were traced without one. It also blocks the feed and
asserts the opposite: still drawing, naming no model, staying inside the
internal budget. See the comment below for details.

Also green on the surfaces this touches: `qa-layer-panel` (0 failures),
`qa-layer-token-twochar` (10 pass, 0 fail) and `qa-weather-journey` (19 steps,
exit 0), since the layer sits in the Weather group.

## Reviewing this

42 files is a lot, but most of it is generated or transliterated and not
hand-written logic:

- `src/layers/magnetosphere/t96.js` (2,386) and `t89.js` (605) are
  transliterations; the coefficient tables inside them were extracted
  programmatically rather than retyped.
- `igrf-coefficients.json` (1,379) is built by a committed script.
- The three `*-reference.fixture.json` files (2,794) are generated evidence.

The parts that are genuinely new judgement are `external.js` (which model to
run), `trace.js` (the integrator), `magnetopause.js`, `gsm.js` and the layer's
`index.js`.

This is a narrow request-path optimization for identical concurrent terrain-height batches.

Before:
`N identical concurrent callers -> N transport requests`

After:
`N identical concurrent callers -> 1 shared transport -> N independent results`

Cancellation remains per-caller: one waiter can abort without cancelling work still needed by another; the shared loader aborts only when its final waiter leaves.

Scope is intentionally small:
- terrain height requests only;
- no TTL, SWR, or stale-data policy;
- settled keys are not cached by the singleflight primitive;
- existing terrain freshness/cache semantics remain authoritative.

title: fix(hud): label the summary's longitude zone as a nautical zone, not a UTC offset
body:
Fixes #775.

## What

The deterministic HUD summary line computes `Math.round(lonDeg / 15)`, which is a nautical time zone, but printed it as `UTC+N` and described it in comments as the "local timezone". As the issue shows, that reads as a civil offset and is wrong for most places (Madrid `UTC+0`, Delhi `UTC+5`, and so on).

- `src/hud.js`: the token is now `ZONE+7` / `ZONE-4` instead of `UTC+7` / `UTC-4`. The arithmetic is unchanged.
- The JSDoc and inline comment now say nautical time zone instead of local timezone.
- `CHANGELOG.md`: one entry.

title: feat(search): place search through an operator's SearXNG instance
body:
## What

Place search can use an operator's own SearXNG instance. With `SEARXNG_URL` set (Provider Settings → SEARXNG, or `.env`), location search, voice fly-to and annotation landmark lookup ask that instance first, before Google, Photon and Nominatim. Without the setting nothing changes.

## How

- `server/providers/places/searxng.js` adds `/api/searxng/geocode` and `/api/searxng/text-search`. The instance URL stays server-side; the browser never supplies or sees it.
- Requests use the map category with `format=json`, refuse redirects, time out after 8 s, cap bodies at 1 MB, are limited to 60/min per client and cached for five minutes. Upstream errors are returned as a generic message.
- Results are normalized to Nominatim-shaped hits, so the existing consumers are unchanged. Geocoding prefers a hit inside the bias bounds; text search keeps hits inside the radius.
- The reusable `./search` package only adds the SearXNG step when its caller supplies the endpoints.
- `npm run doctor` reports which search chain is active.
- Docs: `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`, `DATA_SOURCES.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `.env.example`.

## Verification

- `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run layer-token:check`, `npm test` and `npm run build` pass on this branch.
- New unit tests cover URL normalization, hit normalization, the unconfigured case, caching, redirect refusal, bias and radius selection, sanitized failures, and a malformed request path.
- Manually tested against a real SearXNG instance: the search bar and voice fly-to resolve through it, and a repeated query is answered from the cache.
- **Not run:** `npm run test:track` and the `qa-*.mjs` gates. The machine this was developed on has no browser, so I could not run the headless gates.

## Notes

- A request path such as `/api/searxng/geocode//?q=a` reaches the handler as `//?q=a`, which `new URL()` rejects. This route answers it with 400 (covered by a test). `server/providers/places/google.js` parses `req.url` the same way and looks exposed to the same unhandled rejection; I left it alone to keep this PR focused and can send a separate fix.
- This PR, the Gemini Live PR and the HTTPS PR each add an entry at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` and touch neighbouring lines in a few shared files, so whichever merges later needs a trivial rebase. Happy to do that.

title: feat(voice): Gemini Live as a switchable voice provider
body:
## What

Voice control can run on Google Gemini Live as an alternative to OpenAI Realtime. A provider chip on the voice control (`OPENAI` / `GEMINI`) switches the session adapter; the choice is remembered per browser and defaults to OpenAI. Without a `GEMINI_API_KEY` nothing changes for existing users.

## How

- `server/providers/gemini.js` keeps `GEMINI_API_KEY` server-side and mints a single-use ephemeral token at `/api/gemini/token`. Model, optional voice, the shared instructions and the tools are locked into the token's setup. Errors are sanitized and `GEV_RATELIMIT_GEMINI_PER_MIN` adds an opt-in per-client limit.
- `src/voice/geminiSession.js` implements the existing common session interface over the constrained Live WebSocket. Tool calls go through the same action runner as OpenAI, using the same schemas converted to Gemini's subset (`src/voice/geminiTools.js`).
- `src/voice/geminiAudio.js` captures 16 kHz PCM16 through an AudioWorklet and plays the 24 kHz replies gaplessly. Capture takes the loudest input channel, so a microphone on any input of a multi-channel interface is heard.
- The listening detail names the captured microphone. After six seconds without sound it says whether capture did not start, the browser receives no audio, or the signal is silent. Browsers keep the microphone choice per origin, and this made a wrong-device case obvious during testing.
- Provider Settings and `npm run doctor` know the new key.
- Docs: `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `.env.example`.

Cost display, push-to-talk, viewport screenshots and the HUD summary remain OpenAI-only.

## Verification

- `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run layer-token:check`, `npm test` and `npm run build` pass on this branch.
- New unit tests cover schema conversion, the token route (locked setup, missing key, sanitized failures), the session against a fake WebSocket (setup order, tool calls, cancellation, interruption, transcripts, unexpected close, stop or close during the microphone prompt), the silent-microphone notice and the provider toggle.
- Manually tested with a real free-tier key in Chrome on Windows: voice commands work through Gemini on `https://localhost` and from another machine over HTTPS. The default model id `gemini-3.8-live` was accepted.
- **Not run:** `npm run test:track` and the `qa-*.mjs` gates. The machine this was developed on has no browser, so I could not run the headless gates.

## Notes

- The token's lock relies on Google's constrained-endpoint semantics; the server also returns the setup so the client can send the matching first frame.
- After a provider switch, `debug.voiceCommands` in `src/app/tools.js` still points at the previous (disposed) controls. The new session is disposed through the shared signal, so nothing leaks, but the debug handle is stale.
- This PR, the SearXNG PR and the HTTPS PR each add an entry at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` and touch neighbouring lines in a few shared files, so whichever merges later needs a trivial rebase. Happy to do that.

title: feat(server): optional HTTPS for the dev and preview server
body:
## What

The dev and preview server can serve HTTPS when `HTTPS_CERT_FILE` and `HTTPS_KEY_FILE` point at PEM files (for example from `mkcert`). Browsers grant the microphone only to HTTPS or localhost pages, so this is what makes voice control usable when GEV is opened from another machine with `HOST=0.0.0.0`. Without the settings nothing changes.

## How

- `server/standalone/vite.config.js` reads the two paths and passes the PEM contents to `createBrowserViteConfig({ https })`. Setting only one fails at startup.
- `fs.deny` now also covers `*.key`, so key material inside the checkout is not served.
- Vite serves HTTPS over HTTP/2, which has no `Host` header. The loopback-only Provider Settings gate read only `Host`, so over HTTPS it refused every request and the panel disappeared. `keySetupRequestAuthority` now takes the authority from `:authority` or `Host` and refuses a request where the two disagree. The loopback-socket, local-hostname, proxy-header and exact-Origin checks are unchanged.
- Docs: `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `.env.example`.

## Security notes

- TLS is not authentication. Everyone who can reach the server can still spend the configured keys; `SECURITY.md` says so next to the existing LAN opt-in.
- Vite does not install its `allowedHosts` check when `server.https` is set and relies on certificate validation against DNS rebinding. This is documented in `SECURITY.md` rather than worked around; say if you would prefer an explicit host check in this repo.

## Verification

- `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run layer-token:check`, `npm test` and `npm run build` pass on this branch.
- New unit tests cover the option parsing, the passed-through config and the authority helper, including HTTP/2-shaped requests through the admission gate.
- Manually tested with an `mkcert` certificate: the app, the API routes and Provider Settings work on `https://localhost`, a LAN client is still refused by Provider Settings, and the microphone works from another machine in Chrome on Windows.
- **Not run:** `npm run test:track` and the `qa-*.mjs` gates. The machine this was developed on has no browser, so I could not run the headless gates.

## Notes

- `scripts/dev-fresh.sh` still prints `http://` URLs when HTTPS is enabled.
- This PR, the SearXNG PR and the Gemini Live PR each add an entry at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` and touch neighbouring lines in a few shared files, so whichever merges later needs a trivial rebase. Happy to do that.

title: feat(draw): import GPX, KML and GeoJSON onto the whiteboard, and export the board
body:
Closes #890.

## What

DISPLAY ▸ Draw gains **Import** and **Export** beside Clear.

- **Import** reads a GPX, KML or GeoJSON file in the browser and puts its tracks, areas and points on the whiteboard. Nothing is uploaded.
- Each imported file gets a row with **Hide/Show** and **Remove**, which is the show/hide/delete the issue asks for.
- **Export** saves the marks on the board as a GeoJSON file that imports back unchanged, so a drawing can outlive the session.

## How it fits the existing design

Imported features go through the same `annotationEngine.annotate()` that Draw and the voice agent use, as `manual: true` specs. `featuresToSpecs` produces exactly what `finishSpec` produces for a hand-drawn shape, and a test compares the two. Imported marks therefore drape, de-dup, list and clear like any other mark, and no renderer changed.

The one engine change is `remove(ids)`: it takes named marks off the board without clearing the rest and without superseding in-flight work for other marks. Hide is `remove` plus the retained specs; Show annotates them again.

## Decisions worth a look

- **XML is scanned, not passed to `DOMParser`.** `pathXml.js` builds a plain tree with node and depth ceilings and never expands document-declared entities. It also runs without a DOM, so the whole import is unit tested under node.
- **Limits are reported, not silent.** 16 MB per file, 60 marks per file, 12 files, and lines over 2,000 points are simplified with Visvalingam–Whyatt (keeps corners, O(n log n) on any input). The status line says what was simplified or skipped and why.
- **A file only claims marks it created.** A feature that duplicates an existing mark is not tracked, so removing a file cannot delete something drawn by hand.
- **Clear empties the file list too**, and a board cleared by voice is reconciled before the list is acted on.
- **I changed one existing test.** `drawTool.test.mjs` forbade the docs from mentioning GeoJSON near the Draw description, because Draw had no export. The board now has one, so that guard keeps the draw modules from claiming it and no longer restricts the docs.

## Not included

- KMZ (zip) is refused with an instruction to unzip it.
- Polygon holes, elevation, timestamps and KML styling are not carried.
- Imports are not persisted across reloads; Export is the way to keep a board.
- No rendered `scripts/qa-*.mjs` gate for import yet.

## Verification

- `npm test`: 5,463 tests, 0 failures (93 new tests across 10 files)
- `npm run build`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`: pass
- Live on `npm run dev` (keyless, Esri imagery): imported a 400-point GPX track with a waypoint and a KML polygon through `window.__gevPathImport`, confirmed the marks drape on the map, then hid, re-showed, exported and removed them and cleared the board.
- Not run: `npm run test:track` and `scripts/qa-draw-tool.mjs`. I also did not drive the native file picker by hand; the `change` handler is covered by the behaviour test.

The 20 commits are ordered so each reader, the import core, export, the engine change, the UI, wiring and docs can be reviewed on their own.

title: Add a shared tool catalog and MCP server, with God's Eye View inside Claude and ChatGPT
body: ## Summary This adds MCP support to God's Eye View: a shared tool catalog, a local MCP server, and the live globe inside AI conversations. - **Tool catalog** (`gods-eye-view/tools`): queries defined once over the layers' existing source factories — aircraft, ships, satellites, earthquakes, fires, launches, cameras, weather, cyclones, terrain, infrastructure, military awareness, situation briefs and more. Voice uses the same catalog next to its app actions; a per-tool table chooses which tools each surface (MCP, voice) offers. - **MCP server** (`gods-eye-view/tools/mcp`): `npm run mcp` serves the catalog over stdio, and the development and preview servers answer `/mcp` for local requests. Answers report partial or stale data honestly. - **Views and links**: answers that can be shown include a view (camera, layers, style, map, marks, an aircraft or satellite to follow, or an aircraft's cockpit view) in the share-link format, and every view has a link that opens the full app there. - **God's Eye View in the conversation**: `show_in_gods_eye_view` displays a view as the live globe in clients that support MCP Apps — Claude Desktop and the Codex and ChatGPT desktop apps — and as a link everywhere else. - **Embed mode**: `?embed=1` shows the globe alone and takes new views from the page that frames it. ## Screenshots Claude Desktop: Codex desktop: ## How the panel works Hosts render MCP Apps panels on their own sites under strict content security policies, and some refuse any address on the user's machine. So the panel never contacts the app's server: it loads the app's panel build and its data through `panel_request`, a tool only the panel may call, and the MCP server fetches each path from the app's server. A local server therefore needs no HTTPS, certificates or tunnel. `panel_request` stays on the app's server, refuses `/api/setup`, does not follow redirects, and bounds response size and time. `npm run build:panel` writes the panel build to `dist/panel` (served at `/panel/`): one app script, one stylesheet and Cesium's script, which starts its workers from memory. Files those workers load themselves are embedded in a prelude the panel runs ahead of them. Host differences the panel works around, inside the panel only: images load as `data:` URLs, the globe keeps drawing when a host reports the panel hidden, and 2D canvases are kept in memory so overlays cannot turn black over the globe. Details are in `docs/TOOLS.md`. ## Try it [`docs/MCP_SETUP.md`](docs/MCP_SETUP.md) has one-page setup for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, the Codex CLI and the Codex and ChatGPT desktop apps. In short: `npm run build:panel`, `npm run dev`, add `server/mcp/stdio.js` to the client, quit it fully, and ask in a new chat to show a place in God's Eye View. ## Verification - `npm run build`; `npm test` (5,542 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped); format and boundary checks; `npm run test:track` (109 passed, 0 failed, no console errors). - Tested by hand in Claude Desktop and Codex desktop, inline and expanded, with flights, military aircraft, vessels, traffic and the CRT style. `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` and `docs/TOOLS.md` describe the changes.

title: Integration question: supported opt-in trusted-local embedding for Hermes Desktop
body:
## Integration question: supported trusted-local embedding design

We maintain a community Hermes Desktop wrapper around the separate, unmodified official GEV checkout. Is there a supported opt-in trusted-local embedding mode, or a recommended integration architecture that preserves the provider-settings/clickjacking boundaries?

### Observed behavior

On October 2, 2026 (Pacific), the tested local engine answered its document with HTTP 200 and:

```text
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Frame-Options: DENY
```

The Electron host console reported:

```text
Framing 'http://localhost:4173/' violates the following Content Security Policy directive: "frame-ancestors 'none'". The request has been blocked.
```

The standalone browser visibly renders and responds to camera controls. The header refusal occurs before we can exercise provider requests/storage in the embedded frame. `build/vite.js` and `server/standalone/key-setup.js` explicitly establish these protections; we have not altered them.

### Separate host constraint

Hermes catalog review required moving from a historically functioning Electron webview to SDK `SandboxedFrame`, with its default opaque-origin sandbox. Raw webviews, shared private preview partitions and guest scripting are not approved plugin APIs. This is a distinct host restriction; the engine's anti-framing policy is the immediate observed blocker, not a claim that GEV cannot render in Electron.

[v0.1.3-legacy.1](https://github.com/cygnostik/Hermes-Plugin-Gods-Eye-View/releases/tag/v0.1.3-legacy.1) is a clearly labeled separate legacy compatibility prerelease, using the historical renderer with a dependency-marker repair. It is not SDK/catalog approved or freshly native-certified. The accepted catalog pin remains SDK v0.1.2. The original renderer had live verification in September, including [September 25 results](https://github.com/cygnostik/Hermes-Plugin-Gods-Eye-View/issues/1).

### Research and request

I checked embedding/iframe/frame-ancestors/SandboxedFrame discussions and current README/source. #748 proposed same-origin sub-path embedding but is closed without merge; it is not a shipped solution for an opaque-origin host frame. #242 discusses strengthening CSP and same-site gates. Pinokio discussions such as #789 concern a different embedded-browser path.

We recognize why provider setup, local paid-provider endpoints and clickjacking need protection. We are NOT requesting blanket header removal, permissive CORS, weakening all local endpoints, or a proxy that strips policy. Would you recommend an explicitly enabled, narrowly scoped trusted-local embed design (possibly keeping provider setup outside the embed), a supported integration API, or standalone-browser-only operation? We are separately asking Hermes about an approved isolated webContents/partition primitive or a reviewed exception, rather than assuming either maintainer has granted one.

No provider values, private sessions or user configuration are needed for this question. Happy to supply a small keyless reproduction if useful.

title: Tighten the local MCP server and embed mode
body:
Follow-up hardening for the v0.2.0 MCP server, panel and embed mode.

- **Panel requests:** `panel_request` requires a key each MCP server places in its panel page, which keeps the tool from clients that list it without loading the panel (it is not access control; see SECURITY.md). Provider Settings, credential and model endpoints, `/mcp` and development-server internals are refused to every caller, in any letter case or encoding.
- **Embed mode:** no longer framable unless `GEV_EMBED_FRAME_ANCESTORS` allows the framing page; view answers go only to the origin that sent the view. The MCP Apps panel does not use framing.
- **`/mcp` gate:** applies Provider Settings' proxy and sharing checks (now shared helpers in `keySetupCore`), requires a Host on the port reached and an Origin matching that host.
- **Limits:** panels on one server share six in-flight requests and further requests wait their turn; held responses are per server; `/mcp` request bodies time out after 30 seconds; stdio honors `notifications/cancelled`.
- **Docs:** SECURITY.md gains an MCP server and panel section; TOOLS.md, CURRENT-STATE.md, `.env.example` and the changelog are updated.

Note: a panel page opened before this change has no key and needs a reload.

Validation: `npm test` on Node 24 (5,552 pass, 0 fail), `format:check`, `check:boundaries`; each commit passes its affected tests; local smoke test against a dev server with the panel build.

title: Harden the local server: cross-site gate, CSP, default throttles, LAN host check
body:
Consolidates four community security PRs onto current `main`, keeping each author's credit.

| Commit | Credit | Change |
|---|---|---|
| fix(server): gate cost/log endpoints against cross-site requests and ship a full CSP | **@jasas1** — salvaged from #242 | Cost-bearing and debug-log endpoints refuse cross-site browser requests; one shared CSP for dev and preview; embed-mode framing rewrites only `frame-ancestors`. |
| fix(server): throttle the cost-bearing proxies by default | **@daikaginza** — salvaged from #683 | 30/min OpenAI and 120/min Google per IP by default (the Pinokio values); `0` opts out; unreadable values fall back to the default. |
| fix(server): keep the Host-header check when binding to all interfaces | **@puspoaditya** — ported from #97 | `HOST=0.0.0.0` no longer sets `allowedHosts: true`; IP addresses and `localhost` work, LAN hostnames are listed in `GEV_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Fixes #21. |
| fix(server): keep debug-log timestamps server-owned and send nosniff | from findings by **@Sunil56224972** in #710 | The server's `loggedAt` can no longer be replaced by a record; `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`. |
| refactor(server): share one proxy-header check across the local gates | maintainer | One `hasProxySignals` (in `localRequestGate.mjs`) for Provider Settings, the cross-site gate and `/mcp`. |
| fix(mcp): refuse panel requests to routes reached through a dot suffix | maintainer | The server routes `/mcp.json` to `/mcp` (a dot after a mounted route still matches); `panel_request`'s refusals now cover that for `/mcp`, Provider Settings and the credential/model routes. Regression test against a real Vite server. |
| fix(server): apply the Host check before the app's own routes | maintainer | Vite installs its Host check after plugin middleware, so `/api` routes answered any Host (including DNS-rebinding names) in every mode. A first-running `hostCheckPlugin` applies Vite's rule on dev and preview. Test drives a real Vite server. |
| fix(server): gate Google text search against cross-site requests | maintainer | `/api/google/text-search` joins nearby-places behind the cross-site gate. |
| fix(server): keep cost throttles on for positive fractional limits | maintainer | `0.5` no longer floors to unlimited; positive values below 1 count as 1. |
| fix(server): let the CSP load the Nepal event's embedded media | maintainer | `script-src` adds exactly the YouTube, Facebook and X scripts and a new `frame-src` their embeds; verified in Chrome with each provider's API and zero violations, and a test ties the policy to the frames the media module builds. |

**Behavior change:** names ending in `.local` are no longer accepted by default; add them to `GEV_ALLOWED_HOSTS`. Documented in the changelog and `.env.example`.

Validation on Node 24: `npm test` 5,587 pass / 0 fail, `format:check`, `check:boundaries`. Dev server bound to `0.0.0.0`: `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and the LAN IP answer 200 on pages and `/api` routes; unlisted hostnames get 403 on both. The app loads in Chrome under the new CSP and `nosniff` with no violations.

Supersedes #242, #683, #97 and the remaining fixes in #710; those will be closed with credit once this lands.

title: build: ship each bundled data pack once
body:
The production build emitted every bundled data pack twice: the `.json` the browser fetches, and a JavaScript copy nothing loads. The copy came from a literal `import('./….json')` each caller passed to `loadBundledJson` as a Node-only fallback, which the bundler followed.

- `loadBundledJson(url, { signal })` now reads `file:` URLs itself under Node via `process.getBuiltinModule('node:fs')` (synchronously, as promptly as the cached import it replaces), and callers pass only the URL. The browser path (`fetch` of the `.json`) is unchanged.
- On a Node too old to provide `getBuiltinModule`, it reports that Node 24.14 or newer is needed instead of a cryptic error.
- Callers updated: `adminBoundaries`, `naturalEarthRegions`, `militaryNames`, `neighborhoodPolygons`.
- A test keeps app code from importing a pack as a module (verified to fail on a planted import).

**Result:** `dist/` 54 MB → 42 MB; the regions, marine, countries, states/provinces, counties, military-names and San Francisco neighborhood packs ship once.

**Validation:** `npm test` on Node 24 (5,590 pass / 0 fail), `format:check`, `check:boundaries`, `build`. In Chrome all seven packs load as JSON and region, admin, military-name and neighborhood lookups resolve. In plain Node 24 (the MCP server and dev-server providers load these modules) the same lookups resolve, matching `main`.

title: bug: one TLE set missing a line drops every satellite after it in the group
body:
### What happened

`parseTleText()` reads a group in fixed steps of three lines, so one set that is missing a line puts every later set out of step and each is skipped: the rest of the group is dropped, and nothing reports it.

Eight sets with the second one's line 2 removed give one entry, where the same text whole gives eight. The satellites layer then logs the group as loaded with one satellite, and `next_satellite_pass` says a satellite that is in the text is not in the group. The loop is at `src/sources/tle.js:12`. Its test covers a broken block of three lines, which keeps the step; a block of two does not.

Found with the corrupt-input case of https://github.com/hneogy/gp-omm-conformance. I can send a patch that reads each set from its line 1 and line 2, so that a short set costs only itself, if you want one.

### Steps to reproduce

From the repository root at v0.2.1, save this as `repro.mjs` and run `node repro.mjs`. It prints `8`, then `[ 'SAT 0' ]`.

```js
import { parseTleText } from './src/sources/tle.js';

const set = (n) =>
  `SAT ${n}\n` +
  `1 ${25544 + n}U 98067A   24001.50000000  .00016717  00000-0  30270-3 0  9994\n` +
  `2 ${25544 + n}  51.6416 247.4627 0006703 130.5360 325.0288 15.50377579432414\n`;
const whole = Array.from({ length: 8 }, (_, n) => set(n)).join('');
const broken = whole.replace(/\n2 25545[^\n]*/, ''); // SAT 1 loses its line 2

console.log(parseTleText(whole).length); // 8
console.log(parseTleText(broken).map((entry) => entry.name)); // [ 'SAT 0' ]
```

### How you installed

Terminal (git clone + npm)

### OS, Node version, browser

macOS 27.0.1, Node 26.5.0, no browser (the module was called directly)

### Version or commit

v0.2.1 (aa16b7c); the same loop was in `src/layers/satellites/orbits.js` before v0.2.0

### Output of `npm run doctor`

```text
Not pasted: no provider is involved. The reader was called directly with the text above, and no server was running. I will run it and paste the output if you want it.
```

### Server log and browser console

```text
None from the snippet beyond the two lines it prints. With a group of that shape served as stations, the satellites layer logs "[Data:Satellites] Loaded stations:1" and does not list stations among the groups that failed or came back empty.
```

title: fix: resolve bundled data URLs when used, not at import
body:
## Summary

The submarine cable source and the infrastructure data URLs (datacenters and dams) built their asset URLs from `import.meta.url` while the module loaded. Importing `@gods-eye-view/core/tools/services` therefore threw `Invalid URL` in any runtime without a usable module URL, even for tools that never read those files.

The URLs are now built when they are read:

- `src/layers/submarineCables/bundledSource.js`: the two URLs are functions called from `fetch`.
- `src/sources/infrastructureData.js`: `INFRASTRUCTURE_DATA_URLS` keeps its shape; its entries are getters.
- `src/data/infrastructure.js`: reads the URLs when creating the layers.

Vite still rewrites `new URL('…', import.meta.url)` inside functions, so browser builds are unchanged.

## Testing

- `npm test`: 5,601 passed, 0 failed.
- A bundle of the tool services, loaded with `import.meta.url` unavailable, previously failed with `Invalid URL` and now loads.

title: feat(desktop): standalone Windows app built by GitHub Actions
body:
## Summary

Adds a standalone Windows desktop build: an Electron shell around the same local server `npm run dev` runs, packaged by a GitHub Actions workflow into an NSIS installer and a portable zip. It is not a link to a hosted site. The application source, its production dependencies and a pinned Node runtime ship inside the installer, so every provider and the in-app key setup (POWER UP) work as they do from a checkout.

Everything lives under `desktop/` and a new workflow, so nothing else in the app changes except one small hook described below. Nothing needs to be installed on a developer machine: the workflow builds on a Windows runner.

## How it works

- `desktop/main.cjs` and `desktop/lib/`: single-instance lock, splash window, window-state persistence, application menu, and a child process that runs `desktop/runtime/serve.mjs` (Vite's dev server, bound to `127.0.0.1` on a stable port so localStorage survives restarts).
- `desktop/scripts/stage.mjs`: assembles the payload (source plus `win32-x64` production dependencies installed with `npm --os/--cpu`) and downloads a pinned Node runtime, verified against the published SHA-256.
- `desktop/scripts/after-pack.cjs`: writes the icon and version resources into the executable with `resedit` (pure JavaScript), so no Wine or rcedit is needed.
- `desktop/scripts/smoke.mjs`: starts the staged server with the bundled `node.exe` and requests the pages and the setup API, before packaging.
- `.github/workflows/desktop.yml`: unit tests, build, smoke test, packaging, SHA-256 sums, artifact upload; pushing a `desktop-v*` tag also publishes a GitHub release.

## The one change outside `desktop/`

`GEV_STATE_DIR` is an optional directory for the writable `.env` store. `server/standalone/key-setup.js` writes provider keys there and `server/standalone/vite.config.js` loads the `.env` from there. Unset, behavior is unchanged (the repo-root `.env`), and a test covers both cases. The desktop app needs it because the installed source tree must not hold user data, which would be lost on upgrade.

## Security model

- The server binds to loopback only.
- The window runs with `contextIsolation`, `sandbox` and no Node integration, and has no preload script.
- Navigation is locked to the local origin; external links open in the system browser, and only `http(s)` links are handed to the OS.
- Only microphone capture (voice control) and fullscreen are granted; camera, geolocation and everything else are refused. The behavior is covered by unit tests in `desktop/lib/*.test.cjs`.
- The page keeps the application's own Content-Security-Policy.

## What has and has not been verified

- The workflow builds green on a Windows runner (installer and zip are produced), and the smoke test passes there: the staged server starts with the bundled Node and serves `/`, `/src/main.js` and `/api/setup/status`.
- The 9 unit tests under `desktop/lib` and the new `GEV_STATE_DIR` test pass.
- I have not installed or run the produced `.exe` on a real Windows machine, and the installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen will warn. Please treat it as a draft until someone has launched it. First launch prepares Cesium for the dev server and is slower than later ones.

## Not covered

No auto-update, no code signing, no macOS or Linux packaging.

title: test: make Recent Imagery live gate rail-reflow safe
body:
The existing `scripts/qa-recent-imagery.mjs` live gate can mistake right-rail reflow for movement within Recent Imagery, producing a false failure on an otherwise valid UI.

This is **QA-only** (one script; no runtime/application change).

- Measure controls **relative to the Recent Imagery panel**, so sibling rail motion cannot masquerade as an internal control shift.
- Preserve the existing 1% camera-destination threshold and **2 s** ZOOM IN wait by default. `QA_RECENT_IMAGERY_SLOW_RENDER=1` opts loaded SwiftShader environments into **4 s**.
- Keep the default panel-height stability tail at **1.2 s**, with a separately opted-in **0.8 s** tail for the slow-render environment.
- Drop the fork-only proof workflow that was requested to be removed upstream.

Review feedback from @asturksever (P0/P2) was addressed in `76b003bc`. The branch was mechanically reconciled against upstream `main@6dd4d015` as `36fcabcd`, preserving the same one-file QA change.

## Validation / limitations

- The original failures were observed on untouched upstream `main@aa16b7c3`.
- Earlier fork CI and live-gate evidence: [CI](https://github.com/kvnloo/gods-eye-view/actions/runs/37133725722) · [Recent Imagery browser gate](https://github.com/kvnloo/gods-eye-view/actions/runs/37133722751). **These runs predate the current head**, so they are not exact-head CI signoff.
- A source-level layout-reflow check on the prior amended head showed that a 60 px sibling-rail shift falsely changed absolute control coordinates on main but preserved panel-relative coordinates on the patch.
- Current-head upstream [CI](https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view/actions/runs/38602834408) is `action_required`, pending maintainer approval. A new live browser-gate run is still needed.

Credit: @asturksever for the actionable review and the requirement to keep normal timeout/stability thresholds unchanged.

title: fix(ui): ignore CSS-hidden panels in right rail layout
body:
A CSS-hidden right-rail panel can remain logically expanded (`collapsed` absent). The rail currently filters the `hidden` attribute but still counts `display: none` panels, which can incorrectly enable tactical `layout-exclusive` and hide every collapsed launcher.

This keeps CSS-hidden panels out of the active rail set and adds a focused regression proving they contribute no exclusivity or height allocation.

Found while validating the motion-safe Recent Imagery work; kept as an independent two-file UI fix.

## Validation

- exact-head downstream CI (Node 24, Node 26, Windows): https://github.com/kvnloo/gods-eye-view/actions/runs/37172451657
- with this fix stacked on the motion-safe imagery recut, the live Recent Imagery gate passes **107 checks / 0 failures**: https://github.com/kvnloo/gods-eye-view/actions/runs/37172387776

No Recent Imagery or camera-motion behavior changes are included in this PR.

A server serves the panel build at `PANEL_BASE` and passes the same key to the resource and to `createToolServices({ panelKey })`. The local MCP server now imports from the same entry point. Neither module has imports or load-time side effects.
