title: perf(traffic): stop clipping and re-parsing the whole road set in one task
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

Open `/?welcome=0#lat=40.7549&lon=-73.9840&alt=250&pitch=-25&v=2&l=t` (Street Traffic over Manhattan) and zoom in and out with the wheel. The page stutters, with single freezes of up to three quarters of a second. London is similar.

## Cause

Three costs ran in one task after the detail tiles arrived:

- `outsideDetailTiles` clipped every coarse road against every detail tile (up to 16) for four regions.
- The composed road set was handed on with `replace: true`, so every road was parsed again although each tile had been parsed as it streamed.
- `parseRoads` and the flow pass asked the ground floor service once per coordinate, and each call builds several string keys.

## What changed

- A road lying wholly inside one region of a tile is answered from its extent; only a road that reaches a tile's core or edge is clipped. The output is the same road set, vertex for vertex.
- Records parsed during a pass are remembered per source record, so the final snapshot parses only what is new to it (the clipped coarse roads).
- Within one parse the floor is read once per floor cell. This is used only when floors are per cell; on a map where the mesh answers per point, each coordinate is still asked.

`src/services/groundFloor.js` is not touched.

## Before and after

Keyless dev server, headless Chrome at 1440 x 900 (Apple silicon, Metal), same script on `main` (`188f0ccd9`) and on this branch. Two runs each.

| | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Manhattan zoom, 24 s: long tasks | 30 / 19 | 16 / 11 |
| Manhattan zoom: longest | 751 / 427 ms | 185 / 120 ms |
| Manhattan zoom: total | 5,981 / 3,082 ms | 1,628 / 1,022 ms |
| London pan: long tasks | 25 | 6 |
| London pan: longest | 349 ms | 162 ms |
| London pan: total | 3,600 ms | 545 ms |

Vehicle dot counts are equal in the browser (2,216 and 2,216; 442 and 442).

## Tests

- The clip's output is `deepStrictEqual` to the previous algorithm's in a unit test and a 300-case fuzz.
- New tests in `roadLoadCost.test.mjs` fail on the unfixed files.
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## Not tested

- Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles (the floor memo is off there by design).
- TomTom flow and hybrid road modes.

This is separate from the one-viewport-tile-at-a-time loading in `docs/KNOWN-ISSUES.md`, which is unchanged.

title: perf(alpr): read anchors from the terrain globe and sample outside the paint
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

With ALPR cameras on, the overlay took `scene.sampleHeight` depth renders inside its paint: 63 on load over Manhattan, 128 over Atlanta, and all of them again each time the layer was switched off and on (240 samples and about a second across eight toggles).

## Cause

`anchorFor` and `refineAnchors` in `src/layers/alpr/overlay.js` sampled from `paint()`, up to six per paint, and kept the answers on the entities, which a refresh or a re-enable rebuilds.

## What changed

- On a terrain globe an anchor is read with `globe.getHeight` from the loaded mesh; `sampleHeight` is used only where there is no terrain globe (photorealistic tiles).
- Answers are kept per camera id (up to 2,048) until the map source changes, so a rebuild asks nothing.
- What sampling remains runs after the paint from `requestAnimationFrame`, one sample per frame.

## Before and after

Keyless dev server, headless Chrome at 1440 x 900 (Apple silicon, Metal), same script on `main` (`188f0ccd9`) and on this branch.

| `sampleHeight` | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Manhattan, load | 63 calls, 219 ms | 0 |
| Atlanta, eight off/on toggles | 240 calls, 997 ms | 0 |
| Pan, zoom, settle | sampling continues | 0 |

Long tasks did not change: the longest is about 190–205 ms on both, over three runs. The 0.8–1.9 s first-sample freeze recorded in the audit did not reproduce on `main` on the day this was measured, so what this removes is the depth renders, not a freeze.

## A visible difference

Of 63 anchors over Manhattan, 45 are identical to `main`'s and 18 move by 1.0–4.3 m. Where `main`'s sample answered, it equalled `globe.getHeight` exactly; for those 18 `main`'s sample returned nothing, so `main` leaves the badge at the height of its ~111 m floor cell, and this branch puts it on the rendered terrain.

## Tests

- New tests in `overlay.test.mjs` fail on the unfixed file.
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## Not tested

Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles, where `sampleHeight` is still the only source; there the change is one sample per frame outside the paint, and remembered answers.

title: perf(cables): show landing markers a few per frame
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

Open `/?welcome=0`, let the globe load, then switch Submarine cables on. The page freezes for about 1.4 seconds.

## Cause

1.2 s of that task is Cesium reading the terrain height for the 1,917 ground-clamped landing markers. They were all shown in the first frame, including the ones behind the globe, and a shown ground-clamped billboard reads the terrain as Cesium creates it.

## What changed

Landing entities start hidden. The existing horizon sweep already decides which are visible; it now shows those 48 per rendered frame (`CABLE_LANDING_REVEALS_PER_FRAME`) and asks for another frame while any are left. Hiding is still immediate.

## Before and after

Keyless dev server, headless Chrome at 1440 x 900 (Apple silicon, Metal), same script on `main` (`188f0ccd9`) and on this branch. Two runs each.

| Switching the layer on | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| First time: longest task | 1,436–1,450 ms | 156–216 ms |
| First time: `getHeight` | 1,917 calls, 1,190 ms | 1,002 calls, 108–117 ms |
| Second time: longest task | 494–503 ms | 97–129 ms |
| Third time: longest task | 247–255 ms | 111–199 ms |

Same on both: 1,913 cable, 1,917 landing and 2,629 reference entities; 986 / 1,002 / 1,404 shown; every landing marker still ground-clamped; clicking a landing marker flies the camera to it.

## Tests

- New unit tests cover the staged reveal (in `src/data/telegeographySubmarineCables.test.mjs`).
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## What is left

The audit proposed batched primitives in place of the entity data sources. That is not done here: unclamped points at ellipsoid height sit under the terrain wherever it is higher, so they need either the depth test off (far-side markers would show through the globe during a drag) or a per-frame horizon cull, which is a behaviour decision. Still open, and needing that rewrite: a transient heap of about 1 GB on load, a task of about 150 ms on switch-off, visualiser tasks of 100–250 ms, and about 160 ms of re-clamping during zoom.

Not tested: Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles.

title: perf(flights): make the fleet pass's ground-floor reads cheap
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

Open `/?welcome=0#lat=40&lon=-40&alt=22000000&pitch=-90&v=2&l=f&dm=DENSE&dd=100` (whole globe, Live Flights, detection labels) and wait for the full feed, about 10,000 aircraft. With Chrome's CPU throttled 4x the globe runs at 6.5 frames a second.

## Cause

Every 80 ms the Flights and Military fleet passes dead-reckon each aircraft in view. A coasting one (most of them, between keyless polls a minute apart) goes through `floorCoastedPosition`, which converts the position to geodetic and reads `cachedGroundFloor`, although an aircraft at cruise can never be lifted by the ground.

Each `cachedGroundFloor` read then:

- rounded the coordinate to its coarse cell twice (`coarseFloorCoord`: two `toFixed(3)` calls, two `Number` parses and a new object each time),
- built a string key for the mesh cells and another, through two `toFixed(5)` calls, for the terrain cache,
- and on a hit deleted and re-inserted the terrain cache entry to keep it least-recently-used.

In a 15.3 s busy profile at 4x throttle, `cachedGroundFloor` was 5.9 s.

## What changed

- `src/data/motionModel.js`: `floorCoastedPosition` returns at once for a position certainly above 9,000 m (`COAST_FLOOR_CEILING_M`; Everest is about 8,821 m above the ellipsoid). The test is three multiplications on the scaled position, with no geodetic conversion.
- `src/services/groundFloor.js`: `cachedGroundFloor` works the coarse cell out once, as two integers (`coarseCellIndex`), and uses them for both the mesh read and the DEM read. Mesh cells are keyed by one packed number. `coarseFloorCoord` itself and the returned object are untouched.
- `src/services/terrainHeights.js`: the synchronous reads find entries through a numeric index kept beside the string-keyed cache, and promote an entry only once half the bound's worth of stores and promotions have passed since it was last newest. The string keys, the proxy `points` string and the batch resolver are unchanged.
- `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md`: the terrain cache paragraph says how a synchronous read now promotes.

Where the fast arithmetic could round differently from `toFixed` (within 1e-6 of a half step, a negative value that rounds to zero, a coordinate out of range), the read goes through the string as before.

## Before and after

`main` 188f0ccd9 against this branch, same script, keyless, headless Chrome 1440×900, camera still, about 10,400 aircraft with detection DENSE at 100%:

| | `main` | This branch |
|---|---|---|
| 1x, 15 s: frames drawn | 776 (52 fps) | 900 (60 fps) |
| 1x: average frame work | 13.7 ms | 10.7 ms |
| 1x: long tasks | 1 (51 ms) | 0 |
| 4x throttle, 15 s: frames drawn | 97 (6.5 fps) | 275 (18.3 fps) |
| 4x: average frame work | 160.7 ms | 55.7 ms |
| 4x: longest task | 246 ms | 128 ms |
| 4x profile: `cachedGroundFloor` | 5,933 ms | 340 ms |
| 4x profile: `floorCoastedPosition` | 5,093 ms | 900 ms |
| 4x profile: `_fleetTick` per frame | 120 ms | 28 ms |
| `toFixed` calls per floor read | 6 | 0 |

At 4x every frame is still over 50 ms, so the count of long tasks goes up with the frame rate (88 to 149); their total time goes down (14.7 s to 10.6 s).

## Tested

- `src/services/groundFloor.test.mjs` (new): `cachedGroundFloor` gives the same answer as the string-keyed read for about 2,000 probes, on cell edges, either side of zero, at -0, out of range and not finite, with mesh cells on and off; a read formats no numbers; a mesh reading is found from anywhere in its cell.
- `src/services/terrainHeights.test.mjs`: a synchronous read finds exactly the entry its 5-decimal key names (including "-0.00000" against "0.00000" and half-step coordinates); a read formats no numbers; an entry read repeatedly still outlives unread ones; an evicted entry is gone from the synchronous read.
- `src/data/motionModel.test.mjs`: nothing above the ceiling reads the ground, from pole to equator; nothing at or below it skips the read; below the ceiling the result matches the old function for 6,000 positions.
- The "formats no numbers" tests and the above-the-ceiling test fail on the unfixed files; the equivalence tests pass on both, which is what shows the floors are the same.
- `node scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`.

## Not tested

- The Google 3D Tiles mesh-floor path in the browser (no key); unit tests only.
- Grounded and landing aircraft by eye at an airport. The floors they read are covered by the equivalence tests; I only looked at the whole-globe view.
- Military alone (about 120 aircraft); it shares `floorCoastedPosition`.

## Decided differently from the plan

- No per-aircraft, per-fix floor cache. A coast moves across cells, and terrain can rise under it, so a floor kept from the fix would change results. The read is cheap enough now that it is not needed.
- Eviction order in the terrain cache differs when an entry goes unread for between half and all of the bound's worth of cache moves. With the default bound of 20,000 that needs 10,000 other cells stored or promoted between two reads of one cell.

## Follow-up

- The rest of `_fleetTick` (dead reckoning, rotation, billboard writes) is now most of the pass.
- The detection overlay's share is next: see the note on finding 8, cause B in #1697.

title: perf(radio): work out a station's tags and categories once
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

Switch Radio on anywhere. When the station directory loads, the page hitches: about 450 ms in one task.

## Cause

`stationTags()` in `src/layers/radio/categories.js` split and normalised a station's tags on every `hasTag` call, and category matching ran that for every needle of every category of every station, twice, and again for the active filter on each horizon scan.

## What changed

A station's normalised tags, detected genres and category set are worked out once and kept against the station record, and read again only if the record's tags change.

## Before and after

Keyless dev server, headless Chrome at 1440 x 900 (Apple silicon, Metal), same script on `main` (`188f0ccd9`) and on this branch. London at 20 km, two runs each.

| | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Long tasks on load | 3 | 2 |
| Longest task | 454 / 457 ms | 179 / 181 ms |
| Total | about 805 ms | about 350 ms |
| `stationMatchesRadioCategory` in the load profile | 1,005 ms | 18 ms |

## Tests

- Category counts and filter results equal a copy of the previous matcher over 1,500 generated stations and every category id.
- The new tests fail on the unfixed file.
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## Not tested

Category counts were not compared in the browser beyond the same 753 stations loading on both.

title: perf(cctv): hold continuous rendering for video only
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

Switch CCTV on over London. A nearby still-image camera activates, and from then on the scene renders 60 times a second with the camera still, although the picture changes about every ten seconds.

## Cause

`startProjectionLoop` in `src/layers/cctv/projection.js` held continuous rendering for as long as any projected camera was active, video or still.

## What changed

Only a video feed holds the continuous loop. A still asks for frames for half a second after a new image is swapped onto the plane (and after the loop is re-armed), and a focus fade asks for a frame on the ticks that restyle an icon.

## Before and after

Keyless dev server, headless Chrome at 1440 x 900 (Apple silicon, Metal), same script on `main` (`188f0ccd9`) and on this branch. London, a TfL still camera.

| Camera still, 15 s | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Renders per second | 60 | 0 between stills |
| Render hold | `cctv-projection` | none |
| Renders around a new still | continuous | about 31 in 10 s |

Fed synthetic solid-colour stills, each of 8 appeared on the plane 0.1–0.2 s after it was served, on both. Over Manhattan a video camera activates and the hold is kept, as intended.

## Tests

- New tests in `projectionLoop.test.mjs` fail on the unfixed files.
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## Not tested

Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles; a video feed's frame rate was checked only for the hold being present.

title: perf(firms): serve a cached body and gzip instead of serialising per request
body:
## What was slow

`/api/firms` filtered every fire record, built the payload and ran `JSON.stringify` over it on every request, and sent it uncompressed. In a heavy season that is tens of megabytes per response, blocking the server's event loop while it serialises and the browser while it parses.

## What changed

- The response bytes are kept (one slot) and reused for the same cache entry and stale flag while the clock stays inside the span over which the trailing-24-hour filter keeps the same records. `trailing24hWindow` in `src/data/firmsCsv.js` returns that span; `filterTrailing24h` is unchanged in what it returns.
- The body is gzipped once per kept body, on the first request that accepts gzip, through `common/compress.js` as the OpenSky provider does, with `Vary: Accept-Encoding`.

A request never gets a body that serialising for it would not have produced.

## Before and after

No FIRMS key was available, so this is measured with synthetic records over loopback, median of 20 requests.

| 100,000 records | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Same span, identity | 88 ms | 12 ms |
| Same span, gzip | 95 ms | 1.8 ms |
| New span each request, identity | 78 ms | 76 ms |
| New span each request, gzip | 77 ms | 237 ms |
| Bytes sent with gzip | 19.9 MB | 2.8 MB |

With 300,000 records: same span 274–595 ms → 49–63 ms (identity) and 442–527 ms → 8–12 ms (gzip); new span with gzip 309–352 ms → 710–922 ms; 59.6 MB → 8.4 MB.

## What this does and does not buy

The filter's span changes about once a minute as detections cross the 24-hour edge, so "serialise once per refresh" is not possible with identical output. Bursts and several clients are served from the kept bytes. A single tab polling every ten minutes still serialises each time, and with gzip spends more server time per request in exchange for about seven times fewer bytes; on loopback that reads as slower, on a real network the transfer dominates.

## Tests

- Four new tests in `src/data/firmsProxy.test.mjs`; three fail on the unfixed provider.
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## Not tested

- A live FIRMS feed.
- Memory: the server now holds one extra payload and its gzip.

title: perf(vessels): prune the AIS store on a timer and evict in insertion order
body:
## What was slow

Every AIS position message walked the whole vessel map and the pending-track map to expire stale entries. Once the store passed its 50,000 cap, each message also copied and sorted every row to find the ones to evict. The static-data map (`_aisStreamStatic`) was never pruned, so it grew for as long as the server ran.

To see it: feed synthetic messages through `ingestAisStreamEnvelope` (table below).

## Cause

`server/providers/vessels/ais-store.js` called `pruneAisStreamCache()` at the end of every ingest that wrote a vessel row; the prune did the two walks and, past the cap, the sort. Nothing ever deleted from `_aisStreamStatic`.

## What changed

- Ingest re-inserts the vessel row on update, so the map stays least recently updated first, and enforces the cap by dropping from the front. That is O(1) per message and the 50,000 bound still holds at all times.
- The expiry walk moved to the existing 15 s AIS watchdog tick in `ais-live.js` (no new timer).
- A vessel's static entry is dropped with the vessel, on expiry and on eviction. Static entries that never got a position are held to the same cap, oldest first.
- Readers do not depend on the walk: `aisStreamRows` already filtered by age, `readAisTrack` now returns nothing for an expired vessel, and a first fix older than the window no longer seeds a track.

Eviction outcome is the same as before: the least recently updated vessel goes first. Two differences: vessels updated in the same millisecond now go in update order rather than first-seen order, and a vessel that returns after more than 30 minutes no longer gets its old type, destination and IMO until its next static message (that is what dropping the static entry means).

## Before / after

200,000 synthetic messages (one in ten `ShipStaticData`, the rest `PositionReport`) through the real `ingestAisStreamEnvelope`, same script against `origin/main` and this branch. The baseline is `origin/main`'s file with a walk counter added.

| Scenario | Version | Total ms | ms/message | Prune walks | Vessels | Static entries |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 20,000 vessels (under the cap) | main | 56,067 | 0.280 | 182,000 | 20,000 | 2,000 |
| 20,000 vessels (under the cap) | this PR | 450 | 0.002 | 0 | 20,000 | 2,000 |
| 80,000 vessels (past the cap) | main | 1,016,515 | 5.083 | 200,000 | 50,000 | 8,000 |
| 80,000 vessels (past the cap) | this PR | 2,931 | 0.015 | 0 | 50,000 | 5,000 |

The script does not run the timer, so 0 walks is expected there; in production it is one walk per 15 s. The baseline's past-the-cap run overlapped with other work on the machine, so its 1,016 s is inflated by an unknown amount.

## Tested

- New `server/providers/vessels/ais-store.test.mjs` (7 tests): no full walk per message; readers never see an expired vessel between prunes; a stale first fix never seeds a track; past the cap the least recently updated vessels are evicted; an evicted or expired vessel takes its static entry with it; position-less static entries are capped. Five fail against the unfixed file; the other two are guards that the outcome is unchanged.
- `node scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`: all pass.

## Not tested

- **No live AISStream feed: there is no AISStream key available, so this is verified by unit tests with synthetic messages only.**
- The one-line call from the watchdog tick in `ais-live.js` has no unit test of its own.

title: perf(weather): apply the infrared cloud transfer from a lookup table, in place
body:
## What was slow and how to see it

Satellite clouds on the 3D Tiles map run a CPU pass over the whole cloud image: 4096 x 2048 for the regional image and for the detail window, back to back, on enable, on each camera move that shifts the detail window, and every two seconds during history playback. Each pass took about 150 ms.

## Cause

`infraredAlpha` copied the pixel buffer, ran a `** 2.2` power curve and a smoothstep for each of 8.4 million pixels, and `infraredImage.js` wrote the copy back.

## What changed

The alpha scale depends only on a pixel's brightest channel, so it is worked out once for each of the 256 byte values and applied in place (`applyInfraredAlpha`). `infraredAlpha` keeps its copying behaviour for its other callers.

## Before and after

`processInfraredImage` in Chrome, median of 6.

| Image | `main` | this branch |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4096 x 2048 | 150–153 ms | 67–93 ms |
| 2048 x 1024 | 40 ms | 18–19 ms |

The output is byte-identical: the same hash on `main` and on the branch for both sizes at strength 100 and 50.

## Tests

- A unit test compares the table against the old per-pixel formula for every byte value, 7 alphas and 7 strengths.
- A new test in `infraredImage.test.mjs` covers the in-place transfer.
- Unit suite, `format:check`, `check:boundaries` and `build` pass locally.

## Not tested, and what is left

- The real 3D Tiles path needs a Google key; only the function was measured.
- A 4096 x 2048 image is still a long task: what remains is `drawImage`, `getImageData` and `putImageData`. Doing the transfer in the shell's fragment shader would remove it; that is a follow-up.

title: Procedural fleet models for aircraft, vessels, transit and rail
body:
Every 3D model God's Eye View draws is now one of the project's own procedural fleet models: 121 of them (1.96 MB, meshopt-compressed), under the repository's MIT license. They replace the eight CC BY aircraft models, and their attribution goes with them.

**What changes**
- **Aircraft** (Flights, Military, Local ADS-B): the model is chosen by ICAO type designator, then aircraft class, then ADS-B emitter category, and drawn life size. A parked aircraft stands on its wheels.
- **Vessels, Transit and Rail** get models too, under the same 3D toggle and distances as aircraft:
  - **Vessels:** chosen by AIS ship type and sized to the reported length and beam. The AIS store now passes the A+B and C+D dimensions through. Each ship is clipped at its waterline.
  - **Transit and Rail:** vehicles stand on the road or rail, painted in their mode or category colour.
- **Loading and interaction:** the whole set loads once at layer start (about 0.2 s). A vehicle drawn as a model keeps its card, selection and detection-overlay entry, and follows NVG/FLIR.

**Files**
- `public/models/fleet/`: the models, `catalog.json` (bounds, length, beam, clearance, icon class) and `types.json` (type → model and length).
- `src/data/fleetModels.js`: the resolver.
- `src/data/fleetModelInstances.js`: the shared model handoff for vessels, transit and rail.

**Checks**
- Full test suite, format, boundaries and i18n pass.
- Headless QA screenshots at SFO gates, San Francisco Bay and Kraków trams.
- Median frame time with models stays within about 1 ms of icons only.

title: Draw a vessel of unknown length at its ship type's typical size
body:
Most live vessel feeds send no length. The fleet resolver then fell through every length rule to the range's last model, drawn as built, so a cruise ship or a container ship showed as the smallest model of its range (a 9 m boat).

- `public/models/fleet/types.json`: each passenger (140 m), cargo (300 m), tanker (250 m), fishing (40 m), pleasure craft (19 m), dredging (100 m), law-enforcement (40 m) and towing (24 m) range gets a `typical_len`.
- `resolveVessel` uses it in place of an unknown or out-of-range length, both to pick the rule and as the drawn length. A reported length still wins.
- Tests: unknown and out-of-range lengths in a range with a typical length, a range without one, and the set's passenger, cargo and tanker ranges.

`npm test`: 12,783 pass, 0 fail.

title: feat(transit): add 306 feeds and a coverage heat-map
body:
## What

Adds 306 feeds to the Transit layer, taking the registry from 52 to 358: 112 French networks from the national access point, 139 feeds from the catalogue's "terms to read" wave (Part 2), and 55 Japanese bus networks (Part 3).

## Part 1: French networks

Every one of the 112 is a keyless GTFS-Realtime VehiclePositions feed listed on the national access point, transport.data.gouv.fr, under a dataset record whose licence field is Licence Ouverte 2.0 (79 feeds) or ODbL (33 feeds).

Coverage runs from metropolitan networks (Nice, Dijon, Angers, Brest, Le Mans, Metz, Amiens, Avignon, Valenciennes, Perpignan, Troyes, Quimper, Vannes) to small-town networks, three regional coach networks (liO Occitanie, Aléop Pays de la Loire, Rémi Centre-Val de Loire) and the overseas departments (Réunion, Martinique, French Guiana).

## How the feeds were chosen

Source list: the 267 keyless, open-licence vehicle-position candidates from a catalogue export (Mobility Database + Transitland). Each URL was fetched and decoded with the repo's own `gtfsRealtime.js` on 2026-11-13, then filtered:

| Outcome | Feeds |
| --- | --- |
| Added | 112 |
| Already in the layer through the operator's own endpoint (Bordeaux, Montpellier, Rouen, Toulon, Le Havre, Tours, Rio) | 7 |
| Same feed listed twice in the catalogue, or the Atoumod aggregate that repeats Normandy networks added one by one |16 |
| No vehicle positions at probe time (51 Japanese feeds at midnight JST; the rest carry trip updates or alerts only, or were empty) | 97 |
| Republished by bus-tracker.fr rather than the operator | 8 |
| Plain HTTP only | 5 |
| Positions too old (three Fluo Grand Est feeds running 7 to 15 minutes behind, two others over an hour) | 5 |
| Unreachable, or not a GTFS-RT body | 3 |
| Outside France: licence needs reading feed by feed (follow-up) |12 |
| Catalogue record points at a different realtime URL, or licence claim not verifiable | 2 |

## No duplicates

- A candidate whose redirect ends at a URL already registered was dropped.
- No new row cites a dataset record an existing feed cites.
- A test asserts that no two registered feeds fetch the same upstream.

## What each row carries

- `src/data/transitFeedsFrance.js`: plain rows (id, name, operator, region, centre, radius, URL, licence field, record slug, vehicles seen). `transitFeeds.js` turns them into registry entries, so licence name, record link and terms note are built one way for all of them.
- Centre and radius come from the stops in the same record's GTFS, not from where the buses happened to be.
- Trams and boats take their mode from `route_type` in that GTFS: Dijon T1/T2, Brest A/B, Le Mans T1/T2, Nice L1 to L3, Angers A to C, Avignon T1, Valenciennes T1/T2, the Île d'Yeu boat and the Martinique Vedettes. An unlisted route stays a default, never a resolved "bus".
- Five feeds publish km/h (Dijon, Le Mans, Bourg-en-Bresse, Blois, Montluçon). Two samples 75 s apart showed reported speeds at 3.3 to 6.6 times the measured movement, so they are marked `speedUnit: 'km/h'`.
- `src/data/transitRouteNamesFrance.js`: line names for the 58 feeds that publish internal route keys (1,275 entries), copied from each record's `routes.txt`. An id missing from a table renders unchanged.
- `DATA_SOURCES.md`: one row per feed, and the feed count paragraph updated.

## Request budget

The proxy admits 40 upstream requests a minute across all feeds, and a browser polls each in-range feed four times a minute. The densest spot after this change has four feeds in range (16 a minute). A test fails if any viewpoint could exceed the budget.

## Verification

- All 112 feeds were run through the real `createTransitService` handler against the live upstreams: 112 of 112 answered 200 with vehicles, 3,806 vehicles in total.
- `npm test`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries` and `npm run build` pass locally.
- New tests in `src/data/transitFeedsFrance.test.mjs`: licence and record per row, no duplicate upstreams, request budget, modes, km/h set, route-name tables, DATA_SOURCES rows.

Browser check: live vehicles seen over Paris at 900 km on a local dev server; no wider visual pass. Thirty-seven feeds are served from `proxy.transport.data.gouv.fr`, which my local DNS resolver blocks, so those were verified with a pinned address rather than through a local dev server.

## Part 2: the "terms to read" wave

The same catalogue export lists 538 further keyless vehicle feeds. Each was probed live on 2026-11-13; 209 returned vehicles, and after removing duplicates, plain-HTTP and stale feeds, 154 were candidates. Their rows are in `src/data/transitFeedsCatalogue.js`.

| Outcome | Feeds |
| --- | --- |
| Added | 139 |
| Excluded: terms do not allow keyless public display | 7 |
| Held: terms page unreachable or empty | 8 |
| Excluded before that: BusOne republisher (14), data.gov.my rate limit (5), not an operator endpoint (4), same fleet already here (3), other (4) | 30 |

**Operator terms read (10).** Metro Bilbao (CC BY 4.0, source and update date credited), Metro St. Louis, Madison Metro Transit, MVgo (ODC-BY), Valley Regional Transit (CC BY 3.0), Greater Portland Metro, Greater Cleveland RTA, Fairfax Connector (its required "Visit fairfaxconnector.com" line is in the credit), Zagreb ZET (Croatian open licence) and Bustang (RTD's agreement). Each row quotes the grant and says when it was read.

**Catalogue feeds (129).** Keyless endpoints the catalogue lists as the operator's own, mostly on the operator's tracking vendor (Avail, Passio, Connexionz, TransLoc), mostly United States agencies: Sacramento, Spokane, Louisville, Fresno, Broward County, Riverside, Grand Rapids, Lexington and many smaller systems. Each row links its catalogue record and ships on the same basis as the existing Metro Transit, OVapi, Kraków and Vilnius entries.

**Excluded on their terms (7).** MTA New York City Bus (API key required; apps may not serve data straight from MTA servers), Detroit DDOT (use only with permission), Everett Transit (registration), Duluth Transit (written consent for displaying arrival information), Greater Dayton RTA (unpublished developer agreement), CTtransit and Pittsburgh Regional Transit (licences cover static GTFS only). A test asserts none of these hosts is registered.

**Held (8).** Sofia, Lviv, Saint-Avold, Des Moines DART, Springfield SMTD, Knoxville KAT, Pioneer Valley PVTA, Lafayette CityBus: the terms page returned 403/404 or an empty body.

Checks for this part: all 139 feeds ran through the real `createTransitService` handler against live upstreams, 139 of 139 answering with vehicles (4,730 in total). A two-sample speed check found no km/h feed among them. Route ids are shown as the feed sends them (no line-name tables for this batch), and centres and radii come from live vehicle positions, not stops. The densest viewpoint (Los Angeles) now has five feeds in range.

## Part 3: Japan

55 Japanese bus networks in `src/data/transitFeedsJapan.js`: Toyama (28, including Chitetsu Bus, Kaetsunō Bus and the municipal community buses), Mie (10, the Mie Kōtsū offices plus Ise and Komono), Kumamoto (4), Kōchi (4), Aichi (3), and one each in Chiba, Gunma, Nagano, Miyagi, Ibaraki, Okinawa and Aomori. The Mobility Database records 28 under CC0 1.0 and 27 under CC BY 4.0; each row links that record and credits the operator in Japanese.

**Verified live: 34 of 55.** The rows were added at about 01:40 Japan time, when buses are not running, and probed again at 08:00 Japan time on Saturday 2026-11-14. All 55 answer through the real `createTransitService` handler with a well-formed message.

- 33 carried vehicle positions in the morning probe (435 vehicles in total; Sankō Bus 132, Mie Kōtsū Chūsei 31, Kumamoto Toshi Bus 31, Chitetsu Bus 26). The 19 seen with five or more vehicles are now centred on them with a radius that covers the farthest one; the 14 seen with fewer keep the catalogue centre, with the radius widened where a vehicle fell outside it. Aomori was seen around midnight and is unchanged.
- 21 were empty both times and keep `liveSeen: false`: 16 Toyama community and municipal buses, plus Komono, Nagano city, Owariasahi, Takeya Kōtsū and Yanbaru Express. One Saturday-morning sample does not show a feed is dead (several of these are weekday services), so they stay registered but get no heat-map spot. They should be probed on a weekday and removed if still empty.

Each row's note says which case it is.

Toyama is still the densest viewpoint: ten feeds in range, the proxy's full 40 upstream requests a minute.

The catalogue's 20 other Japanese entries are trip-update feeds, not vehicle positions, and are not added.

## Part 4: coverage heat-map

Above the 3,000 km altitude gate the layer polls nothing and draws no vehicles, so from orbit there was no way to see where Transit has anything to show. With 358 feeds that matters more.

- `src/layers/transit/coverage.js` draws one soft Gaussian disc per feed, in two sets that cross-fade by camera height (`COVERAGE_OPACITY_STOPS`):
  - **far**: wide spots (150 to 230 km radius) so coverage reads from orbit; full above the gate.
  - **near**: patches the size of each feed's own polling radius (clamped 22 to 75 km), drawn under the vehicles between about 250 km and 3,000 km, so neighbouring covered cities stay visible while browsing a region. Off below 60 km.
- `src/data/transitCoverage.js` (pure) sets each spot's heat from how many other feeds lie within 150 km, on a log scale normalized so a lone network always looks the same. Spots in a crowd are thinned so a cluster sums to a smooth field instead of clipping.
- Only feeds whose live positions have been seen get a spot: the 21 Japanese rows not yet seen with vehicles carry `liveSeen: false` and stay out until confirmed.
- It is built once from the registry on first need. No feed is polled for it.

Two approaches were tried and dropped, which is why it is built the way it is:
- A draped raster (as Active Fires uses) does not render on the photoreal tiles, the default map.
- Translucent billboards go through Cesium's order-independent transparency, whose weights clamp at orbital distances and turned each faint spot into a dark disc with a rim.

So the discs are drawn in the opaque pass with ordinary alpha blending, with no depth test (the coarse photoreal mesh speckled them) and back-face culling to hide spots over the horizon.

Checked in the browser on a local dev server, photoreal map: smooth at 15,000 km (no spots leaking from the far side), smooth service-area patches at 1,300 km over France with live vehicles on top. Not checked: tilted views near the horizon, other visual presets, the Esri map after the rework, and performance on low-end GPUs (12 draw batches, about 675 discs).

## Follow-ups

- Japan: probe the 21 still-empty feeds on a weekday; remove any that stay empty (see Part 3).
- The 8 held feeds above, once their terms can be read.
- Outside France from the open-licence wave (Phoenix, Santa Cruz, Córdoba, San Sebastián, Ełk, Kuala Lumpur, Colombo): live, licence still to be read on the operator's page.

title: perf(wind): decode forecast GRIB in a worker and reuse the cycle's wind
body:
## What was slow

Every `/api/wind` refresh froze the whole server for 43 to 164 ms, and for 316 to 974 ms when all six model/overlay keys refreshed together. While it was frozen, no other API route answered. Choosing a color field (temperature or pressure) also downloaded and decoded the wind again, although only the color field was new.

The finding estimated 200 to 600 ms per refresh from reading the code. Measured, a single warm refresh is smaller than that; the first refresh in a process (230 to 381 ms) and the six-key burst are in or above that range.

## Cause

The server runs as Vite middleware on one thread. A refresh fetched two or three 0.25° GRIB2 messages and then, on that thread and synchronously: decoded each with ecCodes WASM (about 37 ms per message), checked all ~1.04 M values of each (about 6 ms per field) and resampled to 1° (about 20 ms for three fields, most of it the same check again). Nothing kept the decoded wind between keys of the same model.

## What changed

- Decode, validation and resampling run on one `node:worker_threads` worker (`server/providers/wind/decoder.js`, entry `decode-worker.js`). It hands back only the 1° samples (65,160 doubles per field, transferred, not copied). The server thread is left with narrowing those to Float32 and the existing final checks.
- Each `windProxy()` owns a worker. It starts on the first wind request and is referenced only while a job is pending. When the dev or preview server that mounts the proxy closes, its HTTP server’s `close` event stops the worker. In middleware mode, Vite’s `closeBundle` hook stops it. A decode error rejects that one job. A crash, an exit, or a job that takes longer than 30 s rejects every pending job and retires the worker. The next decode starts a new one.
- Each `windProxy()` keeps the sampled U and V of the last forecast file per model. A request for the same file and byte ranges fetches the inventory and the scalar only. Retained: 2 × 65,160 × 8 B = 1.04 MB per model, 2.1 MB for both. It is written only after the pair has passed every wind check, and replaced when the forecast step changes.
- `decodeImpl`, `fetchImpl` and `models` injection, single-flight per key, abort on timeout and on last-waiter disconnect, and the 8 MB budget are unchanged. Injected decoders also receive `{ targetDx, signal }` and may ignore both. Models also receive `scalarSignal` for the optional field.

## Before / after

Same script, unchanged between runs (sha256 checked), driving the real `windProxy()` handler for all six keys with real GFS and IFS messages cached on disk, so both sides decode the same bytes. 3 runs × 5 repetitions each, Node 24.14.0. Another benchmark was running on the machine, hence the ranges. "Block" is the largest event-loop delay during the refresh (`monitorEventLoopDelay`, 1 ms resolution); a 5 ms heartbeat gave the same figures before, and 5.8 to 12.6 ms after (its own period is 5 ms).

| Scenario | main: block, median (range) | this PR: block, median (range) |
|---|---|---|
| One refresh, per key, warm (6 keys) | 68 ms (43–164) | 3 ms (1.8–10.6) |
| First refresh in the process (starts ecCodes) | 248 ms (230–381) | 11.6 ms (11.4–11.6) |
| All six keys at once | 407 ms (316–974) | 4 ms (3.4–8.4) |

| Overlay chosen after wind is loaded | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| GRIB ranges fetched and decoded | 3 | 1 |
| Time to answer, median (range) | 120–138 ms (112–241) | 42–43 ms (40–78) |

Time to answer a refresh that has to load everything is unchanged or slightly lower (79–123 ms against 91–136 ms): the work moved, it did not shrink. The six-key burst still takes about 0.6 s end to end, because one worker decodes the messages one after another.

In a running server (this PR only, live upstream, cold): pinging a trivial route every 5 ms while all six keys refreshed, the slowest ping was 8.7 ms under `npm run dev` and 31 ms under `npm run preview`, and the process went from 13 to 14 threads.

## Output is byte-identical

For the same upstream bytes the manifest (minus `fetchedAt`) and the grid `.bin` are identical to main. The script saved both for every case on each side and `diff -r` over the two folders reports no difference: 34 manifests and 28 grid bodies. Cases, for each of the six keys where they apply: success; scalar bytes corrupt, scalar refused with 404, scalar corrupt after the wind-only key was already served, scalar replaced by other bytes (all four give wind-only with `scalarError`); U corrupt with nothing cached (`unavailable`); a good refresh followed by an upstream outage after the TTL (`stale`).

## Behaviour changes and caveats

- Within one forecast file the wind is fetched once. A later request for that file does not ask upstream for U and V again, so it succeeds for wind even if those two ranges would now fail. The inventory is still fetched every time. IFS steps are 3-hourly, so its hourly refreshes now reuse the wind for up to three hours; GFS steps are hourly.
- Two keys of one model refreshing at the same moment still each fetch the wind, as before. Only a finished load is reused.
- An unusable message is now rejected as soon as it is decoded, not after all three have loaded. The outcomes are the same (bad wind fails the refresh, a bad scalar leaves wind-only).
- The optional scalar has 12 s to download. Its decode has the worker’s 30 s job deadline, and the refresh stops waiting for it 2 s before the 40 s refresh deadline. If the decode hangs, the proxy serves ready wind with `scalarError`.
- A cancelled or timed-out refresh stops waiting at once. A decode already posted to the worker still runs there and its result is discarded. A decode that hangs is stopped at the worker's 30 s job deadline, which retires the worker and rejects the jobs queued behind it.
- ecCodes runs in the worker’s memory. The worker stays up between requests until its server closes.

## Tested

- `src/data/windDecoder.test.mjs` has 14 offline tests, including real ecCodes over small synthetic GRIB2 messages. They cover a blocking decode leaving the server responsive, a caller’s Buffer view reaching the worker intact, and byte-identical results for all three overlays and for partial and failed refreshes. They check U/V reuse across overlay changes and hourly IFS refreshes, fetching wind again at a new forecast step, and excluding invalid wind from the cache. They exercise decode errors, crashes, exits, job deadlines, recovery after a crash, and retirement of a cancelled hung decode at its own deadline. Closing one decoder leaves another working. Closing the HTTP server or its Vite bundle stops the proxy’s worker, and an idle worker lets the process exit.
- `src/data/windGfs.test.mjs` checks that the scalar download deadline allows an ongoing decode to finish. Two `src/data/windProxy.test.mjs` tests cover a hung scalar decode after a 1 s or 11 s download. Both serve wind with `scalarError` within the refresh deadline. All 47 wind tests passed after these fixes.
- `npm test` before the main merge: 12,800 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped. After merging main (d998dee91): 16,213 passed, 4 skipped, 1 failed. The failure is `isMacPlatform reads the browser’s platform` in `src/render/cesium/commandDrag.test.mjs`, which fails on main too. `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries` pass.
- `npm run dev` and `npm run preview`, keyless, on port 4195: `/api/wind` returned 200 for all six keys and each `/api/wind/grid/….bin` returned 200 with 521,280 bytes (wind) or 781,920 bytes (wind + scalar).

## Not tested

- **Windows.** The worker is located with `new URL('./decode-worker.js', import.meta.url)`, the same pattern other server modules use for sibling files, and Vite's config bundler keeps each file's own `import.meta.url`. The Windows CI job does not start a server or run the wind tests, so a path with a drive letter or spaces is unverified.
- **Docker and Pinokio.** Both start a Vite server from a full checkout, so the worker file is on disk beside its imports; neither was run.
- No "before" figure from a running server; the before/after comparison is the script's.

title: perf(styles): NVG and FLIR bloom in two passes and redraw at 15 Hz when idle
body:
## What was slow

With the NVG or FLIR style on, every pixel of every frame read the scene texture 122 times (NVG) or 108 times (FLIR), and the scene was redrawn 60 times a second even when nothing else moved.

## Cause

- `src/styles/surveillance.js` summed an 11x11 bloom (121 reads) and `src/styles/thermal.js` a 9x9 bloom (81 reads) in one pass.
- Any style with a `time` uniform held continuous rendering while visible (`src/ui/visualEffects.js`).

## Change

- **Two-pass bloom.** Both bloom weights are a row weight times a column weight, and Cesium reads a stage's input with nearest sampling, so every sample is a whole texel from the first. A new `bloomRows` pass sums each row once per texel and the main shader sums the columns. Reads for each pixel: NVG 122 → 23, FLIR 108 → 45. The row sum is packed into two 8-bit channels, so the render target is the default one.
- **Composite stage.** A style that declares `passes` is built as a `PostProcessStageComposite` that answers to the style's name, `enabled` and `uniforms` as the single stage did, so the callers in `visualSettings.js` and `cockpitVisionPolicy.js` are unchanged.
- **15 Hz clock.** A style that declares `timeHz` (NVG and FLIR, at 15) steps its clock at that rate and asks for one frame a step. Crossfades and the CRT style are still drawn every frame.

Not changed: FLIR's 5x5 soft blur (25 reads). Splitting it needs another full-resolution pass, which costs about what it would save on the GPU measured here. A half-resolution bloom was not used because it changes the picture.

## Before / after

Apple M3 Max, headless Chrome (ANGLE Metal), keyless globe over Manhattan, 4x MSAA. GPU ms per frame is the median from `EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2` around `scene.render()`; main's shaders and the branch's stages were timed in the same page over the same scene.

| Canvas | No style | Noir (one trivial pass) | NVG main → branch | FLIR main → branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1440x900 | 2.07 | 3.84 | 4.25 → 3.88 | 4.19 → 3.96 |
| 2560x1440 | 5.71 | 11.27 | 12.19 → 11.02 | 12.07 → 11.49 |
| 5120x2880 (resolution scale 2) | 26.5 | 51.0 | 56.3 → 51.4 | 55.0 → 56.6 (noisy; best run 51.9 → 48.8) |

| Idle, style on | main | branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NVG renders per second | 60 | 15 |
| FLIR renders per second | 60 | 15 |
| CRT renders per second | 60 | 60 |

The bloom loops were a small part of the frame on this GPU: NVG now costs the same as a one-line style. Most of the saving is the idle render rate. Device pixel ratio 2 did not change the canvas size (the app keeps Cesium's browser-recommended resolution), so the 5120x2880 row was forced with `viewer.resolutionScale = 2`.

## Look

Main's shader and the branch's stage were rendered over the same frozen scene with the same `time`, at 1440x900, and compared pixel by pixel. Tolerance: 2/255 on any channel for at least 99.6% of pixels. Re-rendering either side gave a difference of 0.

| Scene, default parameters | Largest difference | Pixels differing at all | Pixels over 2/255 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| City, NVG 50 | 2 | 0.004% | 0% |
| City, NVG 100 | 8 | 3.0% | 0.15% |
| City, FLIR 50 | 5 | 1.2% | 0.007% |
| City, FLIR 100 | 6 | 0.17% | 0.013% |
| Ocean, NVG 50 | 1 | 0.002% | 0% |
| Ocean, NVG 100 | 1 | 0.15% | 0% |
| Ocean, FLIR 50 | 0 | 0% | 0% |
| Ocean, FLIR 100 | 1 | 0.0005% | 0% |

With parameters pushed to their ends (bloom 1, gain 1, pixelation 1 and 6, black-hot, ironbow) the worst case was a largest difference of 20/255, with at most 0.34% of pixels over 2/255 and 0.05% over 8/255. The differences sit where pixelation snaps a sample exactly onto a texel edge: main rounds each of its 121 samples separately there, the branch rounds once per column.

What does change is motion: the grain and sparkle noise now change 15 times a second instead of 60, and FLIR's frame counter advances two at a time. `timeHz` on the two style modules is the only switch for this.

## Tested

- `node scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`.
- New tests in `src/styles/bloomPasses.test.mjs` and `src/ui/visualEffects.test.mjs`: reads per pixel, pass uniforms, the composite's uniforms reaching each pass after Cesium replaces the stage's uniforms object, the 15 Hz clock, and crossfades still drawn every frame. Seven of them fail without the change.
- Both styles switched on and off through the style manager in the running app, with sharpen on, without shader or console errors.

## Not tested

- Any other GPU or OS; a weaker GPU should gain more from the bloom change than the M3 Max did.
- A real high-density display, Google photoreal tiles, keyed feeds.
- The 15 Hz noise judged by eye in motion.
- Frame time under a heavy layer; the numbers above are GPU timer queries on the plain globe.

title: perf(detection): reuse the last sweep's brackets when nothing it was built from has changed
body:
## What was slow

With detection labels on at whole-globe view (about 11,100 aircraft in the sweep), every detection paint projected, faded and bracketed every contact. On a still camera most of those paints rebuilt exactly the paths of the paint before: Live Flights moves the fleet every 80 ms, so at 60 fps about seven paints in ten had nothing new to draw.

## Cause

`_drawOverlay` in `src/data/detection.js` ran its per-object sweep on every paint with no check for whether the view or the contacts had changed. On paints that also solve labels, the sweep additionally hashed every identity from a new string, looked up each layer's identity sets once per object, and called `Cesium.Cartesian3.distance` (two argument checks) per aircraft.

## What changed

- **Reuse of the last sweep** (new `src/data/detectionPaintCache.js`). Each paint still asks every layer for its contacts, then compares them with what the last sweep was built from: the same objects in the same order, the same position coordinates, and the same value in every field the sweep reads, under the same view (profile, style, canvas size, keyhole, camera position, view-projection matrix, UI rectangles). On a match the kept bracket paths, counts and callout candidates are used again; only the strokes and callouts are repainted.
- **Always swept, never kept:** solve paints, any paint while the Cyber sonar sweep or a Global Context echo is live, and any sweep that reached a depth-tested contact.
- **Per-object savings in the sweep** (these apply on every paint): camera distance computed inline, the identity hash worked out once per identity, each layer's identity sets looked up once per run of objects.
- **Diagnostics:** `getDetectionDiagnostics().paintReuseCount` and `data-paint-reuse-count`. `placementBuildCount` is 0 on a reused paint, because none is built.
- `docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` describes the reuse and what must be added to it when the sweep reads something new.

**Deviation from the plan in #1697:** the plan was a revision counter bumped by each layer. This compares the contacts themselves instead, so no layer has to announce a change and none can leave a stale picture by forgetting to. It costs one pass over the contacts per paint (about 0.2 ms for 11,000 in the Node benchmark below). No layer file is touched.

## Before / after

Whole globe, Live Flights, detection DENSE at 100%, still camera, 1440x900, 15 s at 1x then 15 s at 4x CPU throttle, same script for every run. "Solve paint" is the app's own `paintMs` timer, median of 150 samples.

Without #1708 (origin/main against this branch):

| | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| 1x average frame work | 17.7 ms | 14.3 ms |
| 1x paints that reused a sweep | 0 of 853 | 590 of 794 |
| 1x solve paint | 9.3 ms | 7.7 ms |
| 4x average frame work | 197.5 ms | 197.1 ms |
| 4x frames in 15 s | 162 | 162 |
| 4x paints that reused a sweep | 0 | 0 |
| 4x solve paint | 42.4 ms | 36.9 ms |

With #1708 applied to both sides:

| | main + #1708 | branch + #1708 |
|---|---|---|
| 1x average frame work | 13.6 ms | 9.1 ms |
| 1x paints that reused a sweep | 0 of 987 | 677 of 942 |
| 1x solve paint | 10.0 ms | 8.1 ms |
| 4x average frame work | 104.8 ms | 81.4 ms |
| 4x frames in 15 s | 266 | 290 |
| 4x paints that reused a sweep | 0 | 0 |
| 4x solve paint | 43.6 ms | 36.7 ms |

How to read these:

- **The gain is at 1x**, where a still camera reuses about 70% of paints and frame work drops 19% (33% with #1708). Frame rate at 1x was already at or near 60 fps on this machine, so this is headroom, not frames.
- **At 4x throttle no paint is ever reused.** Frames there take longer than the 80 ms fleet step, so every paint sees moved aircraft. The only gain at 4x is the per-object savings: the paint is 13 to 16% cheaper, which is about 3 ms of a 100 to 200 ms frame. Without #1708 the 4x frame did not move at all; the fleet tick dominates it.
- **The 4x frame figure with #1708 (104.8 to 81.4 ms) overstates the change.** The paint saving explains only a few milliseconds of it; the machine was under heavy load from other work during these runs and that pair differs by more than the change can account for.

Node benchmark (11,000 contacts through the real paint path with a mock canvas, minimum of 60 to 120 paints):

| | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| Paint, nothing moved | 2.85 ms | 0.23 ms |
| Paint, fleet moved, no solve | 2.85 ms | 2.78 ms |
| Solve paint, fleet moved | 4.8 ms | 4.0 ms |

## Tested

- `src/data/detectionHost.test.mjs`, five new tests. They fail on main.
  - 41 frames (a contact moves, one is relabelled, one changes tier, the camera turns) painted with reusable contacts and again with equal copies that cannot be reused: every canvas call matches, frame for frame, and at least 28 of 40 paints reused a sweep.
  - A reused paint builds no path, adds no point, and strokes the kept brackets.
  - Fifteen kinds of change (contact moved, replaced, renamed, re-tiered, added, removed, reordered, tracked; camera turned or moved; style; profile) are each swept on the very next paint.
  - Depth-tested contacts, the sonar sweep and echoes are never reused.
  - Turning detection off drops the kept sweep.
- `src/data/detectionPaintCache.test.mjs`, 13 tests of the comparison itself.
- One-off check, not in the suite: the canvas calls of that 41-frame script on this branch equal those of unchanged main, call for call (10,698 calls).
- `node scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs` (12,801 pass, 0 fail), `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`: all pass locally.

## Not tested

- A moving camera in the browser by eye. The tests cover it (a changed matrix is always swept), but I did not compare screenshots.
- Layers other than Live Flights in the browser (vessels need a key; satellites move every frame and are never reused).
- The Cyber theme sonar and Global Context echoes in the browser; unit tests only.
- Quiet-machine numbers. All browser runs were taken with load averages between 6 and 18.

title: feat(aircraft): selection hologram and type card for the selected aircraft
body:
## Why

When you select an aircraft, the globe should tell you what it is at a glance, the way a selected vessel already shows its photo and MMSI. This adds the same for aircraft: the selected aircraft's model gets a holographic highlight, and an info card shows the aircraft **type's** licensed photo and specs alongside live telemetry.

## What

- **Bundled ICAO type library** (`src/data/aircraftTypes/`): 197 ICAO type designators mapped to name, manufacturer, class, specs and a free-licensed photo. About 96% coverage of the common type-frequency snapshot. Produced by a reproducible generator (`scripts/build-aircraft-catalog.mjs`) from ICAO Doc 8643 plus Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons; photos are re-encoded to WebP at most 640px and bundled so it works offline.
- **Selected-aircraft hologram** (`src/data/trackedHologram.js`): a faction-colored holographic shader (cyan for civil, amber for military) baked onto the tracked model at creation, with an alpha ramp so it stays readable as the model shrinks. Mirrored in the flights and military layers.
- **Type card** (Vue panel): the selected aircraft's type photo, specs and live telemetry in the faction accent, shown while an aircraft is tracked.
- **i18n** for the new strings across the shipped locales.
- **Provenance**: `docs/AIRCRAFT-TYPE-LIBRARY.md`, `docs/AIRCRAFT-PHOTO-CREDITS.md`, a `DATA_SOURCES.md` row, and a Data-popover credit entry.

## Licensing

Every bundled photo is CC0, public domain, CC BY or CC BY-SA, each with author, licence and Commons file page recorded in `docs/AIRCRAFT-PHOTO-CREDITS.md` and in the catalog. Share-alike applies per photo.

## Verification

- `npm run build`, `npm test` (full suite green) and `npm run test:track` (111/111) pass.
- `npm run i18n`, `npm run format:check` and `npm run check:boundaries` pass.
- The generator is idempotent: a re-run with a warm cache produces a byte-identical catalog.

## Notes for review

- The diff is large because of the 197 bundled WebP photos and the generated `catalog.json`; the catalog is machine-generated by the committed builder, so it is best reviewed by sampling.
- Non-English translations for the new strings are best-effort; native review is welcome.
- Photos represent the type, not the specific tracked airframe, as the card states.

title: perf(weather): apply the infrared cloud key in the shell's shader
body:
Stacked on #1713.

## Cause

On the 3D Tiles host, every Satellite clouds image the shell shows (4096×2048 for the regional product and for each detail window, 2048×1024 for the global mosaic) was drawn to a canvas, read back with `getImageData`, given its transparency curve on the page and written back with `putImageData`. #1713 halved that pass with a lookup table; the read-back and write-back of 33 MB remained, and so did a long task per image.

## Change

- The shell's material samples the image as it was decoded and applies the same curve in its fragment shader: brightest channel, 2.2 power, smoothstep 0.40–0.70, mixed by a new `infrared` uniform (0–1). The thresholds come from the constants `infraredAlpha.js` already exports.
- `acquireWeatherImage` takes `transfer: false`; the shell passes it, so an infrared frame is drawn to its canvas and never read back. Globe hosts are unchanged and keep the per-pixel transfer for draped imagery.
- The shell's image cache no longer keys on the infrared mode. Changing the filter strength sets the uniform on the image already shown: no fetch, no decode, no second canvas per mode.

## Before / after

Keyless headless Chrome (Metal), same scripts on #1713's head (`ad369eb0d`) and this branch (`e3f28a391`). There is no Google key here, so the shell was exercised by creating the real `createWeatherShell` on the dev page with its host forced to `tileset`, drawing over the keyless globe, with real NOAA frames pinned to one observation time for both runs.

| | #1713 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| Main-thread work per 4096×2048 image after decode (median of 8, two runs) | 60 / 81 ms | 0.1 / 0.3 ms |
| Changing filter strength on a shown regional frame | 51–82 ms, new 33 MB canvas per mode | 1–2 ms, same canvas |
| Shell cache after showing 3 strengths of one regional frame with detail | 128 MB | 64 MB |

Rendered result against the CPU path, WebGL canvas only (1280×800), 12 shots (2 products × 3 strengths × up to 3 camera heights, one with a detail window):

| Strength | Mean channel difference (0–255) | Pixels differing by more than 8 | Largest |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full (0 %) | 0.000 | 0 | 0 |
| Clouds only (100 %) | 0.000–0.10 (close/mid views) | at most 0.06 % | 42, on cloud edges |
| 50 % | 0.95–1.07 | at most 0.03 % | 36, on cloud edges |

The differences sit on cloud edges: the shader applies the curve after the texture is filtered, the CPU path before, and the CPU path also loses colour precision when the canvas stores reduced alpha. Two runs of the CPU path against each other are pixel-identical in the close and mid views; the wide view has a 0.1 % floor from the starfield in both comparisons.

## Tested

- `node scripts/run-unit-tests.mjs` (12,791 tests, 0 failures), `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:boundaries`, `npm run build`.
- New and reworked tests fail without the source change (5 failures): frames reach the material unread with the uniform set per product; a mode change keeps the same image with no fetch; `transfer: false` never calls `getImageData`/`putImageData`; the built Cesium material declares the uniform and the curve.

## Not tested

- Real photorealistic 3D Tiles (no Google key). The shell, its material and its images are the real ones; only the surface underneath it was the globe.
- Browsers other than Chrome.

title: perf(cables): draw with batched primitives instead of entities
body:
Stacked on #1707.

## Cause

Submarine Cables loaded two `GeoJsonDataSource`s and a `CustomDataSource`: 6,459 entities (1,913 cable lines, 1,917 landing markers, 2,629 reference stems and tips).

- Every enable rebuilt all of them: three or four long tasks and about 1 GB of heap that stayed until the next collection.
- Every disable removed them in one 130–150 ms task.
- Each horizon sweep that brought a landing marker back into view made Cesium create its billboard again and read the terrain height under it again, so zooming kept re-reading heights.
- Stem and show changes went through the entity visualizers.

## Change

The layer now makes the primitives Cesium built from those entities itself, and creates no entity or data source:

- **Lines:** one `GroundPolylinePrimitive`, one instance per line with its own colour and show flag, tessellated in a worker. A map-stack change sets its classification in place.
- **Landing markers:** one `BillboardCollection`. A marker starts hidden and unclamped; the sweep clamps and shows the visible ones 48 per frame (the #1707 budget). A marker is clamped once: Cesium then follows the terrain within its own per-frame time budget, and hiding or showing the marker reads nothing.
- **Reference tips:** one `PointPrimitiveCollection`.
- **Reference stems:** one static polyline `Primitive` of the stems in view. A sweep that moved a tip or changed which references are in view builds a replacement in a worker; it replaces the shown stems once ready. Same cadence as before (never mid-drag, once on `moveEnd`).
- **Disable** hides the lines, markers and tips and keeps them; **enable** shows them again without fetching or building. Only the stems are redrawn, for the new view.
- The load has one `await` (the fetch); everything is built in the turn after it, so the four post-fetch race windows the old load guarded no longer exist.

Two details that keep the look identical:

- Lines carry the distance-display attribute the entity display gave them. With a float attribute present Cesium keeps the 2.5 px width; without one the width is stored as a byte and the lines draw 2 px wide.
- Billboards keep their depth test, exactly as the entity billboards had it, so markers stay hidden behind the globe during a drag. Horizon culling stays on the sweep cadence as today; no per-frame cull was needed because the depth test was not turned off.

## Before / after

Keyless headless Chrome (Metal), same script on main (`188f0ccd9`), #1707 (`b6c241a68`) and this branch (`1923547d4`); two runs each for #1707 and this branch, one for main. Layer switched on after the globe had loaded.

| | main | #1707 | this branch |
|---|---|---|---|

title: Collapse the CCTV panel when the layer is switched off
body:
## What this changes

Switching the CCTV layer off now collapses the CCTV panel. The panel opened itself when a camera became active, but nothing closed it when the layer went off: it stayed expanded with an empty frame, a `SOURCE · UNKNOWN` badge and a meta line that still described the last camera. The open state was also persisted and written into the share link (`ui=…v.c.0` with `l=` empty), so it came back after a reload.

- `_renderCctvState` collapses the panel on the on → off change only, so a panel opened by hand while the layer is off stays open.
- A context-mode layer clear keeps the panel as it is, with the same guard Radio uses (`preservePanelStateDuringClear`).
- With the layer off, the meta line reads `N cameras loaded · enable CCTV to activate` instead of the last active camera. The layer keeps its active camera while off, so switching back on reopens the panel on it.

## How I verified it

- [x] `npm run build`
- [x] `npm test`
- [ ] `npm run test:track` (dev server running) — not run
- [ ] Feature gate for the area I touched: not run

In the dev server at London with the Trafalgar Square camera active: CCTV ON → OFF collapsed the panel, the meta line read `7350 cameras loaded · enable CCTV to activate`, and the share link went back to `v.c.1`. Before the change the same steps on production left the panel open. I exercised the panel's own switch in the browser; the data-manager path (Data Layers row) is covered by a unit test only.

Six new cases in `src/ui/cctvPanel.test.mjs`: collapse on switch-off, no collapse for a layer that was never on, collapse when the data manager turns the layer off, no collapse during a context-mode clear, no second collapse of a collapsed panel, and the meta line of a disabled layer.

title: Stories: GEV scenes as stories on the live globe
body:
# Stories: GEV scenes as stories on the live globe

## What this changes

Stories adds an Explore feed and a player for GEV scenes on the live Cesium globe. Explore shows built-in scenes, saved stories and local drafts. The player adds a timeline, chapters, key moments and source context. **Open in GEV** selects the current shot in Authoring, where users can add a thumbnail or tags, save the scene to Stories, or delete it.

Back restores the globe view after playback. Explore links reopen with the selected story, and player links open paused at the shared time. Users can open Stories from the button, by saying “Open Stories,” or through typed AI. Entering Stories turns off active voice and shows a notice.

## Known playback limitations

- Pressing Play after opening a link within the final quarter-second can restart the story from the beginning. The link itself opens paused at the correct time.
- Copying a link immediately after scrubbing can capture the previous position while the scene is still seeking. After the seek settles, Share copies the new position.

## How I verified it

- [x] `npm run build`
- [ ] Full `npm test`. The non-voice sweep passed 11,462 unit and allocation checks with four built-in skips before the final timestamp fix. All 67 affected Stories and share-link tests passed after that fix.
- [x] `npm run test:track` with bundled imagery. 111 checks passed before the final timestamp fix.
- [x] Scene authoring, sharing, and timing browser checks. Verified Back, Explore selection links, paused player links, and draft deletion in Chrome. After the timestamp fix, verified a link at 28.8 seconds in a 29-second story opens paused at 28.8 seconds.
- Manual verification confirmed that entering Stories turns off voice. Automated live voice and macOS TTS checks were skipped in the final pass.

## Docs

`docs/CURRENT-STATE.md` describes Stories and the Authoring changes. The changelog fragment will use the public PR number.
